## Large authenticated state (Poseidon MPF/JMT)

Source: https://zeroj.dev/guides/credentials/authenticated-state/

> Keep millions of entries off-chain, publish one Poseidon root, and prove single-key reads and updates with small Groth16 circuits. Experimental.

Many private applications revolve around a big table: a registry of members, credential status
flags, account balances, or the state of a rollup-like app. You can't put millions of entries on
Cardano, and you can't put them in a circuit. You can, however, keep them in an authenticated tree
off-chain, publish only the tree's **root**, and prove statements about one entry at a time.

ZeroJ's `zeroj-mpf-poseidon` and `zeroj-jmt-poseidon` modules do exactly that. They adapt Cardano
Client Lib's Merkle Patricia Forestry (MPF) and Jellyfish Merkle Tree (JMT) to a Poseidon hash
over BLS12-381, so the same tree the service stores can be opened inside a Groth16 circuit.

> **Caution: Experimental**
>
> Both modules are **experimental**: opt-in, outside the stable BOM, and not externally reviewed.
> The 5-million-entry runs described below used deliberately insecure local setups, and the
> production gates listed at the end are still open. Don't protect value with them.

### How it works

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

```text
OFF-CHAIN (your service)
  RocksDB MPF/JMT, millions of entries
    │  read one native proof path for key K
    ▼
  strict verification + normalization  ──►  bounded, canonical witness
    │
    ▼
  operation-specific circuit  ──►  Groth16 prover  ──►  192-byte proof
                                                           │
ON-CHAIN (Cardano)                                         ▼
  state UTxO datum: old root  ──►  validator: verify proof over (old root, new root)
                                   and check the continuing state UTxO carries new root
```

The circuit never sees the database. It sees one path, padded to a fixed maximum length, and the
root(s) as public inputs. Proving cost depends on that path bound, not on how many entries the
tree holds.

### Operation-specific circuits

Each operation has its own narrow circuit, its own R1CS hash and its own keys. That keeps the
statement explicit and the constraint count small. There is no generic "do anything" circuit whose
behaviour a prover could steer.

| Statement | MPF | JMT | Public inputs |
|---|:---:|:---:|---|
| Inclusion: key/value is in the tree | ✓ | ✓ | `root` |
| Non-inclusion: the path ends empty | ✓ | ✓ | `root` |
| Non-inclusion: a different key occupies the path | ✓ | ✓ | `root` |
| Value update | ✓ | ✓ | `oldRoot`, `newRoot` |
| Insert at an empty spot | ✓ | ✓ | `oldRoot`, `newRoot` |
| Insert beside a different leaf | ✓ | ✓ | `oldRoot`, `newRoot` |
| Tombstone update | — | ✓ | `oldRoot`, `newRoot`, tombstone hash |
| Physical delete, multiproofs, batch updates | deferred | deferred | — |

The circuits are exposed as `PoseidonMpfCircuitTemplates` / `PoseidonJmtCircuitTemplates` factory
methods (`inclusion(maxSteps)`, `valueUpdate(maxSteps)`, …) and as `ZkMpf*` / `ZkJmt*` gadgets.

### MPF or JMT?

| | Poseidon MPF | Poseidon JMT |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | Radix-16 Patricia trie with compressed paths | Versioned Jellyfish Merkle Tree |
| Best for | Membership/read-heavy state, compact native proofs, existing MPF data | Update-heavy state that needs version history, rollback and pruning |
| Measured complete profile at 5M entries | S9 (≤ 9 branch steps) | S12 (≤ 12 levels) |
| Circuit size at that profile | 56,635 constraints | 14,057 constraints |
| Median Groth16 prove | 4.173 s | 2.901 s |
| Native (private) proof size | 805–939 B sampled | 2,744–3,161 B sampled |
| Deletion | No physical delete yet | Tombstones only; a tombstone is **not** proof of absence |

Both produce the same 192-byte compressed Groth16 proof and a 432-byte compressed VK for one public
input, so on-chain cost is the same: ZeroJ measured **2,052,276,435 CPU steps and 138,837 memory
units** in the JuLC VM (JuLC 0.1.0-pre18). The JMT's larger native proof is private prover input and never reaches
the chain.

The two root profiles (`zeroj-poseidon-mpf-v1`, `zeroj-poseidon-jmt-v1`) are incompatible with
each other and with classic Blake2b MPF/JMT roots, including Aiken MPF roots.

### Pick a path bound

A circuit covers paths up to a fixed length ("S9" = 9 steps). Choosing it is a data question:

- **Measure the depth** of your real tree. In the 5M MPF run, S8 covered all but 218 entries; S9
  covered all of them. In the 5M JMT run, S8 covered 99.74 % and S12 covered everything.
- **Plan the overflow.** Approve two or more exact profiles, route each request to the smallest
  one that fits, and reject (or send to an approved fallback) anything deeper. Never silently
  truncate or pad a path outside the canonical rules.
- **Stop key grinding.** Poseidon keeps honest paths roughly balanced, but a user who can choose
  keys freely can try to create deep paths. Derive keys in a way callers can't grind, or use a
  fixed-depth design.

### Prove an inclusion (MPF)

Witness factories first verify the native CCL proof strictly, then normalize it into circuit
inputs. They reject malformed proofs and paths deeper than the bound before any proving work.

```java title="MpfInclusion.java"
import org.zeroj.api.CurveId;
import org.zeroj.circuit.CircuitBuilder;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkInputMap;
import org.zeroj.merkle.mpf.poseidon.ccl.PoseidonMpfTrie;
import org.zeroj.merkle.mpf.poseidon.circuit.PoseidonMpfCircuitTemplates;
import org.zeroj.merkle.mpf.poseidon.profile.PoseidonMpfHash;
import org.zeroj.merkle.mpf.poseidon.profile.PoseidonMpfValueCommitment;
import org.zeroj.merkle.mpf.poseidon.witness.PoseidonMpfBranchWitness;

import java.math.BigInteger;

PoseidonMpfTrie trie = PoseidonMpfTrie.inMemory();   // or PoseidonMpfTrie.create(nodeStore, root)
trie.put(keyBytes, valueBytes);

byte[] root = trie.getRootHash();
byte[] proofWire = trie.getProofWire(keyBytes).orElseThrow();
int maxBranches = 8;

PoseidonMpfBranchWitness witness = PoseidonMpfBranchWitness.inclusion(
        root, keyBytes, valueBytes, proofWire, maxBranches);   // throws on an invalid/too-deep proof

ZkInputMap inputs = new ZkInputMap()
        .put(PoseidonMpfCircuitTemplates.ROOT, PoseidonMpfHash.fieldFromDigestBytes(root))
        .put(PoseidonMpfCircuitTemplates.VALUE, PoseidonMpfValueCommitment.field(valueBytes));
witness.putInto(inputs);

CircuitBuilder circuit = PoseidonMpfCircuitTemplates.inclusion(maxBranches);
BigInteger[] circuitWitness = circuit.calculateWitness(inputs.toWitnessMap(), CurveId.BLS12_381);
// …then compile, set up (ceremony keys in production) and prove as for any Groth16 circuit
```

The JMT flow has the same shape: `PoseidonJmtTree`, `PoseidonJmtInclusionWitness.create(...)`,
`PoseidonJmtCircuitTemplates.inclusion(maxLevels)`.

### What the proof does and doesn't say

- A root-only inclusion proof says "the prover knows *some* entry under this root", and nothing
  public about which one. It doesn't bind a particular key to a user. Add the key, owner,
  nullifier, version or transaction fields your application needs in your own circuit.
- JMT version numbers are storage coordinates, not authenticated state.
  Bind `{chain point, version, root}` in your application, with one logical writer.
- A JMT tombstone is still an included value. Never present it as non-inclusion.

### The state-transition validator

`zeroj-onchain-julc` includes a representative Cardano validator,
`Groth16AuthenticatedStateTransitionValidator`, also experimental. It reads the old root from the
state-token UTxO being spent and the new root from the single continuing state-token UTxO. It
enforces a version increment, the authorized signer, value and token conservation and no minting,
then verifies one operation-specific Groth16 proof over the two roots.

Its release tooling (`Groth16AuthenticatedStateTransitionScriptFactory`) binds the exact circuit
manifest, R1CS and VK identities, validator-template digest, JuLC compiler profile, script hash,
network, state token, signer and a one-shot genesis attestation, and it refuses benchmark bundles
on mainnet. The state token's minting policy is outside Groth16: you must independently ensure it
mints exactly one token, once.

### Add the dependency

Both modules are published outside `zeroj-bom-core`, so pin the version. RocksDB is **not** a
dependency. The persistent load and benchmark tools live in the unpublished
`benchmarks/` projects (`-PincludeBenchmarks`).

```groovy title="build.gradle"
dependencies {
    implementation 'org.zeroj:zeroj-mpf-poseidon:0.1.0-pre13'   // or zeroj-jmt-poseidon
}
```

### Gates that remain open

The local tests cover golden vectors, CCL compatibility, malicious witness mutations, cross-operation
and cross-structure replay, real value transitions and JuLC VM evaluation. They show the
implementation is internally consistent and scales on the measured machine. They do **not** show
production assurance. Before protecting value, ZeroJ's own guide requires:

1. freezing every deployed operation and profile, with published manifest, R1CS hash, VK
   identity, Poseidon fingerprint, compiler version and validator-template hash;
2. independent circuit and cryptographic review;
3. a reviewed Groth16 ceremony for each exact circuit;
4. full state-token transactions validated on Yaci DevKit and a public network under current
   protocol parameters;
5. an enforced one-shot, supply-of-one state-token policy;
6. operational procedures for backup, restore, compaction, retention, rollback and rebuild;
7. monitoring of proof depth, prover latency and memory, and rejected over-bound requests.

### Further reading

- 5M benchmark reports: [MPF](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/poseidon-mpf-5m-2026-08-02.md),
  [JMT](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/poseidon-jmt-5m-2026-08-03.md)
- [Practical large-state guide](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/merkle/practical-large-state-guide.md)
  and the [authenticated-state v1 specification](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/merkle/poseidon-authenticated-state-v1.md)
- Design notes: [ADR-0042](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/adr/0042-operation-specific-poseidon-mpf-and-jmt-circuits.md)

## Pedersen commitments

Source: https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/pedersen/

> Commit to a hidden number, open it later, add commitments together, and prove facts about the hidden value in a Groth16 circuit, with ZeroJ's pedersen-jubjub-v1 profile.

A **Pedersen commitment** is a sealed envelope for a number. You publish the envelope, a 32-byte
curve point, and keep the number and a random **blinding** value to yourself. Later you can open
it to someone you choose, or prove facts about the number while it stays sealed: "at least 500",
"these inputs equal these outputs", "this total is covered by our reserves".

ZeroJ implements commitments on the Jubjub curve, whose arithmetic is cheap inside BLS12-381
circuits, so a Groth16 proof about a committed value costs a few thousand constraints. The
profile is [`pedersen-jubjub-v1`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/specs/pedersen-jubjub-v1.md),
designed in [ADR-0051](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/adr/0051-pedersen-commitment-profiles.md).

New to commitments? Read [Commitments & encryption, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/commitments-and-encryption/)
first. Not sure a commitment is what you need? [Choose how to disclose](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/)
compares it with BBS, predicates, encrypted deliveries and threshold decryption.

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### Status

| Area | Status |
|---|---|
| In-circuit commitment (`ZkPedersen`: `commit`, `commitBits`, `verifyOpening`) | **Ready on BLS12-381 Groth16, pending external review** |
| In-circuit homomorphic API (the `ZkPedersenCommitment` wrapper and its `add`/`subtract`, `ZkPedersen.assertBalanced`, subgroup checks) | **Experimental**, pending review and external review |
| Vector commitments (`ZkPedersenVector`, `PedersenVectorCommitment`) | **Experimental**, pending spec and external review |
| Creating commitments off-circuit (`PedersenCommitment.commit`, `randomBlinding`) | **Offline/isolated only**: variable-time arithmetic on secrets |
| Verifying a disclosed opening (`PedersenCommitment.verify`, `verifyScalar`, `verifyBytes`, vector `verify` and `verifyOpening`) | Where the opening is already public (for example published on-chain), or where nobody it is still secret from can time the verifier. Otherwise offline/isolated too |
| Decoding a received commitment (`PedersenCommitment.decode`, `PedersenScalarCommitment.decode`) | Fine anywhere: the point is public |
| Typed profiles, strict adapters, envelopes and keys (`commitScalar`, `verifyScalar`, vector `verifyOpening`, `CommitmentEnvelope`, `CommitmentKey`) | **Experimental**, pending external review; creating commitments is offline/isolated only. New in 0.1.0-pre14 |
| Committing to bytes or a document (`commitBytes`, `commitBytesToEnd`; profile [`pedersen-jubjub-bytes-v1`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/specs/pedersen-jubjub-bytes-v1.md)) | **Experimental**; creating them is offline/isolated only. New in 0.1.0-pre14 |
| BLS12-381 G1 commitments opened directly on Cardano (`G1Pedersen`, `PedersenG1Lib`; profiles [`pedersen-bls12-381-g1-v1`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/specs/pedersen-bls12-381-g1-v1.md) and `-bytes-v1`) | **Experimental**, pending external review; creating them is offline/isolated only. New in 0.1.0-pre14 |

"Offline/isolated only" restricts *where* you run the secret-handling code: on the user's device or
in a separate process, never in a service an attacker can time. It doesn't weaken the commitment's
hiding or binding.

### Add the dependency

Every Pedersen class is in `zeroj-circuit-lib` (the profile contracts of section 7 are in
`zeroj-api`, which it brings in). Add it next to the modules from the
[quickstart](https://zeroj.dev/start/quickstart/):

```groovy title="build.gradle"
dependencies {
    implementation platform('org.zeroj:zeroj-bom-core:<version>')
    annotationProcessor platform('org.zeroj:zeroj-bom-core:<version>')

    implementation 'org.zeroj:zeroj-circuit-annotation-api'
    annotationProcessor 'org.zeroj:zeroj-circuit-annotation-processor'
    implementation 'org.zeroj:zeroj-circuit-dsl'
    implementation 'org.zeroj:zeroj-circuit-lib'          // PedersenCommitment, ZkPedersen, ...
    implementation 'org.zeroj:zeroj-crypto'
    implementation 'org.zeroj:zeroj-codec'
    implementation 'org.zeroj:zeroj-verifier-groth16'
}
```

Use `0.1.0-pre13` or later for `<version>`.

### 1. Commit and open

```java title="CommitAndOpen.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.JubjubCurve;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.JubjubPoint;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.PedersenCommitment;

import java.math.BigInteger;
import java.security.SecureRandom;
import java.util.HexFormat;

public class CommitAndOpen {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // --- Committer (offline) ---
        BigInteger value = BigInteger.valueOf(1_000);                                   // the secret
        BigInteger blinding = PedersenCommitment.randomBlinding(new SecureRandom());   // fresh, never reused

        JubjubPoint commitment = PedersenCommitment.commit(value, blinding);
        byte[] published = commitment.toBytes();                                       // 32 bytes
        System.out.println("Commitment (32 bytes): " + HexFormat.of().formatHex(published));

        // --- Verifier, later: receives the bytes, then the opening (value, blinding) ---
        // decode() rejects non-canonical encodings and points outside the prime-order subgroup.
        JubjubPoint received = PedersenCommitment.decode(published);

        System.out.println("Opens to (1000, r)?   " + PedersenCommitment.verify(received, value, blinding));
        System.out.println("Opens to (1001, r)?   "
                + PedersenCommitment.verify(received, BigInteger.valueOf(1_001), blinding));
        System.out.println("Opens to (1000, r+1)? "
                + PedersenCommitment.verify(received, value, blinding.add(BigInteger.ONE)));

        // (0, -1) is on the curve but has order 2: never a valid commitment.
        BigInteger minusOne = JubjubCurve.BASE_FIELD_PRIME.subtract(BigInteger.ONE);
        byte[] lowOrder = JubjubPoint.fromAffine(BigInteger.ZERO, minusOne).toBytes();
        try {
            PedersenCommitment.decode(lowOrder);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Low-order point rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
```

```text
Commitment (32 bytes): dd6ad5a52e940bdf5754476f42d1bab89df3391c1282fc26d37ca553d4f21291
Opens to (1000, r)?   true
Opens to (1001, r)?   false
Opens to (1000, r+1)? false
Low-order point rejected: Pedersen commitment is not in the prime-order subgroup
```

The commitment bytes change on every run because the blinding is random. That's the point:
committing to 1,000 twice gives two unrelated envelopes.

> **Caution: Decode received commitments with `PedersenCommitment.decode`**
>
> `JubjubPoint.fromBytes` only checks that the bytes are a point on the curve. It does **not** check
> the prime-order subgroup that commitments live in. Use `PedersenCommitment.decode` for any
> commitment you receive.

### 2. Add commitments

Anyone can add two commitments: `C(30, r1) + C(12, r2) = C(42, r1 + r2)`. There's no
`PedersenCommitment.add`; you add the points with `JubjubPoint.add`.

```java title="Homomorphic.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.JubjubCurve;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.JubjubPoint;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.PedersenCommitment;

import java.math.BigInteger;
import java.security.SecureRandom;

public class Homomorphic {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SecureRandom random = new SecureRandom();
        BigInteger v1 = BigInteger.valueOf(30), r1 = PedersenCommitment.randomBlinding(random);
        BigInteger v2 = BigInteger.valueOf(12), r2 = PedersenCommitment.randomBlinding(random);

        JubjubPoint c1 = PedersenCommitment.commit(v1, r1);
        JubjubPoint c2 = PedersenCommitment.commit(v2, r2);

        JubjubPoint sum = c1.add(c2);
        System.out.println("Sum opens to (42, r1 + r2)? "
                + PedersenCommitment.verify(sum, BigInteger.valueOf(42), r1.add(r2)));

        // The arithmetic is modulo the group order l, not over the integers.
        BigInteger l = JubjubCurve.SUBGROUP_ORDER;
        JubjubPoint wrapped = PedersenCommitment.commit(l.subtract(BigInteger.ONE), r1)
                .add(PedersenCommitment.commit(BigInteger.ONE, r2));
        System.out.println("C(l-1, r1) + C(1, r2) opens to (0, r1 + r2)? "
                + PedersenCommitment.verify(wrapped, BigInteger.ZERO, r1.add(r2)));
    }
}
```

```text
Sum opens to (42, r1 + r2)? true
C(l-1, r1) + C(1, r2) opens to (0, r1 + r2)? true
```

The second line is the most important thing on this page. Commitment arithmetic **wraps around**
at a 252-bit number `l`. A huge "value" plus 1 can look like 0, so a cheat could hide a negative
amount inside a sum. A sum of commitments proves nothing about real-world totals unless every
value is range-bounded. That's what the circuit gadgets below do for you.

### 3. Prove a fact without opening

This circuit proves "the value inside this public commitment is at least the public threshold".
The commitment enters as two public inputs, its affine coordinates `(u, v)`.

```java title="CommittedThreshold.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.Prove;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.Public;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.Secret;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.UInt;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZKCircuit;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkBool;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkContext;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkField;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkUInt;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPedersen;

@ZKCircuit(name = "committed-threshold", version = 1)
public class CommittedThreshold {
    @Prove
    ZkBool prove(ZkContext zk,
                 @Public ZkField commitmentU,                 // the commitment, as affine (u, v)
                 @Public ZkField commitmentV,
                 @Public @UInt(bits = 64) ZkUInt threshold,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 64) ZkUInt value,       // never revealed
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt blinding) { // must be exactly 252 bits
        // 1. Recompute C = [value]G + [blinding]H and pin it to the public (u, v).
        ZkPedersen.commit(zk, value, blinding).assertAffineEquals(zk, commitmentU, commitmentV);
        // 2. The statement about the hidden value.
        return value.gte(threshold);
    }
}
```

The program below commits to 1,000, proves "at least 500", and plays the verifier. It uses a
**development-only** setup, as the quickstart does, so run it with
`-Dzeroj.allowInsecureTrustedSetup=true`.

```java title="ThresholdProof.java"
import org.zeroj.api.CircuitId;
import org.zeroj.api.CurveId;
import org.zeroj.api.ProofSystemId;
import org.zeroj.api.PublicInputs;
import org.zeroj.api.VerificationMaterial;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.JubjubPoint;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.PedersenCommitment;
import org.zeroj.codec.SnarkjsJsonCodec;
import org.zeroj.crypto.groth16.Groth16Keys;
import org.zeroj.crypto.groth16.Groth16ProofBLS381;
import org.zeroj.crypto.setup.PowersOfTauBLS381;
import org.zeroj.crypto.snarkjs.SnarkjsGroth16Json;
import org.zeroj.verifier.groth16.bls12381.Groth16BLS12381PureJavaVerifier;

import java.math.BigInteger;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.SecureRandom;

public class ThresholdProof {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Committer (offline): commit to a balance and publish the 32-byte commitment.
        BigInteger balance = BigInteger.valueOf(1_000);
        BigInteger blinding = PedersenCommitment.randomBlinding(new SecureRandom());
        byte[] published = PedersenCommitment.commit(balance, blinding).toBytes();

        // 2. Compile, then a DEV-ONLY trusted setup (this process knows tau).
        var circuit = CommittedThresholdCircuit.build();
        var r1cs = circuit.compileR1CS(CurveId.BLS12_381);
        BigInteger tau = PowersOfTauBLS381.generate(4).tauScalar();   // only tau is used
        try (var keys = Groth16Keys.setupInMemory(
                r1cs.constraints(), r1cs.numWires(), r1cs.numPublicInputs(), tau)) {
            String vkJson = SnarkjsGroth16Json.verificationKeyJson(keys);

            // 3. Prover: knows (balance, blinding) and proves "balance >= 500".
            JubjubPoint c = PedersenCommitment.decode(published);
            var inputs = CommittedThresholdCircuit.inputs()
                    .commitmentU(c.affineU())
                    .commitmentV(c.affineV())
                    .threshold(500)
                    .value(balance)        // secret
                    .blinding(blinding);   // secret
            BigInteger[] witness = inputs.calculateWitness(circuit, CurveId.BLS12_381);
            Groth16ProofBLS381 proof = keys.prove(witness, r1cs.constraints());
            String proofJson = SnarkjsGroth16Json.proofJson(proof);
            String publicJson = SnarkjsGroth16Json.publicJson(inputs.publicValues().toArray(new BigInteger[0]));

            // 4. Verifier: has the published commitment and its own threshold, never the balance.
            System.out.println("Accepted (balance >= 500)? " + accept(vkJson, proofJson, publicJson, published, 500));
            System.out.println("Accepted as proof of >= 900? " + accept(vkJson, proofJson, publicJson, published, 900));

            // 5. A false claim can't even produce a witness.
            try {
                inputs.threshold(2_000).calculateWitness(circuit, CurveId.BLS12_381);
            } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
                System.out.println("Witness for balance >= 2000 refused");
            }
        }
    }

    /** Rebuild the statement from data the verifier trusts, then check the proof. */
    static boolean accept(String vkJson, String proofJson, String publicJson,
                          byte[] publishedCommitment, long requiredThreshold) {
        JubjubPoint c = PedersenCommitment.decode(publishedCommitment);
        PublicInputs expected = CommittedThresholdCircuit.inputs()
                .commitmentU(c.affineU())
                .commitmentV(c.affineV())
                .threshold(requiredThreshold)
                .toPublicInputs();
        if (!expected.equals(SnarkjsJsonCodec.parsePublicInputs(publicJson))) {
            return false;   // the proof is about a different commitment or threshold
        }
        CircuitId id = CommittedThresholdCircuit.circuitId();
        var envelope = SnarkjsJsonCodec.toEnvelopeFromJson(proofJson, vkJson, publicJson, id);
        var material = VerificationMaterial.of(vkJson.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
                ProofSystemId.GROTH16, CurveId.BLS12_381, id);
        return new Groth16BLS12381PureJavaVerifier().verify(envelope, material).proofValid();
    }
}
```

```text
Accepted (balance >= 500)? true
Accepted as proof of >= 900? false
Witness for balance >= 2000 refused
```

The circuit has 2,671 constraints. Two details carry the security:

- **The verifier rebuilds the public inputs** from the commitment it already holds and the
  threshold it requires. Comparing them with the proof's public inputs is what stops a prover
  from submitting a valid proof about a *different* commitment or a lower threshold.
- **The blinding is declared `@Secret @UInt(bits = 252)`.** ZeroJ refuses to build a circuit
  whose blinding is narrower, public or a constant: `CommittedThresholdCircuit.build()` throws
  `IllegalArgumentException`. A 16-bit blinding could be brute-forced, which would reveal the
  value. The guard can't tell whether *your* blinding is random, though, so always use
  `randomBlinding(new SecureRandom())`.

### 4. Prove that amounts balance

To move value privately, prove that the hidden inputs equal the hidden outputs plus any public
fee. `ZkPedersen.assertBalanced` does this, and it refuses layouts that could wrap around `l`.

```java title="ConfidentialTransfer.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.Prove;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.Public;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.Secret;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.UInt;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZKCircuit;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkContext;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkField;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkUInt;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPedersen;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPedersenCommitment;

import java.util.List;

/** "The hidden input amount equals the hidden output amount plus the public fee." */
@ZKCircuit(name = "confidential-transfer", version = 1)
public class ConfidentialTransfer {
    @Prove
    void prove(ZkContext zk,
               @Public ZkField inU, @Public ZkField inV,          // input commitment (u, v)
               @Public ZkField outU, @Public ZkField outV,        // output commitment (u, v)
               @Public @UInt(bits = 32) ZkUInt fee,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 64) ZkUInt inAmount,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt inBlinding,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 64) ZkUInt outAmount,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt outBlinding) {
        var in = ZkPedersenCommitment.commit(zk, inAmount, inBlinding);
        var out = ZkPedersenCommitment.commit(zk, outAmount, outBlinding);
        in.assertAffineEquals(zk, inU, inV);
        out.assertAffineEquals(zk, outU, outV);
        // in = out + fee over the integers. 64 + 32-bit terms can't reach l, so nothing wraps;
        // assertBalanced checks that when the circuit is built.
        ZkPedersen.assertBalanced(zk,
                List.of(ZkPedersen.Term.of(in)),
                List.of(ZkPedersen.Term.of(out), ZkPedersen.Term.amount(fee)));
    }
}
```

Driven the same way as the threshold example (sending 5,000 as 4,750 plus a 250 fee), it gives:

```text
Transfer accepted (fee 250)? true
Transfer accepted (fee 200)? false
Unbalanced witness refused: Constraint violation: inAmount(w6)=5000 != w17753=5001
Wrapping layout refused: the left side of this balance can reach 1fff…fffe (hex), which is not below
the subgroup order l. A relation mod l would not imply integer conservation; narrow the declared
widths or coefficients (ADR-0051 D3a).
```

The last line comes from a variant whose amounts are declared 252 bits wide. `build()` refuses it
before any proof exists. The rules `assertBalanced` enforces:

- every term has a declared width, through `@UInt(bits = …)`;
- coefficients are positive constants (move a subtraction to the other side);
- the largest possible total on each side stays below `l`.

The circuit has 4,886 constraints. The [confidential loyalty points](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-points/)
demo uses the same pattern for a 1-in, 2-out transfer.

### 5. Commit to several values at once

A **vector commitment** seals up to 16 values in one point, for example a credit profile of
income, score, birth year and country. A proof can then check a rule over some fields and keep all
of them hidden:

```java title="CreditProfileCheck.java (core)"
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPedersenVector;

// SCHEMA lists the fields and their widths: income/64, credit_score/16, birth_year/16, country/16.
var binding = ZkPedersenVector.bindSchema(zk, SCHEMA, schemaDigest);   // schemaDigest is @Public
ZkPedersenVector.commit(zk, binding, List.of(income, creditScore, birthYear, country), blinding)
        .assertAffineEquals(zk, u, v);
income.gte(minIncome).assertTrue();
creditScore.gte(minScore).assertTrue();
```

Vector commitments need two extra checks that single commitments don't:

- **The point doesn't record its layout.** `C([a], r)` equals `C([a, 0], r)`, so every proof binds a
  public **schema digest** with `bindSchema`, and the verifier checks it against a trusted
  `PedersenSchemaRegistry`.
- **A commitment proves nothing about who issued it.** Accept a received commitment only with an
  authenticated issuance record, and fail closed without one.

The full worked example is `AnnotatedVectorCommitment` in
[`zeroj-integration-tests`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/tree/main/zeroj-integration-tests/src/test/java/org/zeroj/examples/annotation),
and the [credit gate](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/prove-a-rule/#over-a-committed-credential) shows it on
Cardano.

### 6. Commit to bytes or a document

> **Note:** the APIs on this page are new in ZeroJ 0.1.0-pre14 and not in a release on Maven Central yet (the latest is 0.1.0-pre13). Use a development snapshot (`0.1.0-pre14-<commit>-SNAPSHOT`) from https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/snapshots to try them.

To commit to a file, a JSON message or any other binary data, use the byte profile
[`pedersen-jubjub-bytes-v1`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/specs/pedersen-jubjub-bytes-v1.md)
([ADR-0058](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/adr/0058-pedersen-jubjub-byte-commitments.md)).
It hashes the exact bytes, followed by their length as 8 big-endian bytes, to a scalar (RFC 9380
hash-to-field with SHA-256; see the spec's §3 for the exact frame) and commits to that scalar with
the same bases as above, so the result is the same 32-byte point format.

```java
BigInteger r = PedersenCommitment.randomBlinding(new SecureRandom());   // offline, fresh every time
PedersenBytesCommitment c = PedersenCommitment.commitBytes(documentBytes, r);
byte[] published = c.toPointBytes();                                   // 32 bytes, the whole wire format

// Someone you disclose the document and r to:
boolean ok = PedersenCommitment.verifyBytes(PedersenBytesCommitment.decode(published), documentBytes, r);
```

Large files don't need to fit in memory. Stream them, with the exact length or with a maximum
when the length isn't known up front; both give the same commitment as the array form:

```java
try (InputStream in = Files.newInputStream(path)) {           // you open and close the stream
    c = PedersenCommitment.commitBytes(in, Files.size(path), r);  // exact length: shorter or longer fails
}
try (InputStream in = generator.open()) {
    c = PedersenCommitment.commitBytesToEnd(in, 100L << 20, r);   // unknown length, at most 100 MiB
}
```

Things to know:

- **Every byte counts.** Nothing is normalized. Pick the text encoding yourself
  (`StandardCharsets.UTF_8`); `"café"` in NFC and NFD commits differently, and so does JSON with
  different whitespace or key order. If you need semantic equality, canonicalize in your own
  versioned format first.
- **The blinding must already be in range** (`0 ≤ r < l`); `commitBytes` rejects anything else
  instead of reducing it. Use `randomBlinding`.
- **`verifyBytes` is for a disclosed opening.** It uses variable-time arithmetic, so run it where
  the opening is already public or nobody it is still secret from can time you. To check a
  document you're keeping private, recompute with `commitBytes` offline and compare the points.
- **The point doesn't say it's a byte commitment.** Whoever knows `(bytes, r)` also knows a
  numeric opening of the same point. If it matters which profile and context a commitment was
  issued under, store that association authenticated (for example in an issuer-signed record)
  and check it.
- **No circuit proves the hashing.** You can prove facts about the hashed scalar, but not that it
  came from particular bytes.

### 7. Profiles, envelopes and safe keys

> **Note:** the APIs on this page are new in ZeroJ 0.1.0-pre14 and not in a release on Maven Central yet (the latest is 0.1.0-pre13). Use a development snapshot (`0.1.0-pre14-<commit>-SNAPSHOT`) from https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/snapshots to try them.

Each kind of commitment above is a registered **profile** with its own identifier:
`pedersen-jubjub-v1` (one value), `pedersen-jubjub-vector-v1` (several values under a schema) and
`pedersen-jubjub-bytes-v1` (exact bytes). The registry, the checks and the byte formats are in
[`commitment-profiles-v1`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/specs/commitment-profiles-v1.md)
([ADR-0059](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/adr/0059-commitment-profiles-and-verification-strategy.md)).
The profiles that share bases produce the same points, so a point never tells you its profile:
**your configuration does.**

#### Strict entry points

`commit` and `verify` reduce their inputs mod `l`, so `commit(l + 5, r)` equals `commit(5, r)`.
The strict forms refuse anything outside `[0, l)` instead, and can also check an amount bound:

```java
BigInteger r = PedersenCommitment.randomBlinding(new SecureRandom());          // offline
PedersenScalarCommitment c = PedersenCommitment.commitScalar(BigInteger.valueOf(250), r);

// Someone you disclose (250, r) to, who also requires the amount to fit in 64 bits:
boolean ok = PedersenCommitment.verifyScalar(c, BigInteger.valueOf(250), r, 64);
```

`verifyScalar` checks a **disclosed** opening with variable-time arithmetic: use it where the
opening is already public or nobody it is still secret from can time you. To check an opening
you're keeping private, recompute with `commitScalar` offline and compare the points.

A value or blinding outside `[0, l)` throws `CommitmentFormatException` with
`NON_CANONICAL_SCALAR`; with a canonical value and blinding, a value at or above `2^64` throws it
with `OUT_OF_RANGE`. Typed commitments add and subtract only with their own type: `c.add(other)`.

A **sum of vector commitments** may no longer open under the schema widths, because its
components can grow past them. Say which bound you expect:

```java
PedersenVectorCommitment total = a.add(b);                                // both under `schema`
BigInteger sumBlinding = rA.add(rB).mod(JubjubCurve.SUBGROUP_ORDER);   // blindings add mod l
boolean ok = total.verifyOpening(List.of(sumAmount, sumAsset), sumBlinding,
        PedersenVectorBoundPolicy.widened(schema, 2));                    // each width + 1 bit
```

Reduce the summed blinding mod `l`: `verifyOpening` rejects any scalar outside `[0, l)`
(`NON_CANONICAL_SCALAR`) instead of reducing it.

`schemaWidths(schema)` is for commitments issued under the schema and `residueOnly(schema)` for
differences, whose negative components open to `l − x`; a residue-only opening says nothing about
integer amounts. The policy must be for the commitment's own schema. This is disclosed
verification too, under the same timing rule as `verifyScalar`.

#### Storing commitments: the envelope

To store or send a commitment off-chain together with its profile, wrap it in an envelope. It
is `0x01`, the identifier's length and the identifier, then the 32-byte point:

```java
byte[] stored = CommitmentEnvelope.encode(c);                                  // 52 bytes
PedersenScalarCommitment back = CommitmentEnvelope.decode(stored, PedersenScalarCommitment.CODEC);
```

`decode` takes the profile you **expect**, from your configuration. An envelope of another
profile fails with `PROFILE_MISMATCH`, even when its point would verify.

A vector envelope carries **no schema**. Decode it with `PedersenVectorCommitment.codec(schema)`
for the schema your configuration or issuance record names. The envelope of a commitment made
under another schema decodes without error and the result simply takes the codec's schema, so no
later check can detect the substitution: `verifyOpening` and `CommitmentKey` reject only mixing
schemas *after* decoding. Getting the schema right, from an authenticated issuance record, is
yours.

Envelopes are an off-chain format: datums and redeemers keep the raw 32-byte point, and circuits
keep their public inputs (the affine `u`, `v`, plus the schema digest for vectors).

#### Map keys and acceptance

Don't key a map by the point bytes: a byte commitment and a numeric commitment can share a
point, and so can vector commitments under two schemas. Use `CommitmentKey`:

```java
CommitmentKey key = CommitmentKey.of(c, PedersenScalarCommitment.CODEC);
```

`CommitmentAcceptance` runs the three checks in order (decode under the expected profile, your
provenance rule, the opening) and returns the first failure as a reason:

```java
boolean acceptDisclosed(byte[] stored, BigInteger value, BigInteger blinding) throws IOException {
    CommitmentCheck check = CommitmentAcceptance.accept(stored, PedersenScalarCommitment.CODEC,
            commitment -> issuer.recorded(commitment) ? ProvenancePolicy.Result.OK : ProvenancePolicy.Result.MISSING,
            commitment -> PedersenCommitment.verifyScalar(commitment, value, blinding, 64));
    return check.accepted();   // otherwise check.reason() says why
}
```

Format failures, provenance results and a non-matching opening become a reason. Exceptions are
not swallowed: anything your provenance rule throws, an opening check that reports a
misconfiguration (`INVALID_CONFIGURATION`, such as an invalid `amountBits`), and I/O errors
propagate. `accept` declares `IOException` because opening checks may read streams.

A matching identifier in the envelope is not provenance. If it matters who issued a commitment,
and under which profile and context, your provenance rule checks an authenticated record. The
opening check is disclosed verification, under the same timing rule as `verifyBytes`.

#### What each profile can verify, and where

From the spec's verification matrix (§14). "V1" checks a disclosed opening, "V3" a public
relation such as a sum, "V4" a proof. Every row leaves authorization, replay protection and
context binding to your application.

| Profile | Class | Java (off-chain) | Cardano | Public afterwards |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pedersen-jubjub-v1` | V1 | `verify`, `verifyScalar` | Not native (no Jubjub builtins); only inside a proof | Value and blinding |
| | V3 | Typed `add`/`subtract`/`negate` (residues mod `l`) | Inside a proof only | The deltas |
| | V4 | Groth16/PlonK with `ZkPedersen` | `Groth16BLS12381Lib.verify` with `(u, v)` as public inputs | The public inputs |
| `pedersen-jubjub-vector-v1` | V1 | `verify`, `verifyOpening` under a bound policy | Not native | Values and blinding |
| | V3 | `add`/`subtract`, same schema only | Inside a proof only | The deltas |
| | V4 | Groth16/PlonK with `ZkPedersenVector` | Groth16 verify with the schema digest as a public input, plus an issuance record | The public inputs, including the digest |
| `pedersen-jubjub-bytes-v1` | V1 | `verifyBytes` (and stream forms) | Not native; no circuit proves the hashing | Payload and blinding |
| | V3, V4 | Not offered | Not offered | — |
| `pedersen-bls12-381-g1-v1` | V1 | `G1Pedersen.verifyScalar` (experimental, ADR-0060) | Native (experimental): `PedersenG1Lib.verifyScalarOpening`/`verifyScalarOpeningBounded`: length check, `uncompress`, canonical round trip, check 1 on `m` and `r` and check 2 if requested, then two `scalarMul`, `add`, `equal`; about 3.4% of a transaction's step limit | Message and blinding |
| | V3 | `withPublicDelta` (`deltaBits ≤ 253`), typed `add`/`subtract`/`negate` (residues mod `q`) | Native (experimental): `applyPublicDelta` with the signed-delta rule, `add`/`subtract`/`negate`; sums with verifier-fixed coefficients | The deltas |
| | V4 | Blocked (ADR-0051 D7; #96) | Blocked / feasibility (#96) | — |
| `pedersen-bls12-381-g1-bytes-v1` | V1 only (no arithmetic on byte commitments) | `G1Pedersen.verifyBytes*`, streaming to `2^61 − 256` octets (experimental, ADR-0060) | Native (experimental): `PedersenG1Lib.verifyBytesOpening` recomputes the mapping with `sha2_256`. The transaction size, not the budget, bounds the payload: about 14 KB in a redeemer with the script inline, 15 KB with a reference script, in a minimal transaction. No scalar-only mode: checking a supplied scalar is a `pedersen-bls12-381-g1-v1` opening and authenticates only that scalar, not the bytes | Payload and blinding |

V1 rows are disclosed, variable-time checks: run them where the opening is already public or
nobody it is still secret from can time the verifier, otherwise offline/isolated. Disclosed
openings on-chain are public forever. A relation proves residues, not balances: integer
conservation needs a range proof per term or a circuit. Documents larger than the on-chain limit
can only be committed and opened off-chain; on-chain references them by commitment.

### 8. Open a commitment directly on Cardano (BLS12-381 G1)

> **Note:** the APIs on this page are new in ZeroJ 0.1.0-pre14 and not in a release on Maven Central yet (the latest is 0.1.0-pre13). Use a development snapshot (`0.1.0-pre14-<commit>-SNAPSHOT`) from https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/snapshots to try them.

A Cardano validator has no Jubjub builtins, so it can only check a Jubjub commitment inside a
proof. The G1 profiles put the commitment on BLS12-381's G1 curve instead, where Plutus V3 has
builtins: a validator can open it, add commitments or apply a public delta **directly**, with no
proof. The profiles are
[`pedersen-bls12-381-g1-v1`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/specs/pedersen-bls12-381-g1-v1.md)
(a number) and `pedersen-bls12-381-g1-bytes-v1` (exact bytes), designed in
[ADR-0060](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/adr/0060-pedersen-bls12-381-g1-profiles.md).
A commitment is a 48-byte compressed point. The trade-off: no ZeroJ circuit proves facts about a
G1 commitment's hidden value, so use it when you will **open** the value or move it by **public**
amounts.

Off-chain (`zeroj-bls12381`):

```java
G1Pedersen pedersen = G1Pedersen.pureJava();                       // or G1Pedersen.withProvider(provider)
BigInteger r = G1Pedersen.randomBlinding(new SecureRandom());      // offline, fresh every time
G1PedersenCommitment c = pedersen.commitScalar(BigInteger.valueOf(1_000), r);
byte[] datum = c.toPointBytes();                                   // 48 bytes

G1PedersenCommitment received = G1PedersenCommitment.decode(datum); // strict: rejects anything off the subgroup
boolean ok = pedersen.verifyScalar(received, BigInteger.valueOf(1_000), r, 64); // value < 2^64 too
G1PedersenCommitment next = received.withPublicDelta(BigInteger.valueOf(-250), 64); // opens to 750 with r
```

On-chain (`zeroj-onchain-julc`, `PedersenG1Lib`):

```java
var c = PedersenG1Lib.decodeCommitment(datum.commitment());        // 48 bytes, canonical, in the subgroup
boolean opened = PedersenG1Lib.verifyScalarOpeningBounded(c, redeemer.value(), redeemer.blinding(),
        BigInteger.valueOf(64));
var moved = PedersenG1Lib.applyPublicDelta(c, redeemer.delta(), BigInteger.valueOf(64));
```

Things to know:

- **Cost on Cardano.** A scalar opening costs about 341 million CPU steps, about 3.4% of a
  transaction's limit; a byte opening about 346 to 395 million. The transaction size, not the
  budget, limits a byte opening's payload: about 14 KB in a redeemer with the script inline, 15 KB
  with a reference script. See the
  [measurements](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/pedersen-g1-2026-10-22.md).
- **An opened value is public forever.** Anyone can read the redeemer.
- **Deltas and sums are residues mod `q`**, not balances. Bound them yourself; `deltaBits` is at
  most 253 so that one delta has only one accepted form.
- **The library checks the commitment, not your application.** Authorization, replay protection,
  binding to the spent output and value conservation are the validator's job. Three example
  validators (an opening, a running total, a byte opening) are in
  [`zeroj-integration-tests`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/tree/main/zeroj-integration-tests/src/test/java/org/zeroj/examples/pedersen/g1).
- **Creating commitments is offline/isolated only**, as for Jubjub; neither the pure-Java nor the
  blst provider is constant-time.

### Commitments you didn't make

If your circuit receives a commitment whose opening it doesn't know, for example another party's
balance, there are three ways in. Pick by who checks the point:

| Situation | API | Who checks the point |
|---|---|---|
| The circuit knows the opening | `ZkPedersenCommitment.commit(zk, value, blinding)` + `assertAffineEquals` | The circuit recomputes it |
| The opening is unknown, the point is a witness | `ZkPedersenCommitment.witnessInSubgroup(zk, u, v)` | The circuit (about 5,500 extra constraints) |
| The opening is unknown, the point is public | `ZkPedersenCommitment.fromVerifierCheckedPublic(zk, u, v)` | **Your verifier** must `PedersenCommitment.decode` it first |

On Cardano, a validator can't run the Jubjub subgroup check, so on-chain consumers use the first
two rows.

### Rules to follow

- **Fresh random blinding, every time.** `PedersenCommitment.randomBlinding(new SecureRandom())`;
  never reuse one, never derive it from public data.
- **Commit offline.** `commit` and `randomBlinding` use variable-time arithmetic on secrets. Run
  them on the user's device or in an isolated process.
- **Decode with `PedersenCommitment.decode`**, never `JubjubPoint.fromBytes`, for received bytes.
- **Take the profile, and for vectors the schema, from your configuration**, never from data that
  travels with the commitment. Decode envelopes with the codec you expect and key maps with
  `CommitmentKey`.
- **Range-bound every value that means a number.** Commitments bind values *modulo* `l`:
  `commit(v, r)` equals `commit(v + l, r)`. Integer meaning comes only from declared widths and
  `assertBalanced`. Off-circuit point sums carry no such check.
- **Rebuild public inputs on the verifier side.** A commitment is two public inputs, `u` then `v`.
- **The identity point is a valid commitment** (to 0 with blinding 0). Check `isIdentity()` if
  your application must exclude it.
- **A proof is not a permission.** Replay protection, nullifiers and binding to the spending
  transaction are still your job. See [Application security](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/application-security/).

### Cost

| Circuit | Constraints | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Commitment with public `(u, v)`, 64-bit value | 2,410 | `zeroj-circuit-lib` README |
| Same, 252-bit value | 4,042 | `zeroj-circuit-lib` README |
| "At least a threshold" (example 3) | 2,671 | measured for this page |
| 1-in, 1-out transfer with a fee (example 4) | 4,886 | measured for this page |
| Vector commitment, 1 / 4 / 16 values | 2,411 / 3,581 / 8,261 | [vector benchmark](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/pedersen-vector-2026-10-03.md) |

Pure-Java proving for circuits this size took about 1.2 to 1.5 seconds per proof in the
[vector benchmark](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/pedersen-vector-2026-10-03.md)
(2,400 to 8,300 constraints, one Apple M4 Max laptop), most of it fixed overhead. On Cardano, the proof is checked by ZeroJ's ordinary Groth16 verifier, and the
commitment is just two of its public inputs. See [Verify proofs on Cardano](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/on-chain/).

### Next steps

- [Confidential notes](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/confidential-notes/): deliver the opening on-chain to
  the owner and an auditor
- [ElGamal encryption](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/elgamal/): encrypt an amount so an auditor can read it
- [Hide a number, prove facts about it](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/hide-a-number/): the pattern, with use cases
- Use cases: [Proof of solvency with hidden balances](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-solvency/),
  [Confidential loyalty points](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-points/)

## ElGamal encryption

Source: https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/elgamal/

> Encrypt small amounts to someone's public key, add ciphertexts without decrypting them, and prove in a Groth16 circuit what a ciphertext contains, with ZeroJ's elgamal-jubjub-v1 profile.

A [Pedersen commitment](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/pedersen/) can only be opened by someone who knows
its opening. **Encryption** solves a different problem: a value that a named party, such as an
auditor, an auctioneer or a group of election trustees, must be able to read later **without
the sender's help**.

Think of a lockbox with a slot. Anyone can drop a value in using the public key; only the holder
of the secret key can open it. ZeroJ uses **exponential ElGamal** on the Jubjub curve, which adds
one more property: ciphertexts under the same key **add up**. A ledger can keep an encrypted
running total, and the key holder decrypts only the total.

The trade-off is that decryption ends in a search, so it only works for **small numbers**: votes,
counters, or a large amount split into 32-bit pieces called **limbs**. The profile is
[`elgamal-jubjub-v1`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/specs/elgamal-jubjub-v1.md),
designed in [ADR-0052](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/adr/0052-exponential-elgamal-jubjub.md).

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### Status

| Area | Status |
|---|---|
| Host API: keys, encryption, homomorphic addition, decryption (`ElGamal`, `ElGamalCiphertext`, key contexts) | **Experimental**, pending review and external review |
| In-circuit encryption and DLEQ proofs (`ZkElGamal`, `ZkElGamalPublicKey`) | **Experimental**, pending review and external review |
| Secret operations (encrypting, decryption shares, decrypting) | **Offline/isolated only**: variable-time arithmetic, no constant-time claim |

"Offline/isolated only" means: run code that touches secret keys or plaintexts on the user's own
device or in a separate process, never in a shared service an attacker can time. See
[Status & maturity](https://zeroj.dev/start/status/).

### Add the dependency

The host API is in `zeroj-circuit-lib`:

```groovy title="build.gradle"
dependencies {
    implementation platform('org.zeroj:zeroj-bom-core:<version>')
    implementation 'org.zeroj:zeroj-circuit-lib'   // ElGamal, ElGamalCiphertext, JubjubDiscreteLog, ...
}
```

Example 4 below also proves a circuit, so it needs the annotation, crypto, codec and verifier
modules listed in the [Pedersen guide](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/pedersen/#add-the-dependency). Use
`0.1.0-pre13` or later for `<version>`.

### 1. Encrypt, add, decrypt

```java title="ElGamalBasics.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamal;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamalCiphertext;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamalSecretKey;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.JubjubDiscreteLog;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.NOfNKeyContext;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.RawElGamalCiphertext;

import java.security.SecureRandom;

/** Exponential ElGamal on Jubjub: encrypt two amounts, add the ciphertexts, decrypt only the sum. */
public class ElGamalBasics {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SecureRandom random = new SecureRandom();

        // 1. A key pair. The context is "the key a ciphertext belongs to"; n-of-n with n = 1 here.
        ElGamalSecretKey secretKey = ElGamalSecretKey.generate(random);
        NOfNKeyContext key = NOfNKeyContext.singleKey(secretKey);

        // 2. Encrypt two amounts. The width (16 bits here) is a promise: 0 <= m < 2^16.
        int width = 16;
        ElGamalCiphertext a = ElGamal.encrypt(key, 1200, width, random);
        ElGamalCiphertext b = ElGamal.encrypt(key, 345, width, random);
        System.out.println("Ciphertext size: " + a.encode().length + " bytes");
        System.out.println("Bound of each ciphertext: " + a.bound());

        // 3. Add without decrypting. The library tracks the bound of the sum.
        ElGamalCiphertext sum = a.add(b);
        System.out.println("Bound of the sum: " + sum.bound());

        // 4. Decrypt the sum: a bounded discrete-log search over [0, bound].
        //    Build the search table once and reuse it for many decryptions.
        long maxPlaintext = sum.bound().longValueExact();
        JubjubDiscreteLog table = JubjubDiscreteLog.forBound(maxPlaintext);
        long total = ElGamal.decryptWithSecret(sum, secretKey, maxPlaintext, table);
        System.out.println("Decrypted sum: " + total);

        // What the safe API refuses:
        try {
            ElGamal.decryptWithSecret(sum, secretKey, 1000);  // search limit below the bound
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Refused: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        try {
            ElGamalSecretKey other = ElGamalSecretKey.generate(random);
            a.add(ElGamal.encrypt(NOfNKeyContext.singleKey(other), 1, 1, random)); // different keys
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Refused: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        try {
            ElGamal.encrypt(key, 70_000, width, random);      // does not fit in 16 bits
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Refused: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        // Bytes carry no key and no bound: decoding gives a *raw* ciphertext, which has no
        // decrypt method. It re-enters the safe layer only through ElGamal.admit(...) with a
        // verifier that checks an encryption proof.
        RawElGamalCiphertext raw = RawElGamalCiphertext.decode(sum.encode());
        System.out.println("Decoded from bytes: " + raw.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
}
```

```text
Ciphertext size: 64 bytes
Bound of each ciphertext: 65535
Bound of the sum: 131070
Decrypted sum: 1545
Refused: the ciphertext's plaintext bound 131070 exceeds the search limit 1000
Refused: ciphertexts are under different key contexts; homomorphic operations need one key
Refused: message must satisfy 0 <= m < 2^16
Decoded from bytes: RawElGamalCiphertext
```

What to notice:

- **Every encryption carries a width.** `encrypt(key, 1200, 16, random)` promises that the
  message fits in 16 bits. The ciphertext remembers the largest value it can hold, its **bound**
  (65,535 here), and adding two ciphertexts adds their bounds.
- **Decryption is a search** over `[0, bound]`. `JubjubDiscreteLog.forBound(...)` builds a lookup
  table once; reuse it for many decryptions.
- **The safe API refuses mistakes** instead of returning a wrong answer: a search limit below the
  bound, ciphertexts under different keys, a message that doesn't fit its width.
- **Bytes carry no key and no bound.** `RawElGamalCiphertext.decode` gives you a *raw* ciphertext,
  which has no decrypt method. Section 3 shows how it gets back in.

### 2. Encrypt to someone else's key

In example 1 one process owns the key, so `NOfNKeyContext.singleKey(secretKey)` is fine. A real
sender only has the recipient's **published** key, and must check a **possession proof** before
using it: a zero-knowledge proof (a DLEQ proof) that whoever published the key knows its secret.

Why bother? Without it, an attacker can publish a "rogue" key crafted from other people's keys,
so that a combined key ends up decryptable by the attacker alone. ZeroJ makes the check part of
the type system: the only way from bytes to a usable key goes through `VerifiedKeyShare.verify`,
which hands your verifier the exact statement to check.

```java title="Admit a published key (shape)"
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.DleqStatement;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamalPublicKey;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.NOfNKeyContext;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.VerifiedKeyShare;

import java.util.List;

// keyBytes and proof come from the auditor's registry entry (or a trustee's announcement).
VerifiedKeyShare share = VerifiedKeyShare.verify(keyBytes, statement ->
        statement.kind() == DleqStatement.Kind.POSSESSION
                && verifyDleqProof(proof, statement.publicInputs()));   // YOUR Groth16 check
NOfNKeyContext auditor = ElGamalPublicKey.aggregate(List.of(share));

// Several key holders (n-of-n): aggregate all their verified shares into one joint key.
// NOfNKeyContext trustees = ElGamalPublicKey.aggregate(List.of(share1, share2, share3));
```

`verifyDleqProof` stands for your own Groth16 verification of the possession proof, over a DLEQ
circuit built with `ZkElGamal.assertDiscreteLogEquality`. The full proven flow (possession
proofs, joint key, proved ballots, proved decryption shares, tally) is the `endToEnd` test in
[`AnnotatedElGamalTest`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/zeroj-integration-tests/src/test/java/org/zeroj/examples/annotation/AnnotatedElGamalTest.java).

> **Danger: A verifier that returns `true` disables the check**
>
> Every `...Verifier` lambda is a promise that *you* checked a proof. `s -> true` compiles, runs and
> silently turns off the protection.

### 3. Receive ciphertexts: admit them with a proof

A ciphertext you receive could encrypt anything: a negative number, a huge number, a value under
the wrong key. Adding it to your total would corrupt the total. So received bytes start as a
`RawElGamalCiphertext`, and become a usable `ElGamalCiphertext` only through `ElGamal.admit`:

```java title="Admit a received ciphertext"
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamal;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamalCiphertext;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.RawElGamalCiphertext;

RawElGamalCiphertext raw = RawElGamalCiphertext.decode(ciphertextBytes);   // 64 bytes
ElGamalCiphertext ballot = ElGamal.admit(raw, electionKey, 1, statement ->
        statement.width() == 1
                && verifyEncryptionProof(proof, statement.publicInputs()));   // YOUR Groth16 check
```

The statement's public inputs are exactly `PK.u, PK.v, A.u, A.v, B.u, B.v`: the key and the
ciphertext's two points. Your proof must be over those values and that width, for example a
circuit that calls `ZkElGamal.encrypt` and `assertAffineEquals`, as in example 4.

When is `s -> true` acceptable? Only when something else already verified a proof for that exact
statement, for example a Cardano validator that refused the transaction unless the proof
verified. The [confidential points](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-points/) auditor does this for
ciphertexts it reads from validated ledger outputs, and says so in a comment.

### 4. Prove what a ciphertext contains

The most useful pattern combines a commitment and a ciphertext: "this ciphertext, encrypted to the
auditor, holds **the same amount** as this commitment". Then the auditor's copy can't be faked,
even by the sender. This circuit is a minimal illustration of that idea for one 32-bit amount; it
is not the reference circuit ZeroJ measured on-chain.

```java title="AuditedAmount.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.Prove;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.Public;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.Secret;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.UInt;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZKCircuit;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkContext;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkField;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkUInt;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkElGamal;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkElGamalPublicKey;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPedersenCommitment;

/**
 * "The public ElGamal ciphertext encrypts, under the auditor's key, the same amount the public
 * Pedersen commitment hides." One secret amount feeds both relations.
 */
@ZKCircuit(name = "audited-amount", version = 1)
public class AuditedAmount {
    @Prove
    void prove(ZkContext zk,
               @Public ZkField commitU, @Public ZkField commitV,
               @Public ZkField auditorU, @Public ZkField auditorV,
               @Public ZkField handleU, @Public ZkField handleV,
               @Public ZkField blindedU, @Public ZkField blindedV,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 32) ZkUInt amount,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt blinding,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt randomness) {
        ZkPedersenCommitment.commit(zk, amount, blinding).assertAffineEquals(zk, commitU, commitV);
        var auditor = ZkElGamalPublicKey.fromVerifierFixedPublic(zk, auditorU, auditorV);
        ZkElGamal.encrypt(zk, amount, randomness, auditor)
                .assertAffineEquals(zk, handleU, handleV, blindedU, blindedV);
    }
}
```

The program commits to 250, encrypts 250 to the auditor, proves the circuit, lets the auditor admit
and decrypt the ciphertext, then plays a cheating sender who encrypts 1 instead. Run it with
`-Dzeroj.allowInsecureTrustedSetup=true` (development setup):

```java title="AuditedAmountMain.java"
import org.zeroj.api.CurveId;
import org.zeroj.api.ProofSystemId;
import org.zeroj.api.VerificationMaterial;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamal;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamalCiphertext;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamalEncryption;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamalSecretKey;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.JubjubPoint;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.NOfNKeyContext;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.NoteOpening;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.RawElGamalCiphertext;
import org.zeroj.codec.SnarkjsJsonCodec;
import org.zeroj.crypto.groth16.Groth16Keys;
import org.zeroj.crypto.setup.PowersOfTauBLS381;
import org.zeroj.crypto.snarkjs.SnarkjsGroth16Json;
import org.zeroj.verifier.groth16.bls12381.Groth16BLS12381PureJavaVerifier;

import java.math.BigInteger;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.SecureRandom;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class AuditedAmountMain {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SecureRandom random = new SecureRandom();
        var circuit = AuditedAmountCircuit.build();
        var r1cs = circuit.compileR1CS(CurveId.BLS12_381);
        System.out.println("Public inputs: " + AuditedAmountCircuit.schema().publicInputs().names());
        System.out.println("Constraints: " + r1cs.numConstraints());

        // DEV-ONLY single-party setup. Production keys come from an MPC ceremony.
        BigInteger tau = PowersOfTauBLS381.generate(6).tauScalar();
        Groth16Keys keys = Groth16Keys.setupInMemory(r1cs.constraints(), r1cs.numWires(),
                r1cs.numPublicInputs(), tau);
        String vkJson = SnarkjsGroth16Json.verificationKeyJson(keys);

        // The auditor's ElGamal key (a separate key from any note viewing key).
        // Demo shortcut: one process plays both parties. A real sender builds this context from
        // the auditor's published key and possession proof:
        //   ElGamalPublicKey.aggregate(List.of(VerifiedKeyShare.verify(keyBytes, proofVerifier)))
        ElGamalSecretKey auditorSecret = ElGamalSecretKey.generate(random);
        NOfNKeyContext auditor = NOfNKeyContext.singleKey(auditorSecret);

        // Sender: commit to 250 and encrypt the same 250 to the auditor, then prove it.
        long amount = 250;
        NoteOpening opening = NoteOpening.random(BigInteger.valueOf(amount), random);
        JubjubPoint c = opening.commitment();
        ElGamalEncryption enc = ElGamal.encryptWithOpening(auditor, BigInteger.valueOf(amount), 32, random);
        List<BigInteger> keyAndCiphertext = enc.statement().publicInputs(); // PK.u, PK.v, A.u, A.v, B.u, B.v
        var inputs = AuditedAmountCircuit.inputs()
                .commitU(c.affineU()).commitV(c.affineV())
                .auditorU(keyAndCiphertext.get(0)).auditorV(keyAndCiphertext.get(1))
                .handleU(keyAndCiphertext.get(2)).handleV(keyAndCiphertext.get(3))
                .blindedU(keyAndCiphertext.get(4)).blindedV(keyAndCiphertext.get(5))
                .amount(amount).blinding(opening.blinding()).randomness(enc.randomness());
        String proofJson = SnarkjsGroth16Json.proofJson(
                keys.prove(inputs.calculateWitness(circuit, CurveId.BLS12_381), r1cs.constraints()));
        byte[] ciphertextBytes = enc.ciphertext().encode();   // what goes on chain, 64 bytes

        // Auditor: admit the ciphertext only if the proof verifies for exactly
        // (this commitment, my key, this ciphertext, width 32), then decrypt it.
        RawElGamalCiphertext raw = RawElGamalCiphertext.decode(ciphertextBytes);
        ElGamalCiphertext admitted = ElGamal.admit(raw, auditor, 32, statement -> {
            List<BigInteger> pub = new ArrayList<>(List.of(c.affineU(), c.affineV()));
            pub.addAll(statement.publicInputs());
            return statement.width() == 32 && verify(vkJson, proofJson, pub);
        });
        System.out.println("Auditor decrypts: " + ElGamal.decryptWithSecret(admitted, auditorSecret, (1L << 32) - 1));

        // A cheating sender: commitment hides 250, ciphertext encrypts 1. No witness exists.
        ElGamalEncryption lie = ElGamal.encryptWithOpening(auditor, BigInteger.ONE, 32, random);
        List<BigInteger> liePub = lie.statement().publicInputs();
        try {
            inputs.handleU(liePub.get(2)).handleV(liePub.get(3)).blindedU(liePub.get(4)).blindedV(liePub.get(5))
                    .randomness(lie.randomness()).calculateWitness(circuit, CurveId.BLS12_381);
            System.out.println("Cheating witness accepted?!");
        } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
            System.out.println("Cheating sender: witness rejected (" + e.getMessage() + ")");
        }
    }

    static boolean verify(String vkJson, String proofJson, List<BigInteger> publicInputs) {
        var circuitId = AuditedAmountCircuit.circuitId();
        String publicJson = SnarkjsGroth16Json.publicJson(publicInputs.toArray(BigInteger[]::new));
        var envelope = SnarkjsJsonCodec.toEnvelopeFromJson(proofJson, vkJson, publicJson, circuitId);
        var material = VerificationMaterial.of(vkJson.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
                ProofSystemId.GROTH16, CurveId.BLS12_381, circuitId);
        return new Groth16BLS12381PureJavaVerifier().verify(envelope, material).proofValid();
    }
}
```

```text
Public inputs: [commitU, commitV, auditorU, auditorV, handleU, handleV, blindedU, blindedV]
Constraints: 8893
Auditor decrypts: 250
Cheating sender: witness rejected (Constraint violation: w30527=2541…7612 != w30513=1358…0935)
```

The cheating sender can't even produce a witness: no secret amount makes both the commitment and
the ciphertext check out. The circuit has 8,893 constraints. Production applications split a
64-bit amount into two 32-bit limbs and encrypt each, so the auditor can decrypt it; the
[confidential payroll](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-payroll/) and
[confidential points](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-points/) demos do exactly that, inside their
transfer and issue proofs.

### Bounds and decryption cost

Decryption recovers `m·G` and then searches for `m`. How far it can search decides what you can
encrypt:

- **Widths are 1 to 64 bits**, and a message must satisfy `0 ≤ m < 2^width`.
- **Bounds add up.** A sum of 1,000 ciphertexts of width 16 has a bound of about 65 million, even
  if the real total is small. Use the narrowest width that fits.
- **`maxPlaintext` must be at least the bound**, not just the value you expect, or `decrypt`
  refuses. If no value in range matches, it throws `ElGamalDecryptionException` instead of
  guessing.
- **The default table reaches about 2⁴³.** A width-64 ciphertext can be admitted and added, but
  not decrypted. Split amounts into 32-bit limbs.

| Operation (Apple M4 Max) | Time |
|---|---|
| Encrypt | 4.7 ms |
| Decryption share | 1.65 ms |
| Decode a ciphertext | 0.22 ms |
| Add, per ciphertext | 1.6 µs |
| Discrete log up to 2³²: build table / solve | 21 ms / 7–19 ms |
| Discrete log up to 2⁴⁰: build table / solve | 108 ms / 0.55–0.9 s |

Source: [ElGamal benchmark](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/elgamal-jubjub-2026-10-05.md).
These are measurements on one machine, not performance claims.

### Rules to follow

- **Verify every key you didn't make** with `VerifiedKeyShare.verify` and a real possession-proof
  check.
- **Admit every ciphertext you didn't make** with `ElGamal.admit` and a real encryption-proof
  check, for exactly that key and width.
- **Verify every decryption share you didn't make** with `VerifiedDecryptionShare.verify` and a
  DLEQ proof. An unchecked share lets a key holder choose the result.
- **Keep widths small** and decrypt only bounded values.
- **Run secret operations offline or isolated.** Encrypting, decryption shares and decrypting
  handle secrets with variable-time code.
- **The key holder can read everything encrypted to them.** If that's too much trust in one
  party, split the key: see [Threshold decryption](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/threshold-elgamal/).
- **Fixed randomness is test-only.** Never pass your own encryption randomness; the API draws it
  from `SecureRandom`.
- **A proof is not a permission.** Binding ciphertexts to transactions, replay and authorization
  are application rules. See [Application security](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/application-security/).

### Cost

| Circuit | Constraints |
|---|---|
| Encrypt to a fixed public key, width 1 / 16 / 64 | 6,558 / 6,650 / 6,938 |
| Encrypt to a key witnessed in the circuit | 12,105 |
| DLEQ (possession or decryption-share proof) | 6,546 |
| Commitment + ciphertext of the same 32-bit amount (example 4) | 8,893 |

A 64-byte ciphertext is two curve points. On Cardano, its four coordinates are public inputs of
an ordinary Groth16 proof; see [Verify proofs on Cardano](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/on-chain/).
