- [Threshold decryption](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/threshold-elgamal/): split the key among trustees
- [Confidential notes](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/confidential-notes/): deliver commitment openings
  on-chain
- [Encrypt for an auditor](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/encrypt-for-an-auditor/): the pattern, with use
  cases
- Use cases: [Sealed-bid auction](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/sealed-bid-auction/),
  [Confidential payroll](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-payroll/),
  [Private voting](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-voting/)

---

## Threshold decryption

Source: https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/threshold-elgamal/

> Split an ElGamal key among trustees so that no single party can decrypt, run the distributed key generation, deliver its private shares over a public board with HPKE, and decrypt only a total.

With [ElGamal encryption](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/elgamal/), whoever holds the secret key can read
every ciphertext. For an election, a sealed-bid market or a shared treasury, that's too much
trust in one party. **Threshold decryption** splits the key among `n` trustees so that:

- any `t + 1` of them can decrypt together;
- any `t` or fewer learn nothing, even if they collude;
- the full secret key **never exists anywhere**, not even during setup.

The trustees create the key together with a **distributed key generation** (DKG): each trustee
deals secret shares to the others and publishes commitments that let everyone check the shares,
so a cheating dealer is caught and excluded. Afterwards each trustee holds one share, and everyone
knows the joint public key that voters encrypt to.

ZeroJ implements the New-DKG protocol of Gennaro, Jarecki, Krawczyk and Rabin
([J. Cryptology 2007](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-006-0347-3)) as the profile
[`elgamal-jubjub-threshold-v1`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/specs/elgamal-jubjub-threshold-v1.md)
([ADR-0053](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/adr/0053-threshold-elgamal-jubjub-dkg.md)).
The private shares can travel over a public board, encrypted with HPKE (RFC 9180), following
[`dkg-share-delivery-hpke-v1`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/specs/dkg-share-delivery-hpke-v1.md)
([ADR-0054](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/adr/0054-hpke-dkg-share-delivery.md)).

### Status

| Area | Status |
|---|---|
| Threshold key generation and decryption (`DkgParticipant`, `ThresholdKeyContext`, `ElGamal.decrypt` with shares) | **Experimental**, pending review and external review |
| Encrypted share delivery over a board (`DkgShareDelivery`, `DkgShareDeliveryKeys`, `DkgKeyDirectory`) | **Experimental**. Assumption A1 (HPKE envelopes can stand in for private channels) and the delivery contract await external review. |
| Secret operations (dealing, decryption shares) | **Offline/isolated only**: variable-time arithmetic, no constant-time claim |

Everything is in `zeroj-circuit-lib`, the same dependency as the
[ElGamal guide](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/elgamal/#add-the-dependency).

### Choose t and n

`t` is the number of **corrupted trustees the scheme tolerates**, not the number needed to
decrypt. Decrypting needs `t + 1`. The protocol requires an honest majority, `2t + 1 ≤ n`, and
supports up to 64 trustees.

| `DkgConfig.create(t, n, …)` | Decrypting needs | Tolerates |
|---|---|---|
| `create(1, 3, …)` | any 2 of 3 | 1 corrupted trustee |
| `create(2, 5, …)` | any 3 of 5 | 2 |
| `create(3, 7, …)` | any 4 of 7 | 3 |

A 4-of-5 policy isn't possible: it would need `t = 3` with `n = 5`, which breaks the honest
majority. And remember the other side of the threshold: any `t + 1` trustees who collude can
decrypt **any single ciphertext**, not just the total.

### 1. Run the key generation and decrypt a tally

This program runs a 2-of-3 key generation in one process, encrypts five 0/1 votes to the joint
key, adds them, and has two trustees decrypt only the total. In a real deployment each trustee is
a separate, isolated machine, and the messages travel over your own channels.

```java title="ThresholdTally.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.DkgConfig;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.DkgMessage;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.DkgParticipant;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamal;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamalCiphertext;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ThresholdKeyContext;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ThresholdKeyShare;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.VerifiedDecryptionShare;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.SecureRandom;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * Three trustees run a threshold key generation (t = 1, n = 3: any 2 can decrypt), voters
 * encrypt 0/1 votes, the ciphertexts are added, and two trustees decrypt only the tally.
 * Everything runs in one process here; in reality each trustee is a separate, isolated host.
 */
public class ThresholdTally {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SecureRandom random = new SecureRandom();

        // 1. Configuration, agreed by everyone (e.g. published in an election manifest).
        //    t = faults tolerated; any t + 1 trustees decrypt; the rule is 2t + 1 <= n.
        List<byte[]> roster = List.of(          // each trustee's authentication key (demo bytes)
                "trustee-1-auth-key".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
                "trustee-2-auth-key".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
                "trustee-3-auth-key".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        DkgConfig config = DkgConfig.create(1, 3, roster,
                "demo-election-2026".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8), 1);

        // 2. Key generation: 7 rounds. Broadcasts go to everyone (sender included);
        //    SHARE messages go privately to one recipient.
        List<DkgParticipant> trustees = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int id = 1; id <= 3; id++) trustees.add(DkgParticipant.create(config, id, random));
        List<DkgMessage> outgoing = new ArrayList<>();
        for (DkgParticipant p : trustees) outgoing.addAll(p.start());
        for (int round = 1; round <= 7; round++) {
            for (DkgMessage m : outgoing) {
                for (DkgParticipant p : trustees) {
                    if (m.kind() != DkgMessage.Kind.SHARE) p.receiveBroadcast(m.sender(), m.encode());
                    else if (m.subject() == p.id()) p.receivePrivate(m.sender(), m.encode());
                }
            }
            outgoing = new ArrayList<>();
            for (DkgParticipant p : trustees) outgoing.addAll(p.closeRound()); // round deadline
        }
        List<ThresholdKeyShare> shares = new ArrayList<>();
        for (DkgParticipant p : trustees) shares.add(p.result());   // each trustee keeps its own
        ThresholdKeyContext election = shares.get(0).context();
        System.out.println("Threshold t = " + election.threshold() + ", qualified trustees " + election.qual());
        System.out.println("All trustees agree on the key: "
                + (election.equals(shares.get(1).context()) && election.equals(shares.get(2).context())));

        // 3. Voters encrypt 0 or 1 (width 1) under the joint key; the ciphertexts are added.
        int[] votes = {1, 0, 1, 1, 0};
        List<ElGamalCiphertext> ballots = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int vote : votes) ballots.add(ElGamal.encrypt(election, vote, 1, random));
        ElGamalCiphertext total = ElGamalCiphertext.sum(ballots);
        System.out.println("Encrypted tally bound: " + total.bound());

        // 4. Any t + 1 = 2 trustees publish decryption shares of the *total* only.
        List<VerifiedDecryptionShare> published = List.of(
                ElGamal.decryptionShare(shares.get(0), total),   // trustee 1
                ElGamal.decryptionShare(shares.get(2), total));  // trustee 3 (trustee 2 is away)
        long yes = ElGamal.decrypt(total, published, total.bound().longValueExact());
        System.out.println("Yes votes: " + yes + " of " + votes.length);

        // One share is not enough.
        try {
            ElGamal.decrypt(total, published.subList(0, 1), total.bound().longValueExact());
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Refused: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
```

```text
Threshold t = 1, qualified trustees [1, 2, 3]
All trustees agree on the key: true
Encrypted tally bound: 5
Yes votes: 3 of 5
Refused: threshold decryption needs at least t + 1 = 2 verified shares, got 1
```

The key generation is seven rounds. In each round every trustee processes what it received and
sends its next messages. `closeRound()` is the round deadline: whatever didn't arrive in time
counts as missing, which is how a silent trustee gets excluded instead of blocking everyone.
Two rules of the in-memory loop matter in real code too:

- **Every trustee also receives its own broadcasts**, and `SHARE` messages go only to their one
  recipient, through `receivePrivate`.
- **An abort is final.** Start a new attempt with a new `attempt` number in `DkgConfig.create`;
  never reuse one.

### 2. Deliver private shares over a public board (HPKE)

Each trustee's `SHARE` messages are secrets meant for one recipient. If you don't have private
channels between trustees, ZeroJ can encrypt them with HPKE (RFC 9180, Base mode, with X25519,
HKDF-SHA256 and ChaCha20-Poly1305) and post the encrypted **envelopes** on the same public board
as everything else. The order of posts is part of the security, so the API enforces round
barriers:

1. **Round 0: announce.** Each trustee generates fresh delivery keys for this attempt and posts the
   announcement (106 bytes). Once the round-0 window is final, every trustee builds the same
   `DkgKeyDirectory` from it.
2. **Round 1: envelopes first.** `DkgShareDelivery.start` replaces `start()`. Post the envelopes
   (223 bytes each, `n(n−1)` per attempt), and post the `COMMITMENTS` broadcasts only after the
   envelopes are final, or atomically with them.
3. **Close round 1 only through `closeRound1`**, passing the round-1 window after its cutoff
   **and** after it's final on the board. Plain `closeRound()` refuses round 1. The delivery keys
   are destroyed here.
4. **Rounds 2 to 7** are plain broadcasts, as in example 1.

This program runs the same 2-of-3 key generation as example 1, with every message on one board.
Posts are signed with each trustee's Ed25519 roster key, and the board doubles as the verifier
the API asks for. Its last step, letting an outsider admit the key, is in section 3.

```java title="EncryptedBoardDkg.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.AuthenticatedDkgMessage;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.DkgAdmissionVerifier;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.DkgConfig;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.DkgKeyDirectory;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.DkgMessage;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.DkgParticipant;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.DkgShareDelivery;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.DkgShareDeliveryKeys;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.DkgTranscript;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ThresholdKeyContext;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.GeneralSecurityException;
import java.security.KeyFactory;
import java.security.KeyPair;
import java.security.KeyPairGenerator;
import java.security.SecureRandom;
import java.security.Signature;
import java.security.spec.X509EncodedKeySpec;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.HexFormat;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * The same 2-of-3 key generation as ThresholdTally, but with no private channels: every message,
 * including each trustee's secret SHAREs (HPKE-encrypted), goes over one public board. Each post
 * is signed with the trustee's Ed25519 roster key. Afterwards an outsider (a voter) admits the
 * joint key from the board alone.
 */
public class EncryptedBoardDkg {

    /** An in-memory public board: posts per round window, each signed by its sender. */
    static final class Board implements DkgAdmissionVerifier {
        final List<List<AuthenticatedDkgMessage>> rounds = new ArrayList<>();
        final List<KeyPair> signers;

        Board(List<KeyPair> signers) {
            this.signers = signers;
            for (int r = 0; r <= 7; r++) rounds.add(new ArrayList<>());
        }

        void post(int round, int sender, byte[] message) throws GeneralSecurityException {
            Signature s = Signature.getInstance("Ed25519");
            s.initSign(signers.get(sender - 1).getPrivate());
            s.update(message);
            rounds.get(round).add(new AuthenticatedDkgMessage(message, s.sign()));
        }

        @Override  // authenticity: a valid Ed25519 signature under the sender's roster key
        public boolean authenticate(int sender, byte[] rosterKey, byte[] message, byte[] authenticator) {
            try {
                Signature s = Signature.getInstance("Ed25519");
                s.initVerify(KeyFactory.getInstance("Ed25519").generatePublic(new X509EncodedKeySpec(rosterKey)));
                s.update(message);
                return s.verify(authenticator);
            } catch (GeneralSecurityException | RuntimeException e) {
                return false;   // never throw on attacker-supplied input
            }
        }

        @Override  // closure: this board is the agreed, complete record of each round window
        public boolean roundClosed(DkgConfig config, int round, List<byte[]> messages, byte[] evidence) {
            List<byte[]> expected = DkgTranscript.deliveredRound(config, round, rounds.get(round), this);
            if (expected.size() != messages.size()) return false;
            for (int i = 0; i < expected.size(); i++) {
                if (!Arrays.equals(expected.get(i), messages.get(i))) return false;
            }
            return true;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws GeneralSecurityException {
        SecureRandom random = new SecureRandom();
        int n = 3;

        // Roster: each trustee's long-term Ed25519 public key (X.509-encoded).
        List<KeyPair> signers = new ArrayList<>();
        List<byte[]> roster = new ArrayList<>();
        KeyPairGenerator ed = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("Ed25519");
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            KeyPair kp = ed.generateKeyPair();
            signers.add(kp);
            roster.add(kp.getPublic().getEncoded());
        }
        DkgConfig config = DkgConfig.create(1, n, roster, "demo-election-2026".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8), 1);
        Board board = new Board(signers);

        List<DkgParticipant> trustees = new ArrayList<>();
        List<DkgShareDeliveryKeys> hpkeKeys = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            trustees.add(DkgParticipant.create(config, j, random));
            hpkeKeys.add(DkgShareDeliveryKeys.generate(config, j, random)); // fresh per attempt
        }

        // Round 0: each trustee announces its HPKE key. Once the window is final, everyone
        // builds the same directory from it.
        for (DkgShareDeliveryKeys k : hpkeKeys) board.post(0, k.id(), k.announcement());
        DkgKeyDirectory directory = DkgKeyDirectory.fromRound0(config, board.rounds.get(0), board);

        // Round 1: envelopes (encrypted SHAREs) first; COMMITMENTS only after the envelopes are final.
        List<DkgShareDelivery.SealedDealing> dealings = new ArrayList<>();
        for (DkgParticipant p : trustees) {
            DkgShareDelivery.SealedDealing d = DkgShareDelivery.start(p, directory, hpkeKeys.get(p.id() - 1), random);
            dealings.add(d);
            for (byte[] envelope : d.envelopes()) board.post(1, p.id(), envelope);  // one per other trustee
        }
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            for (DkgMessage m : dealings.get(j - 1).broadcasts()) board.post(1, j, m.encode());
        }
        // Barrier: after the round-1 window is final, each trustee processes all of it at once.
        List<DkgMessage> outgoing = new ArrayList<>();
        for (DkgParticipant p : trustees) {
            outgoing.addAll(DkgShareDelivery.closeRound1(p, directory, hpkeKeys.get(p.id() - 1),
                    board.rounds.get(1), board));
        }
        System.out.println("HPKE keys destroyed after round 1: "
                + hpkeKeys.stream().allMatch(DkgShareDeliveryKeys::isDestroyed));

        // Rounds 2-7: plain broadcasts, as without encryption.
        for (int round = 2; round <= 7; round++) {
            for (DkgMessage m : outgoing) {
                board.post(round, m.sender(), m.encode());
                for (DkgParticipant p : trustees) p.receiveBroadcast(m.sender(), m.encode());
            }
            outgoing = new ArrayList<>();
            for (DkgParticipant p : trustees) outgoing.addAll(p.closeRound());
        }
        ThresholdKeyContext trusteeView = trustees.get(0).result().context();

        // Section 3: an outsider admits the joint key from the board.
    }
}
```

Output of the full program (the joint key is random):

```text
HPKE keys destroyed after round 1: true
Board posts: 18
Voter's admitted key equals the trustees' key: true
Joint key: 325c41c481f9e3fc49d9cc400cb51928820fa74e4dff86dd8501e8e631b1522e
```

Two rules for your own board verifier: `authenticate` and `roundClosed` must **return `false`,
never throw**, on bad input; and `roundClosed` must only say `true` for the agreed, complete
record of that round. A `roundClosed` that always returns `true` defeats the protection.

HPKE here has no forward secrecy and isn't post-quantum: a delivery key that leaks before it is
destroyed exposes that trustee's shares.

### 3. Let outsiders admit the joint key

Voters, talliers and validators hold no secret, but they need to know that the joint key really
came out of an honest key generation. `ThresholdKeyContext.admit` replays the public record and
returns the same key context the trustees hold:

```java title="EncryptedBoardDkg.java (end of main)"

// A voter, who holds no secret, admits the key from the signed board (rounds 1-6 + confirmations).
List<AuthenticatedDkgMessage> transcript = new ArrayList<>();
for (int r = 1; r <= 6; r++) {
    for (byte[] m : DkgTranscript.deliveredRound(config, r, board.rounds.get(r), board)) {
        for (AuthenticatedDkgMessage post : board.rounds.get(r)) {
            if (Arrays.equals(post.message(), m)) { transcript.add(post); break; }
        }
    }
}
Map<Integer, byte[]> closureEvidence = new HashMap<>();
for (int r = 1; r <= 7; r++) closureEvidence.put(r, new byte[0]);   // our Board needs none
ThresholdKeyContext voterView = ThresholdKeyContext.admit(config, transcript, closureEvidence,
        board.rounds.get(7), board);
System.out.println("Board posts: " + board.rounds.stream().mapToInt(List::size).sum());
System.out.println("Voter's admitted key equals the trustees' key: " + voterView.equals(trusteeView));
System.out.println("Joint key: " + HexFormat.of().formatHex(voterView.jointKey().encode()));
```

`DkgTranscript.deliveredRound` filters each round down to the threshold protocol's own messages,
dropping the HPKE envelopes and announcements that share the board.

### Operating rules

The library enforces the protocol; it can't enforce how you run it. A deployment must:

- **Isolate trustees.** Each one runs on its own machine, under its own control.
- **Fix the configuration in advance.** `t`, `n`, the roster and the application context come from
  a trusted source, such as a published election manifest, never from the network mid-run.
- **Never reuse an `attempt` number** for the same context.
- **Deliver private shares on time.** A missed share triggers a complaint, and answering a
  complaint publishes that share. Timely private delivery is a precondition for secrecy.
- **Decrypt once.** Decrypt only the final total, after the deadline. Decrypting running totals
  and subtracting them reveals individual votes.
- **Verify every decryption share** you receive with `VerifiedDecryptionShare.verify` and a DLEQ
  proof. In example 1 the shares are "verified by construction" because one process made them; a
  separate tallier gets them as bytes.

### Sizes and timings

| Item | Size |
|---|---|
| Delivery key announcement | 106 bytes per trustee |
| Encrypted share envelope | 223 bytes, `n(n−1)` per attempt (about 0.9 MB at `n = 64`) |
| Joint key, key shares, decryption shares | 32 bytes each |

| Key generation, whole run in one process (Apple M4 Max) | Time |
|---|---|
| `t = 1, n = 3` | 62 ms |
| `t = 2, n = 5` | 176 ms |
| `t = 10, n = 21` | 4.5 s |

Key generation times are the plain-channel runs in the
[ElGamal benchmark](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/elgamal-jubjub-2026-10-05.md);
sizes are from the
[share delivery benchmark](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/dkg-share-delivery-hpke-2026-10-09.md),
which also times the HPKE-delivered runs. Network rounds, not computation, dominate a real ceremony.

### Next steps

- [Private voting](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-voting/): an encrypted tally decrypted by trustees
- [Split trust between several parties](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/split-trust/): the pattern, and
  when to use it
- [ElGamal encryption](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/elgamal/): keys, admission and proofs

## Confidential notes

Source: https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/confidential-notes/

> Put a Pedersen commitment on-chain together with its opening, encrypted separately for the owner and each auditor, then recover notes by scanning the chain with a viewing key.

A [Pedersen commitment](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/pedersen/) hides an amount, but whoever owns it needs
the **opening**, the amount and the blinding `(v, r)`, to spend it or prove anything about it later.
Sending that opening over a private channel is fragile: lose the message and the money is stuck.

A **confidential note** puts the opening on-chain too, encrypted separately for each reader. The
owner comes first, then any auditors. Each reader holds a **viewing key**: a key that can read
deliveries but can't spend anything. The rest of the world sees the commitment and a few
random-looking bytes per reader.

That gives you two things:

- **Recovery from the chain.** A wallet that knows only its viewing key can rebuild its balance by
  scanning the ledger. No side channel, no backup of every opening.
- **Chosen readers.** The owner and the named auditors can read the amount. Nobody else can.

ZeroJ's profile is [`confidential-note-jubjub-v1`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/specs/confidential-note-jubjub-v1.md),
designed in [ADR-0055](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/adr/0055-confidential-notes-jubjub.md).

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### Status

| Area | Status |
|---|---|
| Notes: seal, open, scan (`ConfidentialNotes`, `NoteScanner`, `NoteViewingKey`, `NoteReaderKey`, `NoteOpening`) | **Experimental**, pending review and external review |
| Secret operations (sealing, opening, viewing keys) | **Offline/isolated only**: variable-time arithmetic on secrets |
| Assumptions A1–A3 (see [below](#assumptions-in-plain-words)) | Unproved; external review is a production gate |

The delivery format is checked against all 10 Zcash Sapling note-encryption test vectors, an
independent Python reference written from the spec, BouncyCastle's personalized BLAKE2b and the
Wycheproof ChaCha20-Poly1305 vectors. It behaves identically in a GraalVM native image.

### How a delivery works

The construction follows Zcash Sapling's note encryption on the Jubjub curve:

1. For each reader, the sender picks a **fresh one-time key** `e` and publishes `E = e·G`.
2. Sender and reader agree on a shared secret from `e` and the reader's public **reader key**
   (Diffie–Hellman on Jubjub).
3. A BLAKE2b-256 key-derivation step, personalized with `ZeroJ_NoteKDF_v1`, turns that secret into
   a one-time encryption key.
4. ChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypts the 41-byte plaintext `0x01 ‖ v (8 bytes) ‖ r (32 bytes)` into a
   57-byte ciphertext. Because each key encrypts exactly one message, the fixed all-zero nonce is
   safe.

A delivery is `E ‖ ciphertext`, **89 bytes per reader**. A reader who decrypts it doesn't trust the
result blindly: it **accepts the opening only if `commit(v, r)` recomputes the note's commitment**.
A delivery that doesn't decrypt, or decrypts to a wrong opening, is rejected.

### 1. Create, deliver, open, scan

This program plays every party: an owner, an auditor and a stranger make viewing keys, a sender
creates a note for 250, and each reader tries to open it. It needs only `zeroj-circuit-lib`
(plus `zeroj-bom-core`); see [Pedersen commitments](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/pedersen/#add-the-dependency).

```java title="ConfidentialNoteDemo.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ConfidentialNotes;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.JubjubPoint;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.NoteOpening;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.NoteReaderKey;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.NoteScanner;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.NoteScanner.Candidate;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.NoteViewingKey;

import java.math.BigInteger;
import java.security.SecureRandom;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

/**
 * A confidential note: a Pedersen commitment to an amount, plus its opening (amount, blinding)
 * encrypted to each reader. The owner and an auditor can open it; nobody else can.
 */
public class ConfidentialNoteDemo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SecureRandom random = new SecureRandom();

        // 1. Each reader makes a viewing key in its own wallet and publishes the reader key.
        NoteViewingKey ownerKey = NoteViewingKey.generate(random);
        NoteViewingKey auditorKey = NoteViewingKey.generate(random);
        NoteViewingKey strangerKey = NoteViewingKey.generate(random);
        byte[] ownerPublished = ownerKey.readerKey().encode();       // 32 bytes
        byte[] auditorPublished = auditorKey.readerKey().encode();

        // 2. The sender validates the received reader keys, then creates the note:
        //    the commitment C goes in the datum, one 89-byte delivery per reader next to it.
        List<NoteReaderKey> readers = List.of(                         // order: owner, then auditors
                NoteReaderKey.decode(ownerPublished),
                NoteReaderKey.decode(auditorPublished));
        NoteOpening opening = NoteOpening.random(BigInteger.valueOf(250), random);
        JubjubPoint c = opening.commitment();
        BigInteger u = c.affineU();
        BigInteger v = c.affineV();
        List<byte[]> deliveries = ConfidentialNotes.seal(opening, readers, random);
        System.out.println("Deliveries: " + deliveries.size() + " x " + deliveries.get(0).length + " bytes");

        // 3. The owner opens the delivery at its position (0) against the note's (u, v).
        NoteScanner owner = NoteScanner.of(ownerKey);
        Optional<NoteOpening> mine = owner.open(deliveries.get(0), u, v);
        System.out.println("Owner reads amount: " + mine.map(NoteOpening::value).orElse(null));

        // 4. The auditor opens its own delivery (position 1).
        Optional<NoteOpening> audited = NoteScanner.of(auditorKey).open(deliveries.get(1), u, v);
        System.out.println("Auditor reads amount: " + audited.map(NoteOpening::value).orElse(null));

        // 5. Anyone else gets "not mine", for every delivery.
        NoteScanner stranger = NoteScanner.of(strangerKey);
        System.out.println("Stranger opens delivery 0? " + stranger.open(deliveries.get(0), u, v).isPresent());
        System.out.println("Stranger opens delivery 1? " + stranger.open(deliveries.get(1), u, v).isPresent());

        // 6. A wallet scans many notes at once. `ownedByMe` is the wallet's own owner check
        //    (e.g. the datum's owner credential). An owned note that does not open is value the
        //    wallet cannot spend: report it, never drop it silently.
        NoteOpening other = NoteOpening.random(BigInteger.valueOf(99), random);
        JubjubPoint c2 = other.commitment();
        byte[] badDelivery = ConfidentialNotes.seal(other, List.of(readers.get(1)), random).get(0); // not to the owner
        NoteScanner.Scan scan = owner.scan(List.of(
                Candidate.of(deliveries.get(0), u, v, true),
                Candidate.of(badDelivery, c2.affineU(), c2.affineV(), true)));
        System.out.println("Scan: opened " + scan.opened().size()
                + ", owned but unopenable at indices " + scan.unopenableOwned());
    }
}
```

```text
Deliveries: 2 x 89 bytes
Owner reads amount: 250
Auditor reads amount: 250
Stranger opens delivery 0? false
Stranger opens delivery 1? false
Scan: opened 1, owned but unopenable at indices [1]
```

A few details:

- **Readers are positional.** The application fixes the order (owner first, then auditors) and
  each reader opens only the delivery at its own position.
- **Open with the datum's coordinates.** `open` and `Candidate.of` take the commitment's affine
  `(u, v)` as `BigInteger`s, exactly as they appear in the note's datum.
- **`ownedByMe` is your check, not the library's.** The scanner can't know who owns a UTxO. Your
  wallet decides that from the datum's owner credential and the script address before it scans.

### Viewing keys

- **Generate in the wallet.** `NoteViewingKey.generate(new SecureRandom())` creates the secret; publish
  only `readerKey().encode()`, 32 bytes.
- **Back it up.** `exportSecret()` and `NoteViewingKey.restore(bytes)` move the key between devices.
  Call `destroy()` when you're done with an in-memory copy.
- **Verify keys you receive from a registry.** `NoteReaderKey.decode(bytes)` checks that the bytes
  are a valid key. When keys come from a public registry, use
  `NoteReaderKey.verified(bytes, verifier)` with a **proof of possession**, so nobody can register
  a key they don't control. The proof statement carries no context, so the registry itself must
  bind each key to its registrant.
- **A viewing key is only a viewing key.** It can't spend, sign or decrypt ElGamal ciphertexts. An
  auditor that also receives [ElGamal-encrypted amounts](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/elgamal/) has a
  separate ElGamal key.
- **No forward secrecy.** A leaked viewing key reads every past delivery addressed to it.

### What a delivery does and doesn't guarantee

**A validator can only check the length.** Plutus has no Jubjub operations, so an on-chain
validator can require "an 89-byte delivery for each reader" but can't check that it decrypts. A
careless or hostile sender can fill a delivery with random bytes. The owner's wallet then finds a
note it owns but can't open. It must **report** that note as unopenable, never drop it silently,
because it's value the owner can't spend.

**Delivery alone doesn't make the sender honest with the auditor.** The sender writes the
auditor's delivery too, and could put a different (valid-looking) opening there. When the auditor's
view must be *enforced*, add the amount a second time as ElGamal ciphertext to the auditor's
key, and prove inside the transfer's Groth16 proof that it matches the commitment. ADR-0055 calls
this **D3a**:

- the amount is split into two 32-bit **limbs**, so the auditor can decrypt each one quickly;
- each limb is ElGamal-encrypted to the auditor's separate key;
- the transfer circuit proves `limb0 + 2³²·limb1` is the committed amount and that both
  ciphertexts are correct.

D3a is **not a library API**. It's a pattern, with a test-only reference validator
([`AuditedConfidentialNoteValidator`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/zeroj-integration-tests/src/test/java/org/zeroj/examples/notes/onchain/AuditedConfidentialNoteValidator.java)
and [`AuditedConfidentialNoteOnChainTest`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/zeroj-integration-tests/src/test/java/org/zeroj/examples/notes/AuditedConfidentialNoteOnChainTest.java)).
In ZeroJ's test validator, a two-output transfer with one auditor measured 34,184 constraints and
73.4% of the per-transaction step limit in the JuLC VM, before the verifier savings in ZeroJ PRs
#85 and #86. A real ledger script does more work: the points demo's transfer, on the same circuit,
used 75.8% on Yaci DevKit. It covers only notes created by
proof-checked transitions such as transfers. Newly **issued** notes carry whatever audit data the
issuer supplied, unless issuance is proved too, as in
[confidential payroll](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-payroll/).

### Wallet rules

- **Open only your own position**, and only notes your owner check selected.
- **Check the owner credential and the script address yourself**, so a copied note can't pass as
  one of yours.
- **Report unopenable owned notes**; never drop them.
- **Scan only in the user's own wallet process**, never as a shared or network service: a scanner
  holds the viewing key and learns every amount.
- **Run sealing and opening offline or isolated.** They use variable-time arithmetic on secrets.

### Assumptions in plain words

The construction reuses Sapling's components, but ZeroJ's use of them has not been externally
reviewed. Three assumptions carry the security, and all three are open:

- **A1, confidentiality.** A delivery reveals nothing about the amount to anyone without the
  reader's viewing key.
- **A2, integrity.** An opening a reader accepts really opens the note's commitment, and a sender
  can't make two readers accept different openings of the same note. This rests on the
  commitment being binding.
- **A3, no useful multi-key partitioning.** A delivery is accepted under at most one reader key,
  whatever its contents, except with negligible probability. ChaCha20-Poly1305 isn't
  key-committing, so this doesn't follow from the cipher alone. If two keys accepted different
  openings, A2 would be broken; the case where two keys accept the *same* opening rests on ZeroJ's
  own argument about the key derivation. A3 is unproved, and that argument hasn't been reviewed.

### Sizes and timings

| Item | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Delivery | 89 bytes per reader (32-byte `E` + 57-byte ciphertext) | spec |
| Reader key | 32 bytes | spec |
| Extra minimum ADA, owner + one auditor | about 0.8 ADA (estimate) | ADR-0055 |
| Seal for 2 readers | about 5.6 ms | [benchmark](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/confidential-note-jubjub-2026-10-09.md) |
| Accept a delivery (decrypt + recompute C) | about 5 ms | benchmark |
| Reject a delivery that isn't yours | about 1.7 ms | benchmark |
| Scan, one thread, every delivery rejected | about 660 deliveries per second (accepting one costs more; threads scale sublinearly) | benchmark |

Timings are from one Apple M4 Max laptop and are only a rough guide.

- Use cases: [Confidential loyalty points](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-points/),
  [Confidential payroll](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-payroll/),
  [Proof of solvency with hidden balances](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-solvency/)
- [Share a value with chosen readers](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/share-with-chosen-readers/): when to use notes
- [ElGamal encryption](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/elgamal/) and [Pedersen commitments](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/pedersen/)

## Use cases

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/overview/

> What zero-knowledge proofs, commitments and encryption unlock on Cardano — worked use cases, Web2 record integration, the building blocks behind each, and runnable demos.

A zero-knowledge proof lets you prove a fact without revealing the data behind it. "I'm over 18"
without a birth date. "I'm on the voter list" without saying which voter. "Our reserves cover every
deposit" without publishing a single balance. A Cardano validator can check that kind of proof in
one transaction. The secret inputs never leave the prover's machine.

This section walks through what that makes possible. Each page explains the real-world problem, the
statement being proven, what stays private, how the proof reaches the chain, and the security
questions you still have to answer. Most pages also link a runnable demo.

> **Caution: Research software**
>
> ZeroJ is experimental and has not been externally audited. The demos run against a local
> [Yaci DevKit](https://github.com/bloxbean/yaci-devkit) devnet with development-only trusted setups.
> Treat them as blueprints to learn from, not as systems for real identities, votes or funds. See
> [Status & maturity](https://zeroj.dev/start/status/).

> **Note: The demos were hardened**
>
> The original demos were reviewed for published values that can be guessed, values that link
> users, and missing on-chain bindings, and then fixed: salted leaves, random issuer and voter keys,
> vouchers that pay exactly what they owe. Each page describes the demo as it now behaves and what
> remains. The demo servers hold users' keys, so privacy is claimed against chain and mempool
> observers, not the demo server. See
> [zeroj-usecases ADR-0009](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/blob/main/docs/adr/0009-privacy-and-binding-hardening-of-the-original-demos.md).

### Identity & compliance

  - [Age & KYC eligibility](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/age-and-kyc/): Prove you're old enough and live in an approved country, using an issuer-signed credential, without revealing either value.
  - [Selective disclosure & reusable KYC](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/selective-disclosure/): Do KYC once, then show each service only the attributes or predicates it needs, with Groth16 predicates or BBS verified on-chain.

### DeFi & finance

  - [Proof of reserves](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/proof-of-reserves/): A custodian proves reserves cover all customer balances without publishing any balance.
  - [Private token transfers](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-payments/): A design walkthrough of a shielded pool: deposit, then withdraw to a fresh address that can't be linked to the deposit.

### Confidential values

Balances, salaries and bids kept private on a public ledger, with Pedersen commitments, ElGamal
encryption and confidential notes. These demos are new in ZeroJ 0.1.0-pre13 and all run in one
app, `pedersen-commitments`, with a tab per use case.

  - [Confidential payroll](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-payroll/): Pay salaries privately on-chain; the tax authority reads every one, and the employer can't under-report.
  - [Sealed-bid auction](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/sealed-bid-auction/): Bids are encrypted to the auctioneer with a proof; the earliest highest bid wins and losing bids are never published (only bounded by the price).
  - [Confidential loyalty points](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-points/): Points move privately between customers; holders recover balances from the chain and an auditor reads every amount.
  - [Proof of solvency with hidden balances](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-solvency/): An exchange proves hidden customer balances are covered by locked reserves; each customer checks their own entry.

### Governance & communities

  - [Private voting](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-voting/): An eligible member votes exactly once, nobody can tell which member cast which ballot, and an encrypted tally keeps choices secret.
  - [One claim per person](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/sybil-resistant-airdrop/): A Sybil-resistant airdrop: a personhood credential claims once per epoch, and the payout is bound to a recipient.

### Ownership & assets

  - [Private NFT ownership](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/nft-ownership/): Prove you hold an NFT from a collection for token-gated access without revealing your wallet.
  - [Prove you own a Cardano account](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/account-recovery/): Prove you know the root key behind an address, without revealing the seed, so a refund can reach the real owner after a hack.

### Supply chain

  - [Digital product passport](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/digital-product-passport/): Prove a product meets carbon, recycled-content and origin rules without exposing supplier data.

### Existing Web2 records

  - [Private proofs for SHA-2 records](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/sha2-web2/): Keep existing SHA-256/SHA-512 digests: explore documents, selective disclosure, eligibility, voting, private state and audits. Includes a runnable approval-record tutorial.

### Pick the right tool

Almost every use case is built from a small set of patterns. Start from what you need to prove:

| You need to… | Approach | ZeroJ building blocks |
|---|---|---|
| Prove a predicate over a hidden value (age ≥ 18, carbon ≤ 50 kg, reserves ≥ liabilities) | Groth16 circuit | `ZkUInt` with `@UInt(bits = …)` and `gte` / `lte` comparisons |
| Prove a fact about a record committed by an existing SHA-2 digest | SHA-2 and policy constraints, plus issuer/registry trust | `Sha256` / `Sha512`, `ZkSha256` / `ZkSha512`; bind the full digest |
| Reveal some issuer-signed attributes and hide the rest | BBS selective disclosure (no circuit, no trusted setup) | `BbsService` in `zeroj-bbs`; `BbsProofVerify` for on-chain checks |
| Prove you're in a set without saying which member | Merkle tree + Poseidon | `ZkMerkle.verifyProofPoseidon` with `PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3.INSTANCE` |
| Allow one action per person, credential or NFT | Nullifier | `ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3.INSTANCE, secret, contextId)`, stored on-chain (sorted list, spent UTxO) |
| Rely on a fact someone else attested | Issuer signature checked inside the circuit | `ZkEdDSAJubjub.verifyWithRegisteredKey` |
| Stop a copied proof from paying someone else | Bind the recipient or the spent UTxO into the public inputs | recipient public input; a spend reference computed from `ScriptContext` in your validator |
| Keep a number private on-chain, but check, add up or open it later | Pedersen commitment + Groth16 | `PedersenCommitment`, `ZkPedersen.commit`, `ZkPedersen.assertBalanced` |
| Let the owner and an auditor read a hidden amount from the chain | Confidential note | `ConfidentialNotes.seal`, `NoteScanner` |
| Let an authority read a value, with no way for the sender to lie | ElGamal encryption + a proof | `ElGamal.encryptWithOpening`, `ZkElGamal.encrypt` |
| Reveal only a total, and only when a quorum agrees | Threshold ElGamal | `DkgParticipant`, `ElGamal.decryptionShare`, `ElGamal.decrypt` |
| Prove facts about large private state (millions of entries) | Poseidon MPF / JMT (**experimental**) | `zeroj-mpf-poseidon`, `zeroj-jmt-poseidon` |

Not sure whether to reveal, prove, commit or encrypt? [Choose how to disclose](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/)
compares the options on one example. Groth16 on BLS12-381 is the default proof system for the circuit-based patterns above. Where a circuit uses Poseidon, pass
explicit BLS12-381 parameters. For the concepts behind these patterns, read
[Circuits, constraints & witnesses](https://zeroj.dev/learn/circuits-and-witnesses/) and
[ZK on Cardano](https://zeroj.dev/learn/zk-on-cardano/).

> **Note: A proof is not a permission slip**
>
> A valid proof only shows that the math checks out. Every validator in these use cases also has to
> bind the proof to its `ScriptContext` (who gets paid, which UTxO is spent), prevent replay and
> enforce its own business rules. [Application security](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/application-security/)
> covers this in depth.

### Run the demos

The [zeroj-usecases](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases) repository has complete Spring Boot
apps for most pages here. Each one covers the circuit, proof generation, a Cardano transaction and
on-chain verification, with a small web UI.

You need Docker (with Compose v2) and a Yaci DevKit devnet running on your machine:

```bash
# 1. Start a local Cardano devnet (outside the demos repo)
devkit start
# then, at the yaci-cli prompt:
#   create-node -o --start

# 2. Run a demo end to end
git clone https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases
cd zeroj-usecases
./demo.sh proof-of-reserves --run

# 3. Stop it (Yaci keeps running)
./demo.sh proof-of-reserves --stop
```

`demo.sh` tops up a devnet-only demo wallet, starts the app, opens its UI and, with `--run`, runs
the happy path. The demo names are `proof-of-reserves`, `identity-kyc`, `nft-ownership`, `voting`,
`airdrop`, `dpp`, `selective-disclosure`, `reusable-kyc` and `pedersen` (the confidential-values app:
payroll, auction, points, credit gate and solvency tabs). The account-ownership demo ships
separately as a desktop app and CLI; see [its page](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/account-recovery/#try-it).

The demos use a single-party development trusted setup (they run with
`-Dzeroj.allowInsecureTrustedSetup=true`, and cached setup files are generated the same way). Real
deployments need keys from a multi-party ceremony; see
[Trusted setup, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/trusted-setup/).

### Ideas to explore

These ideas are **not implemented as demos**. They show how the same building blocks carry over to
new problems.

- **Private credit score for lending.** A borrower proves "score ≥ 700" from a credit bureau's
  signed credential. That needs an in-circuit issuer signature (`ZkEdDSAJubjub`), a `ZkUInt.gte`
  range check and a public input bound to the loan UTxO. BBS is an option if revealing a score band
  is acceptable. The pedersen-commitments demo's credit gate does the committed-credential version;
  see [Prove a rule](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/prove-a-rule/#over-a-committed-credential).
- **Anonymous feedback and whistleblowing.** An employee proves membership in a Merkle tree of staff
  keys and publishes one nullifier per topic. The report's hash is bound as a public input, so
  every report is from a real member and nobody can flood a topic. The shape is the
  [private voting](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-voting/) circuit.
- **Treasury grants within a budget.** A DAO commits to each private grant, proves each one falls
  within an approved band, and proves the committed total stays under the treasury balance, with
  `ZkPedersen.assertBalanced`. Delivering each grant to its recipient and an auditor is the
  [confidential payroll](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-payroll/) pattern.

### Next steps

- New to ZK? Start with [Zero-knowledge in plain English](https://zeroj.dev/learn/zero-knowledge-basics/).
- Build the core patterns yourself: [Prove you're over 18](https://zeroj.dev/tutorials/age-check/) and
  [Private allowlist with a Merkle tree](https://zeroj.dev/tutorials/private-allowlist/).
- Take a proof on-chain: [Verify your proof on Cardano](https://zeroj.dev/tutorials/verify-on-cardano/).

## Private voting

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-voting/

> Let each eligible member vote exactly once, keep every choice secret, and publish only the total, using Merkle membership, nullifiers, ElGamal-encrypted ballots and Groth16 on Cardano.

DAOs, community treasuries and project councils increasingly vote on-chain, and on a public ledger
every ballot is tied to an address. That invites vote buying ("show me your transaction and I'll
pay you"), social pressure from peers and employers, and whales watching the count before they
decide. What you want is a vote where eligibility and one-person-one-vote can be checked by
anyone, but nobody can tell who voted for what, and only the final result is ever revealed.

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### The zero-knowledge idea

**The voter proves "I'm on the eligible-voter list, this is my one nullifier for this election,
and this encrypted ballot holds a 0 or a 1", without revealing who they are or how they voted.**

Four pieces make this work:

- **Voter list.** Each voter's public key is `Poseidon(secretKey, 0)`. The organizer puts all public
  keys into a Merkle tree and publishes only the root.
- **Nullifier.** `Poseidon(secretKey, electionId)`. It's deterministic, so the same voter in the same
  election always produces the same value, and a second vote is caught. A different `electionId`
  gives an unrelated nullifier, so a voter's ballots can't be linked across elections.
- **Encrypted ballot.** The vote, encrypted with exponential **ElGamal** to an **election key** that
  three trustees hold together. Nobody can open a single ballot, but ballots can be **added up while
  still encrypted**.
- **Tally.** After voting closes, the trustees decrypt only the **total**, once, and prove they did
  it honestly.

The circuit ties the first three to one secret key. A voter who switches keys to get a fresh
nullifier isn't in the tree, and a voter who keeps their key gets the same nullifier again.

If ElGamal is new to you, [Commitments & encryption, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/commitments-and-encryption/)
introduces it with an interactive lockbox.

### Why not just hash the vote?

A hash looks like a natural way to hide a vote: publish `Poseidon(vote, nullifier)` and nobody can
undo the hash. The first version of this demo did exactly that, and it doesn't work. **The
nullifier is public and a vote is only 0 or 1, so anyone can hash both choices and see which one
matches.** Hiding a value with a hash only works when there are far too many possible values to
try. A yes/no vote, an age or a small amount can always be guessed this way.

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

| Ballot | Can an observer read one vote? | Can the votes be counted? |
|---|---|---|
| `Poseidon(vote, nullifier)` | Yes: hash 0 and 1 and compare | Yes, by reading every vote, which is the problem |
| `Poseidon(vote, nullifier, salt)` | No, the salt is secret | Only after every voter reveals their salt, and with it their vote |
| ElGamal ciphertext `(A, B)` | No: fresh randomness, and only the trustees together hold the key | Yes: ciphertexts add up, and only the total is decrypted |

A secret random salt stops the guessing, but then nobody can count the votes without every voter
coming back to reveal their salt, which reveals their vote at the end. Encryption solves both
problems at once: each ballot uses fresh randomness, so it can't be matched by guessing, and
ElGamal ciphertexts can be added, so the total can be decrypted without opening any ballot. The
hash version was reported as [issue #7](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/issues/7) and
replaced with the encrypted ballot described on this page
([ADR-0005](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/blob/main/docs/adr/0005-private-ballot-homomorphic-tally.md)).

### What stays private, what's public

| Input | Visibility | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `secretKey` | Secret | The voter's identity; it derives both the public key and the nullifier |
| Merkle path (`siblings`, `pathBits`) | Secret | The path would reveal the voter's position in the list |
| `vote` | Secret | Inside the ciphertext; the proof limits it to 0 or 1 |
| `randomness` (252 bits) | Secret | Fresh for every ballot; it's what makes two ballots for the same choice look unrelated |
| `electionId`, `voterRoot` | Public | The election and its list of eligible voters, fixed in the on-chain script |
| Election key `PK` (`PK.u`, `PK.v`) | Public | The trustees' combined key, also fixed in the script |
| `nullifier` | Public | Recorded on-chain to block a second vote |
| Ballot `(A, B)` (`A.u`, `A.v`, `B.u`, `B.v`) | Public | The encrypted vote; it reveals nothing without the trustees |

### How it works

1. **Trustee keys.** Each of the three trustees generates a key pair and publishes its public key
   with a zero-knowledge *proof of possession* (a DLEQ proof that it knows the matching secret).
   Without that proof, a dishonest trustee could choose its key to cancel the others' and read
   every ballot alone. The election key is the sum of the three public keys.
2. **Register.** The organizer collects each voter's public key `Poseidon(secretKey, 0)`, builds
   the Merkle tree and publishes `voterRoot`. The election ID, the root, the election key and the
   voting deadline become parameters of the on-chain scripts.
3. **Encrypt and prove.** The voter encrypts their vote `v` with fresh randomness `k`:
   `A = [k]·G`, `B = [v]·G + [k]·PK`. A Groth16 proof, made with ZeroJ's pure-Java prover, shows
   that the voter is on the list, that the nullifier is theirs, and that `(A, B)` encrypts a 0 or
   a 1 under `PK`. A ballot that tries to count twice (`v = 2`) has no valid proof. In a real
   deployment this runs on the voter's own device; the demo proves server-side for convenience.
4. **Submit.** A transaction mints one token whose name is the nullifier and creates a list node
   that holds the ballot. The minting policy verifies the proof on-chain before the deadline, and
   the nullifier is inserted into an on-chain sorted list.
5. **Reject repeats.** A second vote from the same key has the same nullifier. The list already
   contains it, so the insert fails.
6. **Add up.** Anyone can add the ballots: `(ΣA, ΣB)` is an encryption of the number of YES votes.
7. **Decryption shares.** After the deadline, each trustee publishes `D_j = [sk_j]·ΣA` together with
   a DLEQ proof that it used the same secret as its registered key. A wrong share fails its proof.
8. **Count.** `ΣB − (D₁ + D₂ + D₃) = [YES]·G`. The number of YES votes is small, so a short search
   recovers it. Anyone can repeat every check from chain data and the published election manifest.

```text
voter (off-chain)                              Cardano
─────────────────                              ───────
secretKey, Merkle path,                        tx: redeemer = proof; new list node = (nullifier, A, B)
vote, randomness  ──encrypt + prove──▶          ├─ minting policy: Groth16 check, deadline, mint 1 token named <nullifier>
                                                └─ list validator: insert <nullifier> between sorted neighbours
after the deadline: anyone adds the ballots ─▶ trustees post verified shares ─▶ YES count
```

The trustees decrypt the total exactly once, after the deadline. Decrypting a running total twice
would let anyone subtract the two results and learn the votes cast in between.

### Counting without opening a ballot

Step through the tally. Switch to **Public view** to see what an observer gets: encrypted ballots,
nullifiers, the trustees' shares, and the total.

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### The ballot circuit

Lightly simplified from the demo's `PrivateBallotProof`: constructor validation is trimmed.
`ZkElGamal.encrypt` is ZeroJ's `elgamal-jubjub-v1` encryption relation, so the demo doesn't
implement any ElGamal itself.

```java title="PrivateBallotProof.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.*;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParams;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkElGamal;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkElGamalPublicKey;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkMerkle;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPoseidon;

@ZKCircuit(name = "private-ballot",
           nameTemplate = "private-ballot-d{treeDepth}-jubjub-elgamal", version = 3)
public class PrivateBallotProof {
    private static final PoseidonParams POSEIDON = PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3.INSTANCE;

    public PrivateBallotProof(@CircuitParam("treeDepth") int treeDepth) {}

    @Prove
    void prove(ZkContext zk,
               @Public ZkField electionId,
               @Public ZkField voterRoot,
               @Public ZkField electionKeyU, @Public ZkField electionKeyV,   // PK
               @Public ZkField nullifier,
               @Public ZkField handleU, @Public ZkField handleV,           // A
               @Public ZkField ballotU, @Public ZkField ballotV,           // B
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 1) ZkUInt vote,                        // 0 or 1
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt randomness,
               @Secret ZkField secretKey,
               @Secret @FixedSize(param = "treeDepth") ZkArray<ZkField> siblings,
               @Secret @FixedSize(param = "treeDepth") ZkArray<ZkBool> pathBits) {

        // Eligibility, and one nullifier per voter and election.
        ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, POSEIDON, secretKey, electionId).assertEqual(nullifier);
        var voterKey = ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, POSEIDON, secretKey, zk.constant(0));
        ZkMerkle.verifyProofPoseidon(zk, POSEIDON, voterKey, voterRoot, siblings, pathBits);

        // The ballot: an encryption of a 1-bit vote under the election key.
        var electionKey = ZkElGamalPublicKey.fromVerifierFixedPublic(zk, electionKeyU, electionKeyV);
        ZkElGamal.encrypt(zk, vote, randomness, electionKey)
                .assertAffineEquals(zk, handleU, handleV, ballotU, ballotV);
    }
}
```

The `@UInt(bits = 1)` on `vote` is what limits a ballot to 0 or 1. The circuit has 9,477
constraints at tree depth 10. The annotation processor generates a `PrivateBallotProofCircuit`
companion that you compile to R1CS and prove with Groth16. Before you trust a circuit like this,
test it with invalid witnesses: a key that isn't in the tree, a nullifier from another election, a
vote of 2, a ballot encrypted to another key. It should reject every one. See
[Testing circuits](https://zeroj.dev/guides/circuits/testing-circuits/).

### On Cardano

The demo uses two Plutus V3 scripts written in Java with JuLC:

- **`VoteZkMintingPolicy`** verifies the ballot proof with `Groth16BLS12381Lib.verify(...)` from
  `zeroj-onchain-julc`. The redeemer carries only the proof. Every one of the nine public inputs
  comes from the script's parameters (`electionId`, `voterRoot`, the election key, and the
  verification key) or from the ledger: the nullifier is the name of the single token minted, and
  the ballot is read from the inline datum of the list node that receives it. The transaction must
  also be valid only up to the voting deadline.
- **`VoteListValidator`** keeps nullifiers in a **sorted linked list**, one UTxO per nullifier, each
  holding its ballot. Inserting between two neighbours proves the new nullifier wasn't there
  before. Votes that land in different parts of the list touch different UTxOs, so they don't
  contend. Each node locks about 2 ADA.

A valid proof is not authorization, which is why the election's values are script parameters and
not redeemer fields: otherwise a voter could prove membership in a tree they built themselves, or
encrypt to a key they hold. See [On-chain verification](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/on-chain/).

### Counting the votes in code

Off-chain, the tally uses ZeroJ's ElGamal API. Simplified from the demo's `TallyService`, with one
trustee's secret shown for brevity (each trustee computes its own share on its own machine):

```java title="Tally (simplified)"
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamal;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamalCiphertext;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.ElGamalPublicKey;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.VerifiedDecryptionShare;

import java.util.List;

// `ballots`: every ballot in the vote list, admitted under the election's key context
ElGamalCiphertext total = ElGamalCiphertext.sum(ballots);

// Trustee j, on its own machine: its share of the decryption, D_j = [sk_j]·ΣA
VerifiedDecryptionShare own = ElGamal.decryptionShare(trusteeSecret, total);
byte[] published1 = own.encode();  // posted with a DLEQ proof of own.statement()

// Anyone: accept each published share only if its proof verifies (repeat for every trustee)
VerifiedDecryptionShare share1 = VerifiedDecryptionShare.verify(total, trusteeKey1, published1,
        statement -> verifyDleqProof(proof1, statement.publicInputs()));
// ... share2 and share3 the same way, then decrypt the total
long yes = ElGamal.decrypt(total, List.of(share1, share2, share3), total.bound().longValueExact());
```

`ElGamal.decrypt` accepts only shares that went through `VerifiedDecryptionShare.verify`, and the
total's bound is the number of ballots, so the final search is tiny. See the
[ElGamal guide](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/elgamal/) for the full API.

### Limits

- **Every trustee is needed, and all of them together could read any ballot.** The demo's key is
  *n-of-n*: if one trustee disappears, nothing can be decrypted, and the three together could
  decrypt a single ballot instead of the total. ZeroJ's
  [threshold ElGamal with a distributed key generation](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/threshold-elgamal/) is
  the *t-of-n* alternative: any `t + 1` trustees can decrypt, and fewer learn nothing. The demo
  doesn't use it yet.
- **The demo server knows every vote.** For convenience it holds every voter's and trustee's secret
  and proves on their behalf. In a real election each voter proves on their own device and each
  trustee keeps its own key.
- **Demo voter keys are random and kept.** The test voters' secret keys come from `SecureRandom`
  and are stored, owner-only, in the demo's data directory. Earlier versions used small fixed
  numbers (`10000 + i`), so anyone could compute each voter's nullifier, match ballots to
  voters, or vote for a voter who hadn't voted yet. Voting "as Alice" by label in the demo is the operator acting for that voter, not the
  voter signing in.
- **Small or unanimous results reveal votes.** If all three ballots are YES, everyone knows how each
  voter voted. The total is always public.
- **The vote list is public.** Anyone can see how many ballots were cast and when.

### Security considerations

- **The voter list is a trust point.** Whoever builds the tree decides who can vote. Publish the
  leaves so members can check their inclusion and spot keys that shouldn't be there.
- **Check the trustees' key proofs.** The election key is only as good as the possession proofs
  behind it; the manifest publishes every key with its proof so anyone can rebuild it.
- **Watch transaction-level metadata.** In the demo a service wallet submits and pays for every
  vote. If voters pay fees from their own wallets, the fee input links them to their ballot. Use a
  relayer and be mindful of timing.
- **No receipt-freeness or coercion resistance.** A voter can prove to a vote buyer how they voted
  by handing over the randomness `k`, or hand over their secret key entirely. Anti-collusion
  designs such as MACI address this. This demo doesn't.
- **Key theft is vote theft.** Anyone who learns a voter's secret key can vote in their place.
- **Trusted setup.** The demo uses a single-party development setup for both its circuits. A real
  election needs keys from a multi-party ceremony ([Trusted setup, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/trusted-setup/)).

### Try it

The demo lives in
[`private-voting`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/private-voting). With Yaci
DevKit running (see [Run the demos](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/overview/#run-the-demos)):

```bash
./demo.sh voting --run
```

At startup the app creates an election with five funded test voters and three trustees, and opens
voting for 10 minutes. With `--run`, `voter1` votes yes and `voter2` votes no. Each ballot is
encrypted and proven in pure Java and verified on-chain. To see double-vote protection, vote again
as `voter1` from the UI, or run:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8086/api/vote \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"voterLabel":"voter1","vote":0}'
```

The second vote is rejected because `voter1`'s nullifier is already in the on-chain list. Cast a
third vote (`voter3` yes) and fetch the tally:

```bash
curl http://localhost:8086/api/results
```

Before the deadline it shows only the encrypted sum. After it, the trustees' shares are posted and
checked, and the result is `yes: 2, no: 1, total: 3, verified: true`, with the list of checks
performed. `GET /api/election/manifest` returns everything needed to re-check the scripts and the
tally yourself.

Design notes:
[Private voting — detailed design](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/usecases/private-voting.md)
(nullifier registries compared, batch rollups, Hydra, MACI).

  nullifier yourself, step by step
- [One claim per person](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/sybil-resistant-airdrop/): the same nullifier idea with a
  personhood credential
- [Application security](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/application-security/): what the validator must check
  beyond the proof

  ciphertext is and why ciphertexts add up

  able to decrypt

## Proof of reserves

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/proof-of-reserves/

> A custodian proves its reserves cover every customer balance without publishing any balance, and each customer can check they were counted.

When an exchange or custodian fails, customers find out too late that the money wasn't there. The
usual remedies are weak. An auditor's report asks you to trust the auditor. Publishing every
account balance destroys customer privacy. A plain Merkle proof lets you see your neighbours'
balances. Stablecoin issuers, bridges, lending protocols and DAO treasuries face the same question:
*can you prove you're solvent without opening your books?*

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### The zero-knowledge idea

**The custodian proves "the balances committed in this published liabilities root are all
non-negative, add up to exactly this total, and that total is covered by our reserves", without
revealing any balance.**

Each customer account becomes a leaf in a Merkle tree, and the root is published. The circuit
rebuilds the whole tree from the private balances, so the root commits to exactly the numbers being
summed. The custodian can't sum one set of balances and publish another. Every balance is a 64-bit
unsigned integer, and range checks rule out a negative "balance" that would quietly shrink the
total.

Customers close the loop. Each gets the Merkle path for their own leaf, recomputes the root, and
compares it with the attestation on the chain. If the custodian left someone out or understated a
balance, that customer can tell.

> **Caution: Reserves are claimed, not proven**
>
> In this design `totalReserves` is a public input the custodian supplies. The circuit proves
> liabilities ≤ that number. It does not prove the custodian controls the funds. On Cardano you can
> check reserves held at known addresses directly; off-chain reserves need an attestation or oracle
> you trust.

#### Why the leaves are salted

A customer's Merkle path contains other customers' leaves: the sibling next to their own leaf is a
neighbour's. If a leaf were just `Poseidon(accountId, balance)`, a customer who can guess the
neighbour's id could hash every plausible balance until one matched the sibling, and so learn the
neighbour's balance. The demo's leaves used to work that way.

Now every account gets a fresh 252-bit salt in every snapshot, and the leaf is

```text
leaf = Poseidon(Poseidon(idTag, salt), balance)
```

where `idTag` is a fixed Poseidon encoding of the account id. A neighbour who doesn't know the
salt has nothing small left to guess. Unused slots get a random id and balance 0, so they look like any other leaf.

### What stays private, what's public

| Input | Visibility | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `accountIds` | Secret | Each is the salted id `Poseidon(idTag, salt)`, so identities stay private and leaves can't be guessed |
| `balances` | Secret | Individual balances; each is range-checked to 64 bits |
| `totalReserves` | Public | The custodian's claimed reserves, which must be checked independently |
| `liabilitiesRoot` | Public | Commits to every leaf; customers check their inclusion against it |
| `totalLiabilities` | Public | The exact sum of all balances |
| `isSolvent` | Public | Proven equal to `totalReserves ≥ totalLiabilities`; the minting policy fixes it to 1 |

### How it works

1. **Snapshot.** The custodian takes the customer balances at a point in time, draws a fresh salt
   for every account and builds the Poseidon Merkle tree.
2. **Prove.** It generates a Groth16 proof over the private balances with the four public inputs
   above.
3. **Attest on-chain.** It mints this period's attestation token into an output at the attestation
   script's address. The minting policy verifies the proof against the values in that output's
   datum, so an insolvent claim can't mint.
4. **Customers verify.** Each customer receives their salt, balance and Merkle path, recomputes the
   root in their browser, reads the attestation from the chain, and compares the two.
5. **Repeat.** Each period gets new salts, a new proof and its own token.

```text
custodian (private)                        public
───────────────────                        ──────
16 × (salted id, balance)  ─prove─▶  mint token I2OSP8(p), locked at the script address
(8 accounts + 8 random padding)
                                     datum: Attestation(p, liabilitiesRoot, totalLiabilities, totalReserves)
                                     redeemer: Groth16 proof, checked against the datum with isSolvent = 1
customer: salt + leaf + path ──────▶ root from the chain indexer = my root? ✓
```

> **Tip: Hide the total too**
>
> This design publishes `totalLiabilities`. If the total is sensitive as well,
> [Proof of solvency with hidden balances](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-solvency/) commits to each balance with
> a Pedersen commitment, proves the hidden total fits under reserves locked for an attestation period,
> and lets each customer open their own entry from an encrypted on-chain delivery. An auditor opens
> only the total.

### The circuit

This is simplified from the demo's `SolvencyProof`: constructor validation is trimmed, and the demo
requires `numLeaves == 1 << treeDepth`. Salting didn't change the circuit. Its `accountIds` witness
now holds the salted ids, so the existing keys still work.

```java title="SolvencyProof.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.*;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParams;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPoseidon;

@ZKCircuit(name = "solvency-proof",
           nameTemplate = "solvency-proof-d{treeDepth}-n{numLeaves}-bls-poseidon", version = 1)
public class SolvencyProof {
    private static final PoseidonParams POSEIDON = PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3.INSTANCE;
    private final int treeDepth;
    private final int numLeaves;

    public SolvencyProof(@CircuitParam("treeDepth") int treeDepth,
                         @CircuitParam("numLeaves") int numLeaves) {
        this.treeDepth = treeDepth;
        this.numLeaves = numLeaves;
    }

    @Prove
    ZkBool prove(ZkContext zk,
                 @Public @UInt(bits = 64) ZkUInt totalReserves,
                 @Public ZkField liabilitiesRoot,
                 @Public @UInt(bits = 64) ZkUInt totalLiabilities,
                 @Public ZkBool isSolvent,
                 @Secret @FixedSize(param = "numLeaves") ZkArray<ZkField> accountIds,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 64) @FixedSize(param = "numLeaves") ZkArray<ZkUInt> balances) {

        // Leaves and running sum over the private balances
        ZkUInt sum = balances.get(0);
        ZkField[] level = new ZkField[numLeaves];
        for (int i = 0; i < numLeaves; i++) {
            level[i] = ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, POSEIDON, accountIds.get(i), balances.get(i).asField());
            if (i > 0) sum = sum.add(balances.get(i));
        }

        // Rebuild the Merkle root from the same leaves
        for (int d = 0; d < treeDepth; d++) {
            ZkField[] next = new ZkField[level.length / 2];
            for (int i = 0; i < next.length; i++) {
                next[i] = ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, POSEIDON, level[2 * i], level[2 * i + 1]);
            }
            level = next;
        }

        return level[0].isEqual(liabilitiesRoot)
                .and(sum.asField().isEqual(totalLiabilities.asField()))
                .and(isSolvent.isEqual(totalReserves.gte(totalLiabilities)));
    }
}
```

The circuit covers a fixed batch. The demo defaults to depth 4, which is 16 accounts. A real book
of accounts needs a much larger circuit or a batching scheme, and proving cost grows with it. See
[Performance](https://zeroj.dev/guides/proving/performance/).

### On Cardano

An attestation is a **minted, locked token**. The demo's `ReserveAttestation` is one JuLC
multi-validator that is both the attestation's minting policy and its script address. Its
parameters are the custodian's key hash, the period clock (`genesisMs`, `periodMs`) and the
verification key. Period `p` covers `[genesisMs + p·periodMs, genesisMs + (p+1)·periodMs)`; the demo
uses five-minute periods.

- **Mint (attest).** The custodian signs. The mint is exactly one token named `I2OSP8(p)` (the
  period as 8 bytes), sent to the single output at the script's own enterprise address (payment
  credential, no stake credential). That output holds only ADA and the token, carries no reference
  script, and has the inline datum
  `Attestation(period, liabilitiesRoot, totalLiabilities, totalReserves)`. The redeemer is the
  proof, which must verify against `[totalReserves, liabilitiesRoot, totalLiabilities, 1]` read from
  that datum. An honest proof of insolvency has `isSolvent = 0`, so it can't mint.
- **Spend (release).** The only spend is a custodian-signed burn of that token, after the period has
  ended. The datum can't change while the token exists.

Why a token? The demo used to lock a plain UTxO with the four public inputs in its datum and check
the proof only when someone spent it. Anyone can create a UTxO with any datum, so a datum alone
proved nothing. Now readers look only for the token, and the token can't exist without a proof over
its own datum.

**One per period.** The script doesn't stop the custodian minting a second token for the same
period, but every mint is visible. The demo's custodian service refuses a second attestation for a
period itself (HTTP 409), and the customer check reads the token's whole mint history from the
chain indexer and refuses a period unless it shows exactly one mint and no burn. Without that check,
a custodian could split its liabilities across several trees against the same reserves.

The mint also doesn't check the transaction's validity range. Only the burn checks time. So a
custodian can mint a future period's token in advance, from today's tree. The customer check looks
only at the current period, so when that period arrives it is checked against the old tree.

**Checking against the chain, not the custodian.** The customer page gets its salt, balance, leaf
index and path from the custodian, and recomputes the root in the browser. It then finds the current
period's token under the known policy id through the chain indexer (Yaci Store), not through the
custodian's API, and compares the attested root with its own. The customer also compares the
balance with their own records.

A valid proof is still not the whole story. The proof checks the sum of the balances the custodian
put in the tree. It doesn't check that those balances are true, or that the reserves exist. See
[Application security](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/application-security/).

> **Caution: Experimental PlonK variant**
>
> An experimental PlonK variant of a reserve statement lives in
> [`examples/minimal-circuits/plonk/proof-of-reserves`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/examples/minimal-circuits/plonk/proof-of-reserves).
> PlonK is experimental in ZeroJ and not a recommended path; use Groth16.

### Security considerations

- **Reserves are custodian-declared.** `totalReserves` is whatever the custodian puts in the datum;
  the demo doesn't check it against on-chain holdings. Check holdings directly, or rely on an
  attestation you trust. Watch for reserves borrowed just for the snapshot. Proving over several
  periods, or at unpredictable times, makes that harder.
- **The proof checks the sum, not the balances.** The custodian chooses the balances in the tree.
  Omissions and understated balances are only caught by customers who check. Make checking easy.
- **The proof isn't bound to its period.** The period is in the token name and datum, not in the
  proof's public inputs, and the mint doesn't check the validity range. A custodian could re-attest
  an old solvent tree (the same root, liabilities and reserves) for a new period, or mint a future
  period's token in advance. Customers would then see old balances, so comparing the balance
  with their own records is what catches it. A real design puts the period in the public inputs.
- **Trust the indexer and the page.** The customer trusts the indexer they point the page at. In the
  demo the custodian serves the customer page, and the policy id and clock it pins on first load come
  from the custodian. A real customer takes them from a published, independent source and runs the
  check from code they trust, such as a wallet or a third-party page.
- **Operator view.** The demo server is the custodian. It holds every balance, every salt and the
  custodian key, and its `/accounts` and `/verify/{id}` endpoints answer anyone. That's the demo
  operator's view; a real custodian gives each customer only their own inclusion data, after
  authenticating. Privacy in the demo holds against chain observers, not against the demo server.
- **Trusted setup.** The demo uses a single-party development setup. Production keys come from a
  multi-party ceremony ([Trusted setup, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/trusted-setup/)).

### Try it

The demo lives in
[`proof-of-reserves`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/proof-of-reserves). With
Yaci DevKit running (see [Run the demos](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/overview/#run-the-demos)):

```bash
./demo.sh proof-of-reserves --run
```

`--run` builds the liabilities tree over the demo accounts and proves solvency against 10,000 ADA of
declared reserves, and mints the current period's attestation token, whose minting policy verifies
the proof. In the UI you can add accounts, try a reserve figure below total liabilities to see the
attestation refused, try a second attestation in the same period (the demo server refuses it, and the customer page
would refuse the period too), and run a customer's
inclusion check against the chain. The first start generates a development setup cache and a
random custodian key, which can take a few minutes. `./demo.sh proof-of-reserves --clean-cache`
removes the key, the deployment state and the attested snapshot together.

Design notes:
[Proof of reserves — detailed design](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/usecases/proof-of-reserves.md)
(Merkle sum trees, stake pool pledge, stablecoin and bridge variants).
