## Age & KYC eligibility

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/age-and-kyc/

> Prove you're old enough and live in an approved country, using an issuer-signed credential, while the validator learns only "eligible".

Regulated DeFi, age-gated content and jurisdiction checks all ask the same thing: *are you allowed
to use this?* Today the answer usually means uploading a passport to every app, which stores it and
can leak it. Credentials fix half of that problem. A KYC provider checks you once and signs your
attributes. Zero knowledge fixes the other half: you prove the signed attributes satisfy the rule,
and the app never sees them.

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### The zero-knowledge idea

**The holder proves "a registered issuer signed my age and country, my age meets the minimum, and my
country is on the approved list". The only public outputs are the issuer's key, the policy and the
result.**

The issuer signs `Poseidon(age, country)` with EdDSA over Jubjub. Jubjub is a curve defined over the
BLS12-381 scalar field, so checking its signatures inside a BLS12-381 circuit is comparatively cheap.
The circuit then does three things:

1. verifies the issuer's signature on the hidden attributes;
2. compares `age ≥ minAge` as 8-bit integers;
3. proves `country` is a leaf of the approved-country Merkle tree, whose root is public.

The demo circuit is about 11,000 constraints. The on-chain check costs the same whatever the circuit
contains, because it's a Groth16 pairing check over a handful of public inputs.

### What stays private, what's public

| Input | Visibility | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `age` | Secret | 8-bit integer, range-checked; only the comparison result matters |
| `country` | Secret | Numeric country code; only membership in the approved set matters |
| Issuer signature (`sigRU`, `sigRV`, `sigS`) and helper witnesses (`kModL`, `kQuotient`) | Secret | Revealing the signature would make every presentation linkable |
| Merkle path (`siblings`, `pathBits`) | Secret | The path would reveal which country |
| `pkU`, `pkV` | Public | The issuer's Jubjub public key; the validator pins it |
| `minAge` | Public | The policy threshold; pinned |
| `countryRoot` | Public | The approved-country set; pinned |
| `eligible` | Public | Proven equal to `age ≥ minAge`; the validator requires 1 |

### How it works

1. **Issue.** The KYC provider verifies the person out of band, signs `Poseidon(age, country)` and
   hands the holder their attributes plus the signature. The issuer keeps its secret key.
2. **Deploy the gate.** The protocol compiles a validator with the verification key, the issuer's
   public key, `minAge` and `countryRoot` as script parameters. Changing the policy produces a new
   script address.
3. **Prove.** The holder generates a Groth16 proof on their own device. The demo does this
   server-side for convenience.
4. **Spend.** The transaction's redeemer carries the proof plus the five public inputs. The
   validator checks the issuer, the policy, `eligible == 1` and the proof.
5. **Reuse.** No nullifier is involved. The same credential can prove eligibility again and again,
   which suits ongoing access.

```text
issuer ──sign(Poseidon(age, country))──▶ holder ──Groth16 proof──▶ validator
  (off-chain, once)                        (local)      params: VK, issuer key, minAge, countryRoot
                                                        checks: registered issuer + policy + eligible==1 + pairing
```

### The circuit

This is lightly simplified from the demo's `CredentialProof`: constructor validation is trimmed and
the steps are reordered for reading.

```java title="CredentialProof.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.*;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParams;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkEdDSAJubjub;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkMerkle;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPoseidon;

@ZKCircuit(name = "credential-verify-eddsa",
           nameTemplate = "credential-verify-eddsa-d{countryTreeDepth}-bls-poseidon", version = 1)
public class CredentialProof {
    private static final PoseidonParams POSEIDON = PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3.INSTANCE;

    public CredentialProof(@CircuitParam("countryTreeDepth") int countryTreeDepth) {}

    @Prove
    ZkBool prove(ZkContext zk,
                 @Public ZkField pkU,
                 @Public ZkField pkV,
                 @Public @UInt(bits = 8) ZkUInt minAge,
                 @Public ZkField countryRoot,
                 @Public ZkBool eligible,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 8) ZkUInt age,
                 @Secret ZkField country,
                 @Secret ZkField sigRU,
                 @Secret ZkField sigRV,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt sigS,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt kModL,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 4) ZkUInt kQuotient,
                 @Secret @FixedSize(param = "countryTreeDepth") ZkArray<ZkField> siblings,
                 @Secret @FixedSize(param = "countryTreeDepth") ZkArray<ZkBool> pathBits) {

        // 1. The issuer signed these exact attributes
        var claims = ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, POSEIDON, age.asField(), country);
        ZkEdDSAJubjub.verifyWithRegisteredKey(zk, pkU, pkV, claims, sigRU, sigRV, sigS, kModL, kQuotient);

        // 2. The country is in the approved set
        ZkMerkle.verifyProofPoseidon(zk, POSEIDON, country, countryRoot, siblings, pathBits);

        // 3. The age meets the minimum
        return eligible.isEqual(age.gte(minAge));
    }
}
```

`verifyWithRegisteredKey` is the right entry point here because the issuer key is a public input
that the verifier pins. If the prover could choose the key, you'd need `verifyStrict`, which also
checks the key's subgroup membership inside the circuit. The name reminds you that "is this a
trusted issuer?" is the validator's job.

> **Tip: Sign a birth year, not an age**
>
> An age goes stale the day after it's signed. The
> [selective-disclosure demo](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/selective-disclosure/) signs `dobYear` and proves
> `dobYear ≤ currentYear − 21`, with `currentYear` pinned by the validator.

### On Cardano

The demo's `CredentialGatedValidator` is a JuLC spending validator. It composes
`Groth16BLS12381Lib.verify(…)` and takes the verification key, the issuer's key coordinates and the
policy values (`minAge`, `countryRoot`) as parameters. It accepts a spend only if the redeemer's
public inputs match the registered issuer and policy, `eligible == 1`, and the pairing check
passes.

A valid proof is not authorization. This is a **stateless, replayable demo gate**: the validator
checks the proof, not the transaction that spends it. Anyone who sees an unlock transaction, on
the chain or still pending, can copy its proof and use it to open any other UTxO locked at the same
gate. A real protocol should bind the proof to its context: add the recipient or the spent
`TxOutRef` as a bound public input that the validator recomputes from `ScriptContext`, or use a
per-epoch nullifier when access should be rate-limited. See
[Application security](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/application-security/).

### Security considerations

- **You trust the issuer.** A dishonest or compromised issuer can sign anything. Plan for key
  rotation and revocation: short-lived credentials, or a periodically refreshed validity tree the
  circuit checks.
- **The issuer key must be secret.** The demo generates its issuer key with `SecureRandom` on first
  start and keeps it, owner-only, in its data directory. Earlier versions derived the key from a
  seed published in the demo's source, so anyone could sign credentials that the deployed validator
  accepted. A credential signed with that old seed is now refused.
- **Keep issuance offline.** The demo signs with `EdDSAJubjub.signCompatibilityOffline`. ZeroJ's
  Jubjub signing isn't constant-time and is meant for offline, isolated use. Don't expose it as a
  network signing service.
- **Credentials can be shared.** A proof shows knowledge of a credential, not identity, and the
  demo credential names no holder. Holder binding helps: include the holder's key in the signed
  message and prove control of it.
- **Unsalted credentials.** The issuer signs `Poseidon(age, country)` with no salt. That message has
  a small domain, so anyone who sees it or its signature, together with the issuer's public key, can recover
  the attributes by trying every age and country. Two holders with the same age and country get the
  same signature. Add a random salt to the signed message in a real deployment.
- **Replay** of stateless proofs, as described above.
- **Demo custody.** The demo server holds the issuer key and every holder's credential, and proves
  on their behalf. Its API is the operator's view. Privacy holds against chain and mempool
  observers, not against the demo server.
- **Linkability outside the proof.** The same wallet, fee payer or timing can still link two
  presentations.
- **Trusted setup.** The demo uses a single-party development setup; production needs an MPC
  ceremony ([Trusted setup, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/trusted-setup/)).

### Try it

The demo lives in
[`identity-kyc`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/identity-kyc). With Yaci
DevKit running (see [Run the demos](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/overview/#run-the-demos)):

```bash
./demo.sh identity-kyc --run
```

`--run` locks 5 ADA at the credential-gated script, proves that Alice (25, USA) is eligible and
unlocks the funds with that proof on-chain. The UI lists five test users. Charlie is 16 and Diana's
country isn't on the approved list, so neither can produce a proof that unlocks the gate.

Design notes:
[ZK identity & credentials — detailed design](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/usecases/identity-and-credentials.md)
(credential lifecycle, revocation options, issuer registries).

### Related

- [Prove you're over 18](https://zeroj.dev/tutorials/age-check/): build the range check yourself
- [Selective disclosure & reusable KYC](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/selective-disclosure/): many predicates from
  one credential, or BBS
- [Gadgets](https://zeroj.dev/guides/circuits/gadgets/): `ZkEdDSAJubjub`, `ZkMerkle`, `ZkPoseidon`
- [Testing circuits](https://zeroj.dev/guides/circuits/testing-circuits/): write the invalid-witness tests

## Private NFT ownership

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/nft-ownership/

> Prove you hold an NFT from a collection for one-time token-gated access, without revealing which NFT or which wallet, and see why the nullifier must absorb a holder secret.

On Cardano, owning an NFT means a UTxO holding it sits at your address. To prove ownership, you
usually connect your wallet or point at that UTxO, and the verifier (plus anyone watching) learns
your address, your balance, every other token you hold and your transaction history. That's a
steep price for a concert ticket, a holders-only chat or a DAO forum. Zero knowledge lets you prove
"I'm a holder" and nothing more.

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### The zero-knowledge idea

**The holder proves "one leaf of this event's ownership snapshot is mine, and this is my one-time
nullifier for the event", without revealing which leaf, which NFT or which wallet.**

Live UTxOs change with every transaction, so the proof is made against a **snapshot**. An indexer
collects registrations from holders and builds a Merkle tree. Each holder has a **holder secret**
`s`: a 252-bit random value that the app draws with `SecureRandom`. For token `t` the leaf is:

```text
leaf = Poseidon(Poseidon(s, 0), t)
```

The root is published, and the holder proves their leaf is in the tree without saying which leaf.

The **nullifier** marks one use per event:

```text
nullifier = Poseidon(Poseidon(s, t), contextId)
```

`contextId` names the event. The same leaf in the same event always gives the same nullifier, so a
second use is caught. A different event gives an unrelated value, so one holder's nullifiers can't
be linked across events. Without `s`, nobody can compute the nullifier for any token.

### Why not just hash the token name?

The first version of this demo used `Poseidon(tokenName, contextId)` as the nullifier. It looks
private, because the token name stays a secret input. But **every input to that hash is public**:
the collection's token names are listed on-chain, and `contextId` is a public input. Anyone could
hash each token name with the event's `contextId` and find the published nullifier. That showed
*which* NFT was used, and because an NFT's holder address is public on Cardano, *which wallet* too.

The fix is to make the nullifier absorb a value nobody else can guess: the holder's 252-bit secret.
It has to be large. A short secret such as `42` could be found by trying every small number, so
the API refuses secrets shorter than 240 bits (below 2^239). Deriving the nullifier from the leaf, as
`Poseidon(leaf, contextId)`, wouldn't work either: if the snapshot's leaves are published, anyone
could recompute it.

### What stays private, what's public

| Input | Visibility | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `secretKey` | Secret | The holder's 252-bit secret; the leaf and the nullifier absorb it |
| `tokenName` | Secret | Which NFT; the nullifier no longer reveals it |
| Merkle path (`siblings`, `pathBits`) | Secret | The path would reveal the leaf's position |
| `snapshotRoot` | Public | The event's snapshot; a parameter of the event's minting policy |
| `contextId` | Public | The event; also a policy parameter |
| `isOwner` | Public | Must be 1 |
| `nullifier` | Public | Minted as a token name and inserted into the on-chain list |

An observer of the chain or the mempool learns that *some* holder in the snapshot used the gate,
and nothing about which NFT or which wallet.

### One use per what?

With the old nullifier, the circuit itself gave each NFT exactly one nullifier per event. Now each
**leaf** gives one nullifier per event, so a holder who registered two leaves for one NFT would get
two uses. Keeping the count right is now the **indexer's** job. In the demo, `SnapshotService`
plays the indexer, and registration:

- **refuses a second registration for a token** already in the snapshot;
- **requires a CIP-8 signature from the holding address.** The holder signs
  `(contextId, tokenName, leaf)` with the payment key of the address that holds the token on-chain,
  and the indexer checks on-chain that this address holds exactly one unit of it;
- **freezes when the snapshot is built.** No leaf can be added after the root is fixed.

So the snapshot has at most one leaf per authenticated holding, and each leaf gets in once.
One limit remains: the leaf hides the token, so the indexer can't check that a leaf registered
under token A really commits to A. A holder of A could register a leaf over another token B. That
changes which token a proof names, not how many uses there are: **one use per authenticated
holding, not one use per specific NFT.** The snapshot is a trust point either way.

### How it works

1. **Register.** For each NFT, the app draws a holder secret and registers the leaf
   `Poseidon(Poseidon(s, 0), t)`, signed (CIP-8) by the wallet that holds the token.
2. **Build the snapshot.** The root is fixed and registration closes. The event's scripts are
   deployed: a minting policy with the root and `contextId` as parameters, and a nullifier list
   whose root can be created only once.
3. **Prove.** The holder generates a Groth16 proof with ZeroJ's pure-Java prover.
4. **Access.** A transaction mints one token named after the nullifier. The policy verifies the
   proof on-chain, and the list inserts a node keyed by that nullifier.
5. **Reuse is rejected.** The same holder in the same event produces the same nullifier, and the
   list already holds it.

```text
holder:   s, t ─sign (CIP-8)─▶ indexer: one leaf per token ─▶ snapshotRoot, frozen
deploy:   ZkProofMintingPolicy(snapshotRoot, contextId, VK) + NullifierListValidator(zkPolicyId, seed)
holder:   s, t, path ─prove─▶ tx: mint 1 × <nullifier>, insert node keyed by <nullifier>
```

### The circuit

This is the demo's `NFTOwnershipProof`, version 2, with constructor validation trimmed.

```java title="NFTOwnershipProof.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.*;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParams;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkMerkle;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPoseidon;

@ZKCircuit(name = "nft-ownership",
           nameTemplate = "nft-ownership-d{treeDepth}-bls-poseidon", version = 2)
public class NFTOwnershipProof {
    private static final PoseidonParams POSEIDON = PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3.INSTANCE;

    public NFTOwnershipProof(@CircuitParam("treeDepth") int treeDepth) {}

    @Prove
    ZkBool prove(ZkContext zk,
                 @Public ZkField snapshotRoot,
                 @Public ZkField contextId,
                 @Public ZkBool isOwner,
                 @Public ZkField nullifier,
                 @Secret ZkField secretKey,
                 @Secret ZkField tokenName,
                 @Secret @FixedSize(param = "treeDepth") ZkArray<ZkField> siblings,
                 @Secret @FixedSize(param = "treeDepth") ZkArray<ZkBool> pathBits) {

        // Leaf (unchanged from version 1): Poseidon(Poseidon(secretKey, 0), tokenName).
        var ownerHash = ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, POSEIDON, secretKey, zk.constant(0));
        var leaf = ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, POSEIDON, ownerHash, tokenName);
        ZkMerkle.verifyProofPoseidon(zk, POSEIDON, leaf, snapshotRoot, siblings, pathBits);

        // Nullifier: Poseidon(Poseidon(secretKey, tokenName), contextId).
        var holderToken = ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, POSEIDON, secretKey, tokenName);
        var computedNullifier = ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, POSEIDON, holderToken, contextId);
        return isOwner.and(computedNullifier.isEqual(nullifier));
    }
}
```

The leaf is the same as in version 1; only the nullifier changed. Token names and event labels
enter the circuit as their bytes read as one big-endian number (1 to 31 bytes, with no leading
zero byte, so each name has one value). The demo builds a
depth-10 tree, which holds up to 1,024 holders. At depth 4, as in the end-to-end test, the circuit
compiles to 1,942 constraints, and each extra level adds one Poseidon hash and doubles the tree's
capacity (and the potential anonymity set).

### On Cardano

Building the snapshot deploys two JuLC scripts for the event. Both run in every access
transaction.

- **`ZkProofMintingPolicy`** takes `snapshotRoot`, `contextId` and the verification key as **script
  parameters**, so there is one policy per event. The redeemer carries only the proof and the
  nullifier. The policy requires the mint under it to be exactly one token, quantity 1, whose
  32-byte name is the nullifier, and verifies the proof with
  `Groth16BLS12381Lib.verifyFour(snapshotRoot, contextId, 1, nullifier, ...)`. A proof against
  another snapshot or event fails, because those inputs come from the parameters.
- **`NullifierListValidator`** keeps nullifiers in a sorted linked list, one UTxO per entry:
  - **One-shot root.** The list is parameterised by a seed UTxO that the root's creation must
    spend, so the root exists once.
  - **The new key is the proved nullifier.** An insert must mint exactly one ZK token, and the
    new node's key is that token's name (its low 31 bytes). The ZK token sits in the new node.
  - **Insert-only.** A node can be spent only as the anchor of an insert, one list input per
    transaction, and nothing is ever burned, so nodes are never removed.

  An insert also proves the key sits between two neighbours, so a nullifier already in the list
  can't be added again.

The first version of the list checked only that the ZK policy minted *something*, not that the new
key was the proved nullifier, and its root could be minted again and its nodes removed, so one
proof could gate any number of accesses.

A token minted under the ZK policy outside a list insert grants nothing: readers count access only
from list nodes. Each node locks about 2 ADA, which stays locked because nodes are never removed.
See [On-chain verification](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/on-chain/) for the verifier side.

### Security considerations

- **The indexer decides the snapshot.** It is trusted to admit one registration per token, from
  the address holding it. The demo doesn't publish the snapshot's leaves; a real deployment should,
  so anyone can rebuild the root.
- **One use per authenticated holding, not per NFT,** as explained above.
- **Front-running.** A mempool observer can copy a holder's proof from a pending transaction and
  submit it first; the access then goes to that transaction. The fix is a fresh one-time
  beneficiary key hash as a public input, with the gate's output paid to it. It is deferred to
  keep circuit version 2 minimal.
- **Using the gate shows that some snapshot holder acted.** Also consider fee payer and timing
  linkability when holders submit their own transactions.
- **Staleness.** A holder who sells after the snapshot can still prove against it. A new snapshot
  is a new event.
- **One event per run.** The demo's event comes from `zk.default-context`; a new event needs a
  restart with a new context.
- **The demo is custodial.** The server holds the custody wallet that holds the NFTs and signs
  registrations. It draws each holder secret and returns it once, without storing it, and it proves
  for the holder. Its API is the operator's view: privacy holds against chain and mempool
  observers, not against the demo server.
- **Trusted setup.** The demo uses a single-party development setup; production needs an MPC
  ceremony ([Trusted setup, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/trusted-setup/)). The demo is not externally
  reviewed.

### Try it

The demo lives in
[`nft-ownership`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/nft-ownership). With Yaci
DevKit running (see [Run the demos](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/overview/#run-the-demos)):

```bash
./demo.sh nft-ownership --run
```

`--run` mints `ZeroJTicket_1` into the custody wallet and registers it. The server draws a fresh
252-bit holder secret, returns it once, and signs the registration with the custody wallet. Then
it builds the snapshot (which deploys the event's scripts), generates a proof for the event
`nft-demo-v1`, and submits the access transaction. The proof is verified on-chain and the
nullifier lands in the sorted list. Submit the same nullifier again and the service answers 403,
"Already accessed (nullifier exists on-chain)"; forcing the insert past that check is rejected by
the list script. Registering `ZeroJTicket_1` a second time is refused, and so is a typed-in secret
such as `42`.

The circuit, scripts and script hashes changed in version 2. If you ran an earlier version, start
fresh with `./demo.sh nft-ownership --clean-cache`.

Design notes:
[`DESIGN.md`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/blob/main/nft-ownership/DESIGN.md) in the
demo, and
[Private NFT ownership — detailed design](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/usecases/private-nft-ownership.md)
(snapshot vs. on-chain registries, threshold "whale" proofs, shielded transfers).

  nullifier pattern, step by step

## One claim per person

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/sybil-resistant-airdrop/

> A Sybil-resistant airdrop where each personhood credential claims once per round with a nullifier even the issuer can't link to a person, and the payout bound to the proved recipient.

Airdrops, faucets and community rewards get farmed. One person spins up a thousand wallets and
claims a thousand times. Checking identity at claim time stops that, but then every claimant hands
over personal data and every claim is linked to a person. What you want is **one claim per real
human per round**, where the nullifier a claim publishes tells nobody, not even the issuer that
vouched for each person, which person claimed.

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### The zero-knowledge idea

**The claimant proves "a personhood issuer signed my credential, and this nullifier is the one my
credential produces for this round", and binds the payout to a recipient, without revealing the
credential.**

A personhood issuer checks, out of band, that each human gets exactly one credential. That's the
part zero knowledge can't do for you. The credential works like this:

- **The holder picks the identifier.** The holder's wallet draws a secret `personhoodId` (252
  bits, `SecureRandom`) and sends the issuer only `m = Poseidon(personhoodId, 0)`. The issuer signs
  `m` with EdDSA over Jubjub and never sees `personhoodId`.
- **Nullifier = `Poseidon(personhoodId, epoch)`.** It's the same for every claim in a round, so
  repeats are caught. A new round gives an unrelated value, so one person's nullifiers can't be
  linked across rounds. The recipient, the fee payer and timing can still link claims (see the
  security considerations).
- **Recipient binding.** The payout's key hash is a public input the proof commits to, and the
  minting policy checks that the transaction really pays it.

This is the same building block behind Semaphore-style signals and "one-per-human" claim tokens.

### Why the issuer mustn't choose the identifier

In the first version of this demo the issuer assigned each person's `personhoodId` (a counter or a
hash of the name). The issuer then knew every identifier it had handed out, and the nullifier
`Poseidon(personhoodId, epoch)` uses only that identifier and the public epoch. **So the issuer
could compute every person's nullifier for every round and link each claim to a name.** Now the
holder chooses `personhoodId` and the issuer signs only its hash, so it can't compute any
nullifier.

Holder-chosen identifiers need one more rule: **one credential per person.** Otherwise a person
could ask for two credentials with two identifiers and claim twice. The issuer keeps a durable
record of each person it has issued to, written before it signs, and refuses a second issuance.
The circuit didn't change: it already proved knowledge of a `personhoodId` whose
`Poseidon(personhoodId, 0)` the issuer signed.

### What stays private, what's public

| Input | Visibility | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `personhoodId` | Secret | Chosen by the holder; the issuer sees only its hash |
| Issuer signature (`sigRU`, `sigRV`, `sigS`) and helpers (`kModL`, `kQuotient`) | Secret | Revealing the signature would link claims |
| `pkU`, `pkV` | Public | The issuer's Jubjub key; pinned by the minting policy |
| `epoch` | Public | This deployment and round (`policyEpoch`); pinned by the policy |
| `nullifier` | Public | One per credential per round; becomes the minted receipt's asset name |
| `recipient` | Public | The payout's 28-byte payment key hash, as a number |
| `eligible` | Public | Must be 1 |

### The epoch is a domain tag

The epoch isn't a small round number. It's a tag for one deployment and one round:

```text
policyEpoch  = Poseidon2(Poseidon2(tag("zeroj.airdrop.epoch.v1"), deploymentId), n)
tag(s)       = blake2b_256(UTF-8(s)) as an integer, top byte cleared
deploymentId = blake2b_256(txId ‖ I2OSP2(index)) of the faucet's seed UTxO, top byte cleared
n            = the round number, 1 ≤ n < 2^32
```

`Poseidon2` is ZeroJ's `PoseidonHash` over `PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3`. Two airdrops, even two
sibling outputs of one transaction used as seeds, never share a nullifier. The policy refuses
`policyEpoch = 0` and any epoch at or above the field order.

### How it works

1. **Enrol.** The holder draws `personhoodId` and sends `m = Poseidon(personhoodId, 0)`. After its
   one-human check, the issuer records the person and signs `m`. A second request for the same
   person is refused.
2. **Claim.** The holder proves with this round's `policyEpoch` and the recipient they choose.
3. **Pay once.** The faucet refuses a nullifier it has already paid, or whose receipt was ever
   minted. Otherwise it records the nullifier, durably, before it signs the payout.
4. **Mint a receipt.** The faucet minting policy verifies the proof, mints one receipt named after
   the nullifier, and requires an output paying the recipient's key hash at least the payout.
5. **Repeat in the same round?** Same credential and same round give the same nullifier, so the
   faucet refuses to pay.
6. **Next round.** A new round number gives a new `policyEpoch` and a new policy, with fresh
   nullifiers.

```text
holder ──m = Poseidon(personhoodId, 0)──▶ issuer (once per person) ──sig(m)──▶ holder
holder ──proof(policyEpoch, recipient)──▶ faucet: nullifier not paid? record it, sign payout
                                          policy: issuer ✓ epoch ✓ eligible ✓ pays recipient ✓ pairing ✓
                                          mint 1 × <nullifier> receipt
```

### The circuit

This is the demo's `PersonhoodAirdropProof`, lightly trimmed (imports and comments):

```java title="PersonhoodAirdropProof.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.*;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParams;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkEdDSAJubjub;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPoseidon;

@ZKCircuit(name = "personhood-airdrop", version = 1)
public class PersonhoodAirdropProof {
    private static final PoseidonParams POSEIDON = PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3.INSTANCE;

    @Prove
    ZkBool prove(ZkContext zk,
                 @Public ZkField pkU,
                 @Public ZkField pkV,
                 @Public ZkField epoch,
                 @Public ZkField nullifier,
                 @Public ZkField recipient,
                 @Public ZkBool eligible,
                 @Secret ZkField personhoodId,
                 @Secret ZkField sigRU,
                 @Secret ZkField sigRV,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt sigS,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt kModL,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 4) ZkUInt kQuotient) {

        var claimsMsg = ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, POSEIDON, personhoodId, zk.constant(0));
        ZkEdDSAJubjub.verifyWithRegisteredKey(
                zk, pkU, pkV, claimsMsg, sigRU, sigRV, sigS, kModL, kQuotient);

        // Bind the public recipient into a real (non-degenerate) R1CS row.
        recipient.mul(personhoodId);

        var computedNullifier = ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, POSEIDON, personhoodId, epoch);
        return eligible.and(computedNullifier.isEqual(nullifier));
    }
}
```

The circuit compiles to 10,467 constraints (from the demo's test runs) and uses a power-14
development SRS.

The line `recipient.mul(personhoodId)` deserves a closer look. The circuit doesn't *compute*
anything with `recipient`, but a Groth16 proof only commits to a public input that appears in at
least one constraint. Multiplying two variables emits a real constraint row. A constant
multiplication such as `recipient * 1` gets folded away and wouldn't bind anything. ZeroJ's native
Groth16 setup refuses a relation with an unbound public input rather than silently producing a key
that ignores it.

### On Cardano

The demo's `FaucetMintingPolicy` is a JuLC minting policy parameterised by the verification key,
the issuer's key, `policyEpoch` and `payout`. It reads the six public inputs from the receipt
output's inline datum and requires:

- the mint under the policy is exactly one entry, quantity 1, named after the nullifier, and the
  receipt sits at the policy's own script address;
- the issuer key and the epoch equal its parameters, with `0 < policyEpoch < r`;
- `eligible == 1`;
- **an output whose payment credential is the key hash `recipient`, carrying at least `payout`
  lovelace.** A script credential never qualifies, and the API accepts only key-credential
  addresses;
- the proof verifies with `Groth16BLS12381Lib.verify(...)`.

**The faucet pays each nullifier once.** The faucet's ADA sits at its admin key's address, so a
payout needs the admin's signature. Before signing, the faucet refuses a nullifier that is in its
paid record or whose receipt was ever minted (from the chain indexer; if that lookup fails, the
claim is refused). It then records the nullifier atomically on disk, so the record survives
restarts.

The policy itself keeps no "minted once" state, so **receipt uniqueness on-chain is deferred**.
Someone replaying a claim with their own funds can mint a second receipt for the same nullifier,
but takes nothing from the faucet. A sorted-list registry like the
[voting](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-voting/) and [NFT](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/nft-ownership/) demos would close that.

### Security considerations

- **The one-human check is out of band.** ZK enforces "one claim per credential". It can't tell
  whether a person holds two credentials. Sybil resistance is only as good as the issuer's
  enrolment checks; the demo stands in for them with the person's name.
- **A lost credential can't be re-issued.** One credential per person is what stops a second
  claim, so a holder who loses `personhoodId` or the signature can't claim again.
- **Stolen credentials claim once per round.** Whoever holds `personhoodId` and the signature can
  claim. Revocation isn't demonstrated.
- **Copied proofs.** A mempool observer can copy a pending claim's proof into its own transaction,
  but the policy still requires the payout to the proved recipient, so the copier can only pay the
  recipient from its own funds.
- **The recipient is public.** It's a public input, written into the receipt's datum, and the
  transaction pays it, so the faucet and every chain observer see it. Use a fresh recipient key
  each round: a reused recipient, the fee payer and timing can link claims even though the
  nullifiers can't. In the demo, `--run` pays every claim to the faucet admin's address.
- **Random, persisted keys.** The issuer's EdDSA-Jubjub key and the faucet admin wallet are
  generated with `SecureRandom` on first start and stored owner-only in the demo data directory.
  The first version derived the issuer key from a seed published in the source, so anyone could
  sign credentials. If deployment state exists but a key is missing or doesn't match, the demo
  stops instead of making a new one. A production faucet keeps these keys in a KMS or HSM.
- **Static round.** The round comes from configuration (`faucet.round`), not chain time, and a new
  round deploys a new policy ID.
- **Keep issuance offline.** The demo signs with `EdDSAJubjub.signCompatibilityOffline`, which is
  meant for offline, isolated use, not a network signing service.
- **The demo is custodial.** The server holds every holder's wallet, so it knows each
  `personhoodId` (the issuer component doesn't). Its API is the operator's view: privacy holds
  against chain and mempool observers, not against the demo server. Even so, `/status` and
  `/history` return no names next to nullifiers.
- **Trusted setup.** The demo uses a single-party development setup; production needs an MPC
  ceremony ([Trusted setup, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/trusted-setup/)). The demo is not externally
  reviewed.

### Try it

The demo lives in
[`personhood-airdrop`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/personhood-airdrop).
Its [tutorial](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/blob/main/personhood-airdrop/SYBIL_AIRDROP_TUTORIAL.md)
walks through the design. With Yaci DevKit running (see
[Run the demos](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/overview/#run-the-demos)):

```bash
./demo.sh airdrop --run
```

At startup the demo enrols five holders (Alice, Bob, Charlie, Diana and Eve), each with its own
`personhoodId`. `--run` has Alice claim for round 1: the proof is generated, the receipt is
minted on-chain and 2 ADA is paid out (to the faucet admin's own address, the demo default when no
`recipient` is given). Claim for Alice again and the service answers 409, because her nullifier
was already paid. Bob's claim succeeds because his credential produces a different nullifier.

The issuer key, the policy parameters and the policy ID changed. If you ran an earlier version,
start fresh with `./demo.sh airdrop --clean-cache`.

### Related

- [Private voting](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-voting/): nullifiers stored in an on-chain sorted list
- [Age & KYC eligibility](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/age-and-kyc/): the same in-circuit issuer signature, without
  rate limiting
- [Circuits, constraints & witnesses](https://zeroj.dev/learn/circuits-and-witnesses/): why unconstrained inputs are
  dangerous
- [Application security](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/application-security/)

## Selective disclosure & reusable KYC

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/selective-disclosure/

> Do KYC once, then show each service only what it asks for, as Groth16 predicates over hidden fields or BBS presentations verified on Cardano.

Every exchange, lending app and marketplace runs its own KYC, and each one keeps a copy of your
documents. A signed credential lets you do KYC once. But if you then show the whole credential
everywhere, you've only moved the problem. Selective disclosure is the missing piece. A library
asks "over 21 and a resident?", a healthcare portal asks "a doctor over 30?", a DeFi app asks
"KYC-verified and from an allowed country?", and each one learns *only* its answer.

ZeroJ supports two complementary ways to do this, and each has a runnable demo.

> **Tip: Not sure which approach fits?**
>
> This page covers revealing signed attributes (BBS) and proving rules over them (Groth16).
> [Choose how to disclose](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/) also covers hidden amounts, values only an
> auditor may read, and decryption that needs several trustees, with code for each.

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### The zero-knowledge idea

**One issuer-signed credential; each verifier learns only the answer to its own question.**

| | Groth16 predicates (`selective-disclosure` demo) | BBS selective disclosure (`reusable-kyc` demo) |
|---|---|---|
| Verifier learns | A computed yes/no, such as `dobYear ≤ currentYear − 21` | Chosen attribute values, such as `country = USA` |
| Computes over hidden values? | Yes: ranges, Merkle membership, any circuit | No: each attribute is either revealed or hidden |
| Signature | EdDSA-Jubjub over a Poseidon hash of all fields, checked in-circuit | BBS (IRTF CFRG draft-10) over all attributes |
| Circuit and trusted setup | One circuit and one setup per predicate | None |
| On-chain | `Groth16BLS12381Lib` | `BbsProofVerify` (fixed profile, see below) |

Use predicates when the verifier needs a fact computed from a value it must not see. Use BBS when
revealing the value itself is fine and you want no circuits and no trusted setup. The two combine
well: reveal some attributes with BBS, and prove a range over another with a small Groth16 circuit.

### What stays private, what's public

**Groth16 "senior doctor" predicate:**

| Input | Visibility | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `dobYear`, `country`, `roleId`, `salaryBracket`, `nameHash` | Secret | The whole credential stays hidden |
| Issuer signature and helper witnesses | Secret | Revealing them would link presentations |
| `pkU`, `pkV` | Public | The issuer's key; pinned by the validator |
| `currentYear` | Public | Pinned by the validator, so the prover can't pick a convenient year |
| `eligible` | Public | The predicate's result; the validator requires 1 |

**BBS reusable KYC:**

| Input | Visibility | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `givenName`, `dob`, `docHash` | Hidden | Proven signed but never shown |
| `country`, `kycLevel` | Revealed | Exactly what this verifier's policy needs |
| Issuer public key, credential `header` | Public | Identify the issuer and schema |
| Presentation header (challenge) | Public | Makes the presentation single-use |

### How it works

**Groth16 predicates:**

1. The issuer signs `Poseidon(dobYear, country, roleId, salaryBracket, nameHash)` once.
2. For each verifier, the holder runs that verifier's predicate circuit. Every circuit recomputes
   the same claims hash, checks the same signature, then asserts its own predicate.
3. Each gate is a spending validator pinned to its own verification key, issuer key and policy
   values.

**BBS:**

1. The issuer signs five attributes as one BBS credential.
2. The verifier sends a fresh random challenge.
3. The holder derives a presentation that reveals only the requested attributes, bound to that
   challenge.
4. The verifier checks the proof, that the challenge is one it issued and hasn't seen before, and
   its policy. On-chain, a validator can do the same natively.

### The circuit

This Groth16 predicate is from the demo's `SeniorDoctorProof`. The `AdultResidentProof` next to it
reuses the same first half and adds a Merkle country check.

```java title="SeniorDoctorProof.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.*;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParams;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkEdDSAJubjub;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPoseidonN;

@ZKCircuit(name = "senior-doctor", version = 1)
public class SeniorDoctorProof {
    private static final PoseidonParams POSEIDON = PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3.INSTANCE;
    private static final int MIN_AGE = 30;
    private static final long DOCTOR_ROLE_ID = 1001L;

    @Prove
    ZkBool prove(ZkContext zk,
                 @Public ZkField pkU,
                 @Public ZkField pkV,
                 @Public @UInt(bits = 16) ZkUInt currentYear,
                 @Public ZkBool eligible,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 16) ZkUInt dobYear,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 16) ZkUInt country,
                 @Secret ZkField roleId,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 8) ZkUInt salaryBracket,
                 @Secret ZkField nameHash,
                 @Secret ZkField sigRU,
                 @Secret ZkField sigRV,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt sigS,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt kModL,
                 @Secret @UInt(bits = 4) ZkUInt kQuotient) {

        // Every predicate recomputes the same signed message over all five fields
        var claims = ZkPoseidonN.hash(zk, POSEIDON, dobYear.asField(), country.asField(),
                roleId, salaryBracket.asField(), nameHash);
        ZkEdDSAJubjub.verifyWithRegisteredKey(zk, pkU, pkV, claims, sigRU, sigRV, sigS, kModL, kQuotient);

        // The predicate: role == doctor AND born no later than currentYear - 30
        var maxDobYear = ZkUInt.wrap(zk, currentYear.asField().sub(zk.constant(MIN_AGE)).signal(), 16);
        var roleOk = roleId.isEqual(zk.constant(DOCTOR_ROLE_ID));
        return roleOk.and(eligible.isEqual(dobYear.lte(maxDobYear)));
    }
}
```

#### The BBS flow

With BBS there's no circuit at all. This is the `zeroj-bbs` API as the reusable-KYC demo uses it,
condensed:

```java
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.SecureRandom;
import java.util.List;
import org.zeroj.bbs.BbsKeyPair;
import org.zeroj.bbs.BbsPresentation;
import org.zeroj.bbs.BbsRevealedMessage;
import org.zeroj.bbs.BbsService;
import org.zeroj.bbs.BbsSignature;

var bbs = BbsService.pureJava();

// Issuer: sign all five attributes as one credential (index = position in the list)
BbsKeyPair issuer = bbs.keyPair(keyMaterial, keyInfo);          // keyMaterial: >= 32 secret random bytes
List<byte[]> attributes = List.of(givenName, dob, country, kycLevel, docHash);
BbsSignature signature = bbs.sign(issuer.secretKey(), issuer.publicKey(), attributes, header);

// Verifier: a fresh, single-use challenge. The verifier picks it, never the holder.
byte[] challenge = new byte[32];
new SecureRandom().nextBytes(challenge);

// Holder: reveal country (2) and kycLevel (3); indexes must be strictly ascending
BbsPresentation presentation = bbs.derivePresentation(
        issuer.publicKey(), signature, attributes, header, challenge, new int[] {2, 3});

// Verifier: check the proof (and that `challenge` is unused), then apply its policy
boolean valid = bbs.verifyPresentation(issuer.publicKey(), presentation);
for (BbsRevealedMessage m : presentation.revealedMessages()) {
    System.out.println(m.index() + " -> " + new String(m.message(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
}
```

`verifyPresentation` checks cryptography only. Issuer trust, schema, expiry, revocation and your
disclosure policy remain application logic. See the [BBS guide](https://zeroj.dev/guides/credentials/bbs/).

### On Cardano

**Groth16 gates.** The demo's `AdultResidentValidator` and `SeniorDoctorValidator` are JuLC
spending validators built on `Groth16BLS12381Lib`. The issuer key, `currentYear` and (for the adult
gate) the approved-country root are script parameters. Changing any of them deploys a new script,
so a caller can't substitute weaker public inputs.

These are **stateless, replayable demo gates**: the validators check the proof, not the
transaction that spends it. Anyone who sees an unlock transaction, on the chain or still pending,
can copy its proof and use it to open any other UTxO locked at the same gate. A real deployment
binds the proof to the output it spends, for example with the spent `TxOutRef` and the payout
address as public inputs that the validator recomputes from `ScriptContext`.

**BBS natively on-chain.** `BbsProofVerify` in `zeroj-onchain-julc` runs BBS `ProofVerify`
inside Plutus V3. `BbsToCardano` in `zeroj-bbs` turns the issuer key into validator parameters and
a presentation into redeemer fields. The demo's `BbsKycClaimValidator` locks a voucher UTxO and
releases it only if four things hold:

- the presentation verifies on the ledger;
- it discloses exactly the required values;
- its presentation header equals `blake2b_256(voucherTxId ‖ I2OSP(index, 8) ‖ recipientPkh)`,
  which the validator recomputes itself rather than trusting the claimer;
- the voucher pays exactly what it owes, as described below.

Spending the voucher is the nullifier. The demo measured about 2.4×10⁹ CPU units for the check,
within Cardano's per-transaction limit. The current `BbsProofVerify` profile is fixed to a
five-attribute credential disclosing indexes 2 and 3; other shapes need a different unrolling.

**How the voucher pays.** The voucher's datum is
`(requiredCountry, requiredKycLevel, recipientPkh, refundAmount, funderPkh, maxFee)`. The demo locks
10 ADA with a 2 ADA refund and a `maxFee` of 2 ADA, so 6 ADA goes back to the funder. A claim counts
only outputs whose inline datum is exactly the spent voucher's `TxOutRef`, called *tagged* outputs:

- tagged outputs to the recipient's key sum to at least `refundAmount`;
- tagged outputs to the funder's key sum to at least the remainder,
  `voucher − refundAmount − maxFee` (no funder output is needed when that is 0);
- the voucher holds only ADA, and `refundAmount + maxFee` is at most the voucher's value.

Why the tags? An earlier version only checked that *some* output paid the recipient at least 2 ADA.
Anyone who saw a pending claim could resubmit the same redeemer, pay the recipient 2 ADA and keep
the other 8 ADA (less fees). One output could also count as the payment for two vouchers in one
transaction. Each tag is unique to one voucher, so no output can pay two vouchers, and the
remainder must go back to the funder.

Two things remain:

- **Fee slack.** Whoever submits the claim can keep `maxFee` minus the actual fee, so a funder
  should set `maxFee` close to the expected fee.
- **Composition.** The tag guarantee holds only between validators that enforce tags. Spending a
  voucher in the same transaction as a script that counts any paying output is unsafe.

A valid proof is not authorization. For the BBS voucher, the header binding and the tagged payout
checks above carry the authorization; the proof alone doesn't. The Groth16 gates have no such
checks, which is why they are replayable. See
[Application security](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/application-security/).

### Security considerations

- **Replay.** A BBS presentation stays valid forever. It's single-use only if the relying party
  chooses the challenge (off-chain) or derives it from the UTxO being spent (on-chain). The Groth16
  demo proofs carry no nonce and aren't bound to the UTxO they spend, so a copied proof opens any
  other UTxO at the same gate. Bind each proof to its session or to the spent output.
- **Unsalted Groth16 credentials.** The issuer signs
  `Poseidon(dobYear, country, roleId, salaryBracket, nameHash)` with no salt, and `nameHash` is
  `Poseidon(name, 0)`. Every field has a small or guessable domain, so anyone who sees the signed
  message or its signature, together with the issuer's public key, can recover the fields by trying
  them. Equal fields give an equal signature. Add a random salt to the signed message in a real
  deployment.
- **Revealed values can identify you.** A rare combination of disclosed attributes may be enough
  to re-identify someone. Reveal the minimum.
- **Credential theft and sharing.** Whoever holds the credential can present it. Neither demo
  binds the credential to a holder. The Groth16 credential names no holder key. A BBS
  presentation proves that the issuer signed these attributes, not that the presenter is their
  subject, so one KYC'd credential can satisfy many vouchers. Bind the credential to the holder's
  key when that matters. BBS per-verifier pseudonyms are out of scope for the demo.
- **Demo custody.** Both demo servers hold the issuer key and the holders' credentials and prove
  or present on their behalf; the reusable-KYC server also holds the funder's wallet. Their APIs
  are the operator's view. Privacy holds against chain and mempool observers, not against the demo
  servers. The voucher funder's wallet and the Groth16 demo's admin wallet come from Yaci DevKit's
  well-known test mnemonic, so anyone can sign as them on a devnet; a real deployment replaces
  them.
- **Issuer keys.** The Jubjub issuer key of the Groth16 demo is random and persisted in the demo's
  data directory. It used to be derived from a seed published in the source, so anyone could sign
  credentials the gates accepted; a credential signed with that old seed is now refused. For BBS,
  the default pure-Java provider isn't constant-time. Prefer the blst provider
  (`BbsService.withBlsProvider(...)`) for issuer keys. The Jubjub demo issuer
  (`signCompatibilityOffline`) is for offline, isolated use only.
- **Maturity.** BBS follows an IRTF draft, not yet an RFC. The Groth16 demos use a single-party
  development setup ([Trusted setup, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/trusted-setup/)).

### Try it

Both demos are in [zeroj-usecases](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases). With Yaci DevKit
running (see [Run the demos](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/overview/#run-the-demos)):

```bash
# Groth16 predicates from one signed credential
./demo.sh selective-disclosure --run

# BBS: reveal a subset of attributes, verified natively on-chain
./demo.sh reusable-kyc --run
```

- [`selective-disclosure`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/selective-disclosure):
  `--run` locks ADA at the "adult resident" and "senior doctor" gates, then has Bob prove each
  predicate and unlock both on-chain. In the UI, Alice passes only the adult gate and Charlie
  passes neither.
- [`reusable-kyc`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/reusable-kyc):
  `--run` issues a credential, gets a verifier challenge, presents only `country` and `kycLevel`,
  then claims a voucher on-chain. The ledger verifies the BBS proof. The UI lets you pick which
  attributes to reveal.

### Related

- [BBS credentials guide](https://zeroj.dev/guides/credentials/bbs/)
- [Groth16, PlonK & BBS](https://zeroj.dev/learn/proof-systems/): when to reach for which
- [Age & KYC eligibility](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/age-and-kyc/): a single predicate from a minimal credential

## Digital product passport

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/digital-product-passport/

> An auditor commits to each product measurement with a Pedersen commitment; the manufacturer proves carbon, recycled-content, origin and inspection claims against them, and one co-signed Cardano transaction mints a locked passport record.

The EU's Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR) introduces Digital Product Passports:
verifiable records of a regulated product's materials, carbon footprint, recycled content and
origin. Regulators, recyclers and consumers need to trust those claims. But the exact numbers
behind them are commercially sensitive. A precise carbon figure reveals manufacturing efficiency,
origin data reveals suppliers, and inspection records reveal defect rates. The tension is real:
*prove it, but don't publish it.*

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### The zero-knowledge idea

**The auditor seals each measurement in a Pedersen commitment. The manufacturer proves "the value
in this commitment is at most 50 kg CO₂e" (or "at least 30 % recycled", "an EU country", "three
approved inspections in order") without opening it.**

The flow, in plain terms:

- **The auditor commits.** It measures the product and, for each claim, computes a
  `pedersen-jubjub-vector-v1` commitment `C = (u, v)` with a fresh 252-bit random blinding `r`.
  It gives the opening `(m, r)` (value and blinding) to the manufacturer with its report.
- **The manufacturer proves.** For each claim, a Groth16 proof shows that the value inside `C`
  passes the rule. A claim that doesn't hold has no proof at all.
- **One transaction mints the passport.** The manufacturer builds it, the auditor co-signs it, and
  the `DppPassport` script mints a passport token into a locked output whose datum holds every
  commitment the auditor attests.
- **Anyone reads it.** Customs, a buyer or a regulator finds the passport on-chain and checks each
  claim's proof against the commitments there. The carbon proof was checked on-chain at mint; the
  manufacturer publishes the other proofs off-chain (in the demo, its server serves them). Only the
  auditor can revoke it.

If commitments are new to you, [Hide a number](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/hide-a-number/) explains them
with an interactive envelope.

### Why not just hash the measurement?

The first version of this demo published `auditorHash = Poseidon(auditorSecret, Poseidon(productId,
m))` in the passport datum, where `m` is the measurement. It leaked in two ways:

- **The key was not secret.** `auditorSecret` was an input to the manufacturer's proof, so every
  manufacturer had to hold it, and the demo hard-coded it (`777777`) in its source.
- **The value was easy to guess.** Carbon and recycled content are 16-bit numbers, and a country
  is one of about 250 codes. Anyone could hash all 65,536 candidates and read `m` off the chain.
  A hash of a small value with a known key hides nothing.

A Pedersen commitment fixes both. The blinding is fresh for each commitment and is never shared
between manufacturers, and for every possible value there is some blinding that gives the same
point, so the commitment says nothing about the value. Try the search yourself:

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

| Published in the datum | Can an observer recover the carbon value? |
|---|---|
| `auditorHash = Poseidon(auditorSecret, Poseidon(productId, carbon))`, with `auditorSecret = 777777` in the demo source | Yes: hash all 65,536 values and compare |
| `C = (u, v)`, a `pedersen-jubjub-vector-v1` commitment with a fresh 252-bit blinding | No: every value matches some blinding |

The old design had binding gaps too. The minting policy fixed neither the threshold nor
`auditorHash`, so a manufacturer could prove against a threshold, or a value, of its own choosing.
The token name was not tied to the product and could be minted again, and the demo's registry and
`/api/dpp/status` returned every measurement. The demo's `PassportBruteForceTest` runs the
65,536-value search: it recovers the carbon value from an old datum and nothing from a new
passport. The redesign is
[ADR-0009](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/blob/main/docs/adr/0009-privacy-and-binding-hardening-of-the-original-demos.md)
D1.

### What stays private, what's public

| Value | Visibility | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Measurements (`carbon_kg`, `recycled_pct`, `country`, inspector ids and times) | Secret | The competitive data; held by the auditor and the manufacturer |
| Blinding `r` (one per claim, 252 bits) | Secret | Fresh from `SecureRandom`; it's what makes the commitment hide the value |
| `productId` | Public | The token name and the first datum field; ties the passport to one product |
| `manufacturerPkh` | Public | In the datum, and fixed by the script |
| Each claim's `(claim, σ, u, v)` | Public | The commitment `(u, v)` and its schema digest `σ`, in the datum |
| Threshold (50 kg) and approved-set roots | Public | Fixed by the script (carbon) or by the reader (the other claims) |

`σ` is the digest of the claim's schema. A commitment point doesn't record what its values mean,
so every proof binds `σ` as a public input, and every verifier takes the expected `σ` from its own
copy of the schemas.

### The four claims

Each claim is one commitment under its own schema. The labels and bit widths are fixed by the
design:

| Claim (id) | Schema | Circuit | Public inputs, in order | Rule | Constraints |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Carbon (0) | `zeroj.demo.dpp.carbon` v1: `carbon_kg`/16 | `CarbonClaimProof` | `σ, u, v, threshold` | `carbon_kg ≤ threshold` | 2,192 |
| Recycled content (1) | `zeroj.demo.dpp.recycled` v1: `recycled_pct`/16 | `RecycledClaimProof` | `σ, u, v, threshold` | `recycled_pct ≥ threshold` | 2,192 |
| Origin (2) | `zeroj.demo.dpp.origin` v1: `country`/16 | `OriginClaimProof` | `σ, u, v, countryRoot` | `country` is a leaf of the approved-set tree (depth 5, the 27 EU states) | 3,344 |
| Inspections (3) | `zeroj.demo.dpp.inspections` v1: `inspector_0`/8, `time_0`/32, … `inspector_2`/8, `time_2`/32 | `InspectionClaimProof` | `σ, u, v, inspectorRoot` | each inspector is a leaf of the approved-inspector tree (depth 3), and `time_0 < time_1 < time_2` | 5,094 |

- **No shared secret, no `isCompliant`.** Every rule is an assertion, so a failing measurement
  simply can't be proved.
- **The auditor commits only passed inspections**, so there is no `passed` entry. An inspector may
  appear at more than one checkpoint.
- **Tree padding.** Unused leaves hold `2^k`, where `k` is the entry's width (`2^16` for countries,
  `2^8` for inspectors). A committed value is at most `k` bits, so it can never equal padding. The
  old trees padded with 0, which made 0 a member of every set.

### The circuit

The carbon claim, as in the demo's `CarbonClaimProof`. It binds the schema, opens the commitment
in-circuit (which also range-checks `carbon_kg` to 16 bits) and asserts the rule:

```java title="CarbonClaimProof.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.Prove;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.Public;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.Secret;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.UInt;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZKCircuit;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkContext;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkField;
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.ZkUInt;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.PedersenVectorSchema;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.PedersenVectorSchema.Entry;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPedersenVector;

import java.util.List;

@ZKCircuit(name = "dpp-carbon-claim", version = 1)
public class CarbonClaimProof {

    public static final PedersenVectorSchema SCHEMA = PedersenVectorSchema.of("zeroj.demo.dpp.carbon", 1,
            List.of(new Entry("carbon_kg", 16)));

    @Prove
    void prove(ZkContext zk,
               @Public ZkField schemaDigest,                     // σ
               @Public ZkField u,                                // the commitment C = (u, v)
               @Public ZkField v,
               @Public @UInt(bits = 16) ZkUInt threshold,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 16) ZkUInt carbonKg,          // never revealed
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt blinding) {       // the auditor's fresh blinding
        var binding = ZkPedersenVector.bindSchema(zk, SCHEMA, schemaDigest);
        ZkPedersenVector.commit(zk, binding, List.of(carbonKg), blinding).assertAffineEquals(zk, u, v);
        carbonKg.lte(threshold).assertTrue();
    }
}
```

The auditor's side, lightly simplified from the demo's `ClaimOpening`: one commitment per claim,
each with its own blinding.

```java title="Auditor: commit to a measurement"
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.JubjubPoint;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.PedersenCommitment;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.PedersenVectorCommitment;

BigInteger carbonKg = BigInteger.valueOf(7);
BigInteger r = PedersenCommitment.randomBlinding(new SecureRandom());   // fresh, 252 bits
JubjubPoint c = PedersenVectorCommitment.commit(CarbonClaimProof.SCHEMA, List.of(carbonKg), r).point();
// (c.affineU(), c.affineV()) goes into the passport datum; (carbonKg, r) goes to the manufacturer
```

The other three circuits follow the same pattern with `ZkMerkle` membership and ordering checks.
See [Commit to several values at once](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/pedersen/#5-commit-to-several-values-at-once)
for vector commitments in general.

### On Cardano

`DppPassport` is a JuLC multi-validator built on `Groth16BLS12381Lib.verify(...)`. Its hash is
both the passport **minting policy** and the passport **address**, so a passport is a public record
that stays where it was minted, not a tradeable token. Its parameters are `manufacturerPkh`,
`auditorPkh`, the gated claim (carbon) with its `σ` and threshold (50 kg), and the carbon circuit's
verification key.

It mints one token named `productId` into an output at its own address with the inline datum

```text
Passport(productId: B, manufacturerPkh: B28, claims: List<Claim(claim: I, σ: B32, u: I, v: I)>)
```

listing every claim the auditor attests (at most 4). The mint redeemer carries only the proof.

**Mint checks:**

- **(a)** the manufacturer and the auditor both sign;
- **(b)** the mint under this policy is exactly `{productId: 1}`, with a 1–32 byte `productId`;
- **(c)** exactly one output holds the token: at the passport address with no stake credential,
  no reference script, only ADA and the token, and an inline datum of exactly the shape above. The
  product id equals the token name, `manufacturerPkh` equals the parameter, every claim has
  canonical `u, v` and a 32-byte `σ`, claim ids are distinct, and the carbon claim is present with
  the parameter `σ`;
- **(d)** the Groth16 proof verifies against `[σ, u, v, threshold]`, with `u, v` from the carbon
  entry and `σ`, threshold from the parameters, never from the manufacturer.

**Revoke.** The only way to spend a passport: the auditor signs and the transaction burns exactly
that passport's token, `{productId: −1}`. A passport is never moved and its datum never changes, so
the datum a reader sees is the one the mint checked.

**The auditor's co-signature.** Before signing, the auditor's `CoSignGuard` checks the finished
transaction: the mint and the passport output are exactly as above, the datum is exactly the
auditor's own commitments for this product and manufacturer, the auditor's key authorises nothing
else (no input or collateral of its own, no withdrawal, certificate or vote), the transaction has a
TTL (the demo sets 180 slots), and the policy has never minted this product. It then reserves the
product for that transaction in one atomic step and only then signs, so concurrent or retried
requests get at most one signature. A reservation is released only after its TTL has passed, so a
failed or timed-out mint blocks a retry for that product for up to three minutes.

| Transaction | CPU steps | % CPU | Memory | % memory |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Issue (mint, Groth16 verification, 4 claims) | 2,789,042,135 | 27.9 % | 1,390,848 | 8.4 % |
| Revoke (spend and burn) | 151,057,197 | 1.5 % | 561,045 | 3.4 % |

Shares of the per-transaction limits, as printed by the demo's `DppPassportVmTest`.

#### Reading a passport

Only carbon is checked on-chain. Recycled content, origin and inspections are proved off-chain,
against the commitments in the passport datum. That datum is the authenticated record of who issued
the commitments: it exists only at the passport address, minted in a transaction the auditor
signed. A reader never accepts a commitment from the manufacturer's API. The demo's
`PassportReader`:

- looks for the passport token at the passport address, and nowhere else;
- reads the policy's whole mint history for the token and refuses a product with more than one
  passport ever minted, including a burn followed by a re-mint. If the history is unavailable, it
  refuses;
- takes each claim's expected `σ` from its own schema registry and never from the datum;
- verifies each off-chain claim's proof against `[σ, u, v, threshold or root]`. In the demo the
  reader endpoint takes those proofs from the manufacturer's records on the same server.

A valid proof is not authorization. The passport's trust comes from the script parameters and the
auditor's signature, not from the proof alone; see
[Application security](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/application-security/).

### Who is trusted for what

| Role | Does | Trusted for |
|---|---|---|
| **Auditor** | Measures, commits each claim with a fresh blinding, gives the openings to the manufacturer, co-signs the passport transaction after checking it against its report, can revoke | Measuring honestly, keeping measurements confidential, co-signing at most one passport per product |
| **Manufacturer** | Proves claims from the openings and builds the passport transaction | Nothing about its measurements |
| **Reader** (customs, buyer, regulator) | Reads the passport from the chain and verifies claim proofs against its commitments | — |

### Limitations

- **The auditor sees every measurement**, could collude with a manufacturer, and alone ensures one
  passport per product, by co-signing once. A second passport under the same policy would be
  publicly visible, and readers refuse that product.
- **The reader's duplicate check needs Yaci Store.** The mint history is read in Yaci Store's
  format, so the reader's check and the auditor's work on DevKit only. Against Blockfrost they
  refuse rather than guess.
- **A passport shows which product has which claims**, but not the values. A very small approved
  set (one country) would reveal the value.
- **Custodial demo.** The demo server holds the manufacturer's and the auditor's keys and the
  openings, and its API is the operator's view. Privacy holds against chain and mempool observers,
  not against this server. The API returns no measurements outside the panel labelled
  "manufacturer (private)".
- **Giving openings to a regulator** is not part of the demo yet; vector openings need their own
  reviewed design.
- **Development setup.** The circuit keys come from a single-party setup; production needs an MPC
  ceremony ([Trusted setup, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/trusted-setup/)).
- **Not externally reviewed.** Vector commitments are experimental in ZeroJ, and the demo hasn't
  been audited.

### Security considerations

- **Bind every claim to an attested value.** A proof that "some country is in the approved set"
  proves nothing about *this* product. Here each proof opens a commitment that sits in the
  product's own passport, which only the auditor could co-sign.
- **Thresholds and roots belong to the verifier.** The carbon threshold is a script parameter, so
  a proof for a looser threshold is refused. Off-chain readers use their own thresholds and roots.
- **Never reuse a blinding.** The same value with the same blinding gives the same point, which
  links products. The auditor draws a new one for every claim of every product.
- **Linkability of batches.** Per-batch passports reveal batch sizes and timing. Decide what you're
  willing to publish.

### Try it

The demo lives in
[`digital-product-passport`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/digital-product-passport).
With Yaci DevKit running (see [Run the demos](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/overview/#run-the-demos)):

```bash
./demo.sh dpp --run
```

`--run` has the auditor attest battery `BAT-SN001`, the manufacturer prove its claims, mints its
passport and prints the status. In the UI (port 8088):

- **`BAT-SN003`** (65 kg, 20 %) has no carbon proof, so no passport. "Skip off-chain check" builds
  the transaction with a proof for a threshold the manufacturer chose (65,535). The demo runs the
  script locally before the auditor co-signs; the script refuses it, and nothing is submitted.
- **Textile batch `TEX-B2024-003`** (made in China, 5 % recycled) gets a passport, because its
  carbon passes, but its recycled-content and origin claims can't be proved, and the reader shows
  no proof for them.
- **Revoke (auditor)** burns a passport. The demo's DevKit end-to-end test also shows that a
  transfer, or a revoke by the manufacturer, is refused.

The measurements appear only in the "manufacturer (private)" panel. Demo state from the old
version isn't read: start fresh with `./demo.sh dpp --clean-cache`.

Broader design notes, written before this redesign:
[Digital product passport — detailed design](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/usecases/digital-product-passport.md)
(multi-party supply chains, lifecycle state machine, comparison with the Cardano Foundation
blueprint).

### Related

- [Hide a number](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/hide-a-number/): Pedersen commitments, explained
- [Pedersen commitments guide](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/pedersen/): the API, including vector
  commitments
- [Private voting](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-voting/): the same "a hash of a small value hides nothing"
  lesson, fixed with encryption

  witnesses
