## Prove you own a Cardano account

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/account-recovery/

> Prove you know the wallet root key behind a Cardano address, without revealing the seed or signing anything, so a refund can reach the real owner.

Picture a wallet hack in which attackers obtain users' address-level signing keys and drain the
funds. An operator such as an exchange or wallet provider wants to refund the victims. Now it has a
hard problem. The attacker can show up and claim too, and a signature from the leaked keys proves
nothing. The genuine owner still has their 24-word recovery phrase, but handing that to anyone
would be a disaster. And a refund submitted on-chain can be copied from the mempool and redirected.

This page explains why zero knowledge is the tool that resolves this, and what ZeroJ's largest
circuit proves.

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### Why a signature isn't enough

Cardano wallets derive keys along the CIP-1852 path `m / 1852' / 1815' / account' / role / index`.
The first three steps are **hardened**, the last two are **soft**, and the two kinds behave very
differently:

- **Soft derivation can be run backwards.** A child private key is the parent key plus an offset
  anyone can compute from the parent's extended public key (xpub). One leaked address key plus the
  account xpub, which some wallets keep on their servers, gives up the **account** private key, and
  with it every address in the account.
- **So everything from the address up to the account is potentially compromised.** A signature
  under any of those keys can be produced by the attacker too.
- **Hardened derivation is a one-way wall.** It feeds the parent *private* key into the derivation,
  so the attack can't climb from the account to the **root key**. Only the real owner has that.

The one claim an attacker can't fake is therefore *"I know the root key this address descends
from"*. You can't reveal the root key. And a verifier can't check the root-to-address link from
public data, because the hardened steps need the private key. That combination is exactly what a
zero-knowledge proof handles.

### The zero-knowledge idea

**The owner proves "I know a wallet root key that derives, along the real CIP-1852 path, to this
address's payment key hash, and I authorise a payout to this recipient". Only the key hash and the
recipient are revealed.**

The circuit takes the root extended private key as a secret witness and replays the whole
derivation inside the proof. That means three hardened and two soft BIP32-Ed25519 steps (HMAC-SHA512
plus Ed25519 arithmetic emulated in the BLS12-381 field), the leaf public key and the Blake2b-224
key hash. It then checks that the result equals the public payment key hash.

### What stays private, what's public

| Input | Visibility | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `rootKL`, `rootKR`, `rootChainCode` | Secret | The root extended private key: the wallet's master secret |
| `account`, `role`, `index` | Secret | The derivation path is private from chain observers; `pkh` already pins the address |
| `recipientBytes` | Secret witness | Constrained to pack exactly to the public `recipient` |
| `pkh` | Public | The address's payment key hash, already public on-chain |
| `recipient` | Public | The payout's payment key hash, bound so a copied proof can't be redirected |

"Private" here means private from people watching the chain. Anyone who holds the account's xpub,
such as a wallet service or a watch-only wallet, can derive the account's addresses, find the one
whose key hash is `pkh`, and so learn its role and index.

The proof also publicly links the compromised address to the recipient. Use a **fresh recipient
address** that isn't tied to your other wallets.

### How it works

1. **Vouchers.** The operator locks a refund voucher UTxO for each affected account. Its datum
   holds `pkh`, `refundAmount`, the funder's key hash `funderPkh` and a fee allowance `maxFee`.
2. **Prove.** The owner runs the desktop app or CLI, enters the recovery phrase at a hidden prompt
   and chooses a recipient address. The seed is used in memory only. It's never written to disk or
   sent anywhere.
3. **Verify.** Anyone can check the proof off-chain in under a second. On-chain, a claim
   transaction spends the voucher.
4. **One claim.** A UTxO can only be spent once, so each voucher pays out once. Anyone, such as a
   fee sponsor, may submit the claim. The refund still goes to the bound recipient, and the rest of
   the voucher, less at most `maxFee`, goes back to the funder.

### The circuit

This is the demo's `OwnershipProof`, unchanged apart from imports and comments:

```java title="OwnershipProof.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.*;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkCip1852;

@ZKCircuit(name = "account-ownership-proof", version = 4)
public class OwnershipProof {

    @Prove
    void prove(ZkContext zk,
               @Secret @FixedSize(32) ZkBytes rootKL,
               @Secret @FixedSize(32) ZkBytes rootKR,
               @Secret @FixedSize(32) ZkBytes rootChainCode,
               @Secret @FixedSize(4) ZkBytes account,
               @Secret @FixedSize(4) ZkBytes role,
               @Secret @FixedSize(4) ZkBytes index,
               @Secret @FixedSize(28) ZkBytes recipientBytes,
               @Public ZkField pkh,
               @Public ZkField recipient) {
        // Root key + full CIP-1852 path -> 28-byte payment key hash, pinned to the public pkh
        ZkBytes derived = ZkCip1852.paymentKeyHash(zk, rootKL, rootKR, rootChainCode, account, role, index);
        pack(zk, derived).assertEqual(pkh);
        // Bind the payout: the proof commits to the recipient's packed key hash
        pack(zk, recipientBytes).assertEqual(recipient);
    }

    // Big-endian packing of a 28-byte hash into one field element (Horner's rule)
    private static ZkField pack(ZkContext zk, ZkBytes bytes) {
        ZkField acc = bytes.get(0).asField();
        for (int i = 1; i < bytes.size(); i++) {
            acc = acc.mul(zk.constant(256L)).add(bytes.get(i).asField());
        }
        return acc;
    }
}
```

The file is short, but the circuit behind it is large. `ZkCip1852.paymentKeyHash` composes ZeroJ's
in-circuit Blake2b, SHA-512, HMAC-SHA512, Ed25519 and BIP32 gadgets. The composed derivation is
validated byte-for-byte against Cardano Client Lib's HD-wallet derivation. Packing each 28-byte
hash into one field element keeps the proof at **two** public inputs, which is what makes the
on-chain check affordable.

#### Size and cost (documented measurements)

| Metric | Measured |
|---|---|
| Circuit size | About 19 million constraints (19,075,097 in the measured runs) |
| Local dev setup | About 6 min on a 12-core, 128 GB machine; about 9.6 GB key bundle on disk |
| Prove | About 1.5 min on that machine; about 2.6 min on an ordinary 16 GB machine |
| Verify off-chain | Under 1 s |
| Verify on-chain | About 2.3×10⁹ CPU steps, under the 10×10⁹ per-transaction limit |

These figures come from the demo's CLI documentation and ZeroJ's prover-memory work, and they depend
on hardware. Proving a circuit this size in commodity memory relies on the memory-mapped proving key
and the streaming setup; see [Performance](https://zeroj.dev/guides/proving/performance/).

### On Cardano

The demo's `OwnershipProofValidator` is a JuLC spending validator parameterized with the
verification key. On a claim it checks all of the following:

1. **The proof verifies** over `[pkh, recipient]`, where `pkh` comes from the voucher's datum.
2. **It's the right voucher.** The datum's `pkh` equals the proof's `pkh`.
3. **The voucher pays exactly what it owes.** Only outputs whose inline datum is exactly the spent
   voucher's `TxOutRef` count as its payments. Tagged outputs to `recipient` must sum to at least
   `refundAmount`, and tagged outputs to the funder to at least the remainder,
   `voucher − refundAmount − maxFee`. The voucher must hold only ADA.

Why the tags? An earlier version only checked that *some* output paid the recipient at least
`refundAmount`. The demo locks 10 ADA and refunds 2 ADA, so anyone who saw a pending claim could
resubmit its redeemer, pay the recipient 2 ADA and keep the rest (less fees). One output could also
satisfy two vouchers in one transaction. A tag is unique to one voucher, so neither works now.

Whoever submits the claim can still keep `maxFee` minus the actual fee (the demo uses a 2 ADA
`maxFee`), so a funder should set `maxFee` close to the expected fee. In the demo the funder
is the admin account whose mnemonic you give the CLI or app (`AOR_ADMIN_MNEMONIC` or a hidden
prompt): a low-value funding wallet, auto-funded on a devnet. The tag guarantee holds only
between validators that enforce tags, so don't spend a voucher in the same transaction as a script
that counts any paying output.

This is a good example of "a valid proof is not authorization". The pairing check alone would let
anyone with a copied proof spend the voucher to any address. The recipient and amount checks bind
the proof to the transaction. See [Application security](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/application-security/).

### Security considerations

- **The whole argument assumes the root seed didn't leak.** If the attacker has the recovery phrase,
  owner and attacker are cryptographically identical, and no scheme can tell them apart.
- **Trusted setup is critical here.** Whoever knows the setup randomness can forge ownership
  proofs. A locally generated key bundle is single-party and for testing only. A refund program
  needs a multi-party phase-2 ceremony (run externally with snarkjs and imported); see the
  [ceremony guide](https://zeroj.dev/guides/proving/trusted-setup-ceremony/).
- **Confirm the recipient.** A production refund program should also confirm the payout address
  through its own authenticated channel.
- **Use a fresh recipient.** The proof links the compromised address to the recipient on-chain.
- **The path is hidden only from observers.** An xpub holder for the account can find which role
  and index the proven address has.
- **Protect the seed on the proving machine.** The tools read it at a hidden prompt and keep it in
  memory only, but the machine itself must be trusted.
- **Review status.** The derivation gadgets are validated against an independent implementation
  but haven't been externally audited.

> **Danger: Experimental**
>
> This is research-grade software. Don't use it to move real value or to run a live refund program
> without an MPC ceremony and external review.

### Try it

The demo lives in
[`account-ownership`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/account-ownership). It
doesn't use `demo.sh`. Instead it ships a desktop app and a CLI (installers and a Java zip on the
repo's [releases page](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/releases)). From source:

```bash
cd account-ownership
./gradlew :ui:run
```

The CLI flow is `setup` (a local, development-only key bundle, which needs `--i-understand-insecure`),
then `prove --recipient <bech32-address>`, then `verify`, or `verify --onchain` against a local Yaci
DevKit. Allow about 10 GB of free disk and use a machine with at least 16 GB of RAM. Test with the
public BIP-39 test mnemonic or a throwaway wallet, never a real recovery phrase.

### Related

- [Performance](https://zeroj.dev/guides/proving/performance/): how multi-million-constraint circuits fit in commodity
  memory
- [Gadgets](https://zeroj.dev/guides/circuits/gadgets/): Blake2b, SHA-512, HMAC, Ed25519, BIP32 and CIP-1852
  in-circuit
- [Trusted setup ceremony](https://zeroj.dev/guides/proving/trusted-setup-ceremony/): producing production keys
- [ZK on Cardano](https://zeroj.dev/learn/zk-on-cardano/)

## Private token transfers

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-payments/

> A design walkthrough of a shielded pool on Cardano. Deposit, then withdraw to a fresh address that nobody can link to the deposit. Design only, no demo.

Every Cardano transaction shows who paid, who got paid, how much and when. That's fine for a lot of
things, but not for payroll, supplier payments, donations to sensitive causes or a treasury that
doesn't want to broadcast its strategy. Using fresh addresses doesn't help much, because change
outputs and timing let chain analysis stitch them back together. A **shielded pool** breaks the
link: many people deposit the same amount, and each later withdraws to a new address without
revealing which deposit was theirs.

> **Note: Design-level page: there is no runnable demo**
>
> Unlike the other use cases, private transfers aren't implemented in
> [zeroj-usecases](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases). This page describes a design built
> from ZeroJ's building blocks. The circuit below is a design sketch, not a tested application.
> Privacy pools also carry legal and compliance questions that are outside the scope of these docs.

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### The zero-knowledge idea

**The withdrawer proves "I know the secret behind *one of* the deposits in this pool, and this is
its one-time spend tag", without revealing which deposit.**

- **Deposit.** Pick two random values, `secret` and `nullifier`. Compute the note commitment
  `commitment = Poseidon(secret, nullifier)` and deposit a fixed amount (say 100 ADA) along with it.
  The commitment joins the pool's Merkle tree.
- **Withdraw.** Later, possibly from a brand-new address, prove the commitment is somewhere in the
  tree and reveal `nullifierHash = Poseidon(nullifier, 0)`. The pool records the hash so the same
  note can't be withdrawn twice.

Nobody learns which leaf was spent. Your anonymity set is every deposit of the same denomination.

### What stays private, what's public

| Input | Visibility | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `secret` | Secret | Proves you own the note; only the depositor (or whoever they share it with) knows it |
| `nullifier` | Secret | Only its hash is revealed, so the spend tag can't be matched to the deposit |
| Merkle path (`siblings`, `pathBits`) | Secret | The path would reveal which deposit is being spent |
| `merkleRoot` | Public | A recent root of the pool's commitment tree |
| `nullifierHash` | Public | Recorded on-chain to block a second withdrawal of the same note |
| `recipient` | Public | Where the funds go, bound into the proof so it can't be redirected |

The design notes also add a public `relayerFee`, bound the same way as `recipient`.

### How it works

1. **Deposit.** Alice sends 100 ADA and her commitment to the pool. Her address is visible, but her
   secret and nullifier stay with her.
2. **Grow the tree.** The pool absorbs deposits into its commitment tree. On Cardano a single shared
   root UTxO would serialize every deposit. The design notes therefore recommend collecting
   deposits as individual UTxOs and folding them into the tree in periodic batches.
3. **Wait.** Time and more deposits grow the anonymity set. Withdrawing right after depositing
   gives most of it away.
4. **Withdraw through a relayer.** A fresh address has no ADA to pay fees, so a relayer submits the
   transaction and takes a fee that the proof also binds.
5. **The pool validator** verifies the proof, checks the root is one it has published, checks that
   `nullifierHash` is new (for example in a sorted linked list, as in the
   [voting demo](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-voting/)), records it and pays the recipient.

```text
Alice ──100 ADA + commitment──▶ pool      (public: Alice → pool)
         ... other deposits, time passes ...
relayer ──proof + nullifierHash──▶ pool ──100 ADA──▶ fresh address   (public: pool → ???)
```

### The circuit

This is a design sketch in the annotation style, adapted from the withdrawal circuit in the design
notes with BLS12-381 Poseidon and an explicit recipient binding. It isn't taken from a runnable
demo.

```java title="PoolWithdrawal.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.*;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParams;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.poseidon.PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkMerkle;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPoseidon;

@ZKCircuit(name = "pool-withdrawal", nameTemplate = "pool-withdrawal-d{treeDepth}", version = 1)
public class PoolWithdrawal {
    private static final PoseidonParams POSEIDON = PoseidonParamsBLS12_381T3.INSTANCE;

    public PoolWithdrawal(@CircuitParam("treeDepth") int treeDepth) {}

    @Prove
    ZkBool prove(ZkContext zk,
                 @Public ZkField merkleRoot,
                 @Public ZkField nullifierHash,
                 @Public ZkField recipient,
                 @Secret ZkField secret,
                 @Secret ZkField nullifier,
                 @Secret @FixedSize(param = "treeDepth") ZkArray<ZkField> siblings,
                 @Secret @FixedSize(param = "treeDepth") ZkArray<ZkBool> pathBits) {

        // 1. My note is one of the pool's deposits
        var commitment = ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, POSEIDON, secret, nullifier);
        ZkMerkle.verifyProofPoseidon(zk, POSEIDON, commitment, merkleRoot, siblings, pathBits);

        // 2. Bind the recipient: a variable x variable product emits a real constraint row
        recipient.mul(nullifier);

        // 3. The public spend tag belongs to this note
        return ZkPoseidon.hash(zk, POSEIDON, nullifier, zk.constant(0)).isEqual(nullifierHash);
    }
}
```

Step 2 is the part people forget. A public input that appears in no constraint isn't committed to
by a Groth16 proof, so anyone could swap the recipient. Multiplying it by a secret variable creates
a real constraint. The [airdrop demo](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/sybil-resistant-airdrop/#the-circuit) uses the same
technique, and ZeroJ's native Groth16 setup refuses a relation that leaves a public input unbound.
Before building on a sketch like this, write invalid-witness tests: a note that isn't in the tree, a
wrong `nullifierHash`, and a proof checked against a changed recipient. All of them must fail. See
[Testing circuits](https://zeroj.dev/guides/circuits/testing-circuits/).

### On Cardano

Verification would use `Groth16BLS12381Lib` from `zeroj-onchain-julc` inside a custom pool
validator, as every demo on this site does. The proof is the easy part. The validator carries most
of the security:

- **Known roots only.** Accept `merkleRoot` only if it's the current root or a recent one the pool
  published. Otherwise a withdrawer can prove membership in a tree they made up.
- **Nullifier registry.** Store each `nullifierHash` so it can't be reused. A sorted linked list
  gives trustless, concurrent inserts.
- **Pay exactly as bound.** Require an output to `recipient` for the denomination minus
  `relayerFee`, and the fee to the relayer, and nothing else leaving the pool.
- **Value accounting.** The pool must never release more than it holds for a denomination.

A valid proof is not authorization. Every one of these checks lives in the validator, not the
circuit. See [Application security](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/application-security/).

### Security considerations

- **Anonymity set size.** With 5 deposits you're 1 in 5. Privacy grows only as the pool is used.
- **Timing and amount fingerprinting.** Withdrawing soon after depositing, or using unusual
  amounts, links you. Fixed denominations help; variable amounts need a more complex circuit.
- **Relayer trust.** A relayer can refuse to submit (censor) but can't redirect funds if the
  recipient and fee are bound. Use more than one.
- **Note secrets.** Whoever holds `secret` and `nullifier` can withdraw. Losing them loses the
  funds.
- **Compliance.** "Privacy pools" designs let users prove their deposit belongs to an approved
  association set. The design notes sketch this. Get legal advice before running anything like it.
- **Trusted setup and review.** A pool holding value would need a multi-party ceremony
  ([Trusted setup, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/trusted-setup/)) and an external audit, neither of which
  exists for this design.

### Try it

There's no demo to run. To experiment with the building blocks:

- Work through [Private allowlist with a Merkle tree](https://zeroj.dev/tutorials/private-allowlist/). It's the same
  membership-plus-nullifier core, and it's runnable.
- Run the [voting demo](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-voting/#try-it) to see a sorted-list nullifier registry
  on Yaci DevKit.
- Read the design notes:
  [Private token transfer — detailed design](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj/blob/main/docs/usecases/private-token-transfer.md)
  (UTxO patterns for commitments, batch deposits, relayers, multi-asset pools). Its code samples
  are older sketches. Prefer the BLS12-381 Poseidon parameters and explicit recipient binding shown
  above.

### Related

- [Private voting](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-voting/): nullifiers and a sorted-list registry, running
  end to end
- [Gadgets](https://zeroj.dev/guides/circuits/gadgets/): `ZkMerkle`, `ZkPoseidon`
- [On-chain verification](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/on-chain/)
- [ZK on Cardano](https://zeroj.dev/learn/zk-on-cardano/)

## Confidential payroll

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-payroll/

> Pay salaries on Cardano without publishing them, while the tax authority reads every salary from the chain and the employer can't under-report one.

Paying salaries on a public ledger is fast and cheap, but it publishes everyone's pay to everyone:
colleagues, competitors and anyone curious. Hiding the amounts fixes that, and creates a new
problem. The tax authority, and often an auditor or a regulator, must still see every salary, and
they shouldn't have to take the employer's word for it. An employer that reports a smaller number
than it paid shouldn't be able to.

This demo pays salaries as **confidential notes**: the chain stores the amount sealed, the employee
can open their own payslip, and the tax authority can read every salary. A zero-knowledge proof
makes the tax authority's copy match the real amount.

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### The zero-knowledge idea

**With each pay run the employer proves "every salary note I'm creating hides some amount, and the
copy of that amount encrypted to the tax authority's registered key is the same amount", without
revealing any salary.**

A salary note has three parts:

- **A commitment.** A Pedersen commitment is a single curve point that hides a number, like a sealed
  envelope. Everyone can see it, nobody can read it, and nobody can later claim it held a different
  number. See [Commitments & encryption](https://zeroj.dev/learn/commitments-and-encryption/).
- **The amount for the tax authority.** The amount is encrypted with exponential ElGamal to the tax
  authority's public key. Decrypting ElGamal ends in a search over small numbers, so the 64-bit
  amount is split into two 32-bit pieces, called **limbs**: `amount = limb0 + 2³²·limb1`. Each limb
  is encrypted separately.
- **Sealed openings.** The opening is the amount plus the random blinding that hides it. It is
  encrypted once for the employee and once for the tax authority. Each reader decrypts their copy
  with a **viewing key**, a key that only reads notes and can't spend them.

The proof ties the first two together. Without it, an employer could commit to 5,000 and encrypt
3,000 for the tax authority. With it, the ledger refuses to mint a salary note unless the limbs
recombine to the committed amount. The openings are a convenience for readers: anyone who opens one
checks it against the commitment, so a wrong opening is detected, not trusted.

### What stays private, what's public

| Value | Employer | Employee | Tax authority | Public |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Each salary amount | Knows it | Their own, from their payslip | Every one, from the limbs | Hidden, until it's cashed out (see below) |
| Blinding (the random part of the commitment) | Knows it | Their own, from their payslip | From its copy of the opening | Hidden |
| Employee's viewing key | No | Yes | No | No |
| Tax authority's secret key | No | No | Yes | No |
| Note owner (the employee's key hash) | Yes | Yes | Yes | **Public** |
| Commitment, limb ciphertexts, sealed openings | Yes | Yes | Yes | **Public**, but unreadable |
| Issuance proof | Yes | Yes | Yes | **Public** |
| Tax authority's public key | Yes | Yes | Yes | **Public**, in the registry |

Owners are public in this demo, so the transfer graph (who paid whom) is visible. The amounts are
not, with one exception: cashing out. A cash-out pays a public amount, so cashing out a whole
payslip publishes the salary it held. A partial cash-out shows that the note held at least the
amount cashed out. Transfers between notes reveal no amounts.

### How it works

1. **Register the tax key.** The tax authority publishes its keys in an on-chain registry, with
   zero-knowledge proofs that it holds the matching secret keys. The payroll ledger reads the key
   from the registry, so the employer can't substitute one it controls.
2. **Pay run.** The employer builds one note per salary, one or two salaries per transaction, and
   proves the limb relation for each. The ledger validator verifies the proof against the
   commitments and limbs in the new notes' datums and the key in the registry.
3. **Payslips.** Each employee scans the chain with their viewing key, opens their note and checks
   that the opening recomputes the commitment. A note that is theirs but won't open is reported, not
   ignored.
4. **Spend.** An employee can transfer part of a salary to a colleague, or cash out at the employer
   for a public amount. Both are proved: the amounts balance, and every new note's limbs are
   encrypted to the current tax key.
5. **Tax view.** The tax authority decrypts the limbs of every salary note: the notes minted by
   pay runs, found in the ledger's mint history, including ones already spent. It totals those
   per employee. It skips notes minted by a transfer or cash-out, whose transaction spent an
   existing note: those are the same salary moving, including change, and counting them would
   count a salary twice. It can still read their amounts. Each amount is **proof-enforced**.

### The circuit

This is the demo's `NoteIssueProof` simplified to a single salary. The demo version handles one or
two notes per pay run with `@CircuitParam` arrays, and keeps the limb relation in a shared
`AuditLimbs` helper.

```java title="SalaryNoteProof.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.*;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkElGamal;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkElGamalPublicKey;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPedersenCommitment;

import java.math.BigInteger;

@ZKCircuit(name = "salary-note", version = 1)
public class SalaryNoteProof {
    private static final BigInteger TWO_32 = BigInteger.ONE.shiftLeft(32);

    @Prove
    void prove(ZkContext zk,
               @Public ZkField noteU, @Public ZkField noteV,   // the note's commitment
               @Public ZkField pkU, @Public ZkField pkV,       // the tax key, from the registry
               @Public @FixedSize(8) ZkArray<ZkField> audit,  // limb 0 then limb 1: A.u, A.v, B.u, B.v
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 64) ZkUInt amount,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt blinding,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 32) ZkUInt limb0,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 32) ZkUInt limb1,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt k0,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt k1) {
        // The note's commitment opens to (amount, blinding)
        ZkPedersenCommitment.commit(zk, amount, blinding).assertAffineEquals(zk, noteU, noteV);

        // The two 32-bit limbs recombine to the same amount
        limb0.asField().add(limb1.asField().mul(zk.constant(TWO_32))).assertEqual(amount.asField());

        // Each limb is an ElGamal encryption to the tax key, matching the public ciphertexts
        var taxKey = ZkElGamalPublicKey.fromVerifierFixedPublic(zk, pkU, pkV);
        ZkElGamal.encrypt(zk, limb0, k0, taxKey)
                .assertAffineEquals(zk, audit.get(0), audit.get(1), audit.get(2), audit.get(3));
        ZkElGamal.encrypt(zk, limb1, k1, taxKey)
                .assertAffineEquals(zk, audit.get(4), audit.get(5), audit.get(6), audit.get(7));
    }
}
```

Every public input comes from data the validator can see: the commitment and the limbs from the new
note's datum, and the key from the registry entry. The blinding is a full 252-bit secret, and each
limb uses its own fresh 252-bit randomness, as the ElGamal profile requires.

The demo's transfer proof (`note-transfer`) adds the balance rule, input = output 1 + output 2, with
`ZkPedersen.assertBalanced`, and the same limb relation for both new notes.

### On Cardano

The demo deploys one `NoteLedger` multi-validator for payroll, with token `SAL` and proved issuance
switched on. In this mode the plain `Issue` redeemer is refused, so `SAL` can't be minted without
a proof. A `ProvedIssue` must:

- carry a `NoteIssueProof` that verifies over the new notes' commitments, the registry key and their
  limbs, taken from the transaction itself;
- use pairwise-distinct handles `A` across every limb ciphertext in the transaction, which catches
  exact reuse of encryption randomness within the transaction (reused randomness would reveal the
  difference between two limbs);
- place each note at the ledger's exact address, with the exact datum shape and exactly one token;
- be signed by the employer.

Transfers and cash-outs use the same ledger's `Transfer` and `Redeem` paths, also proved, and require
the note owner's signature.

| Transaction (demo) | Circuit size | Script budget (steps) | Fee |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pay run, one salary | 15,890 constraints | 50.5% (JuLC VM) | — |
| Pay run, two salaries | 31,773 constraints | 71.3% (Yaci DevKit) | 1.111 ADA |
| Transfer | 34,184 constraints | 75.8% (Yaci DevKit) | 1.163 ADA |
| Cash-out | 18,366 constraints | 57.8% (Yaci DevKit) | 0.984 ADA |

Budgets are shares of the per-transaction step limit, from zeroj-usecases ADR-0007 (r3). Fees were
measured on Yaci DevKit with mainnet protocol parameters after the demo's fee optimization (commit
`814b2f0`). They were measured before ZeroJ PRs #85 and #86 lowered the cost of the on-chain Groth16
verifier, so ZeroJ 0.1.0-pre13 and later should come in somewhat lower.

A valid proof is not authorization. The ledger also checks the employer's signature, the owner's
signature on spends, the registry reference input and the exact output shape. See
[Application security](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/application-security/).

### Security considerations

- **Supply is still trusted.** The proof stops the employer under-reporting what it pays. It doesn't
  stop the employer paying salaries that don't exist, or paying nobody. Payroll truth outside the
  chain is still the employer's.
- **Cashing out reveals amounts.** The cash-out amount is public. Cashing out a whole note
  publishes its amount, which for a fresh payslip is the salary. A partial cash-out bounds it from
  below.
- **Openings are only length-checked on-chain.** A validator can't decrypt a sealed opening, so a
  garbage payslip is accepted. The employee sees an unopenable note, and should treat that as
  evidence against the sender. The tax authority's amount comes from the proved limbs, so it is
  unaffected.
- **The tax key is trusted for confidentiality.** Whoever holds the tax authority's secret key reads
  every salary, past and future. Key rotation stops new notes using a retired key, but doesn't hide
  old ones.
- **Demo custody.** The demo server holds every wallet's spending and viewing keys and the tax
  authority's secrets, and scans the chain for everyone. Its API is the operator's view, so the
  privacy described here holds against chain and mempool observers, not against the demo server. A
  real deployment scans inside each user's own wallet and never ships viewing keys to a server.
- **Unreviewed assumptions.** The confidential-note profile's assumptions A1–A3 (ZeroJ ADR-0055)
  and the demo's protocol haven't had external review.
- **Trusted setup.** The demo uses a single-party development setup, so whoever ran it could forge
  proofs. Production keys need a multi-party ceremony
  ([Trusted setup, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/trusted-setup/)).
- **Not audited.** This is a blueprint of a protocol pattern, not a production payroll system.

### Try it

The demo is the **Confidential payroll** tab of the [`pedersen-commitments`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/pedersen-commitments) app in zeroj-usecases. With Yaci DevKit
running (see [Run the demos](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/overview/#run-the-demos)):

```bash
./demo.sh pedersen
# opens http://localhost:8093; choose "Confidential payroll"
```

To run it without Docker, use Java 25 and `./gradlew -p pedersen-commitments bootRun -PwithFrontend`
from the repository root.

The first start runs development setups for every circuit and takes several minutes; later starts
reuse the cached keys. In the payroll tab, pay a salary, open payslips, transfer and cash out, and
watch the tax authority's table fill in. Then try the cheats: under-report a salary (no proof
exists), send a garbage payslip (unopenable for the employee, still readable by the tax authority)
and use the tax authority's key after a rotation (refused).

- [Commitments & encryption, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/commitments-and-encryption/)
- [Choose how to disclose](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/): payroll is one point on the map
- [Share with chosen readers](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/share-with-chosen-readers/) and
  [Encrypt for an auditor](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/encrypt-for-an-auditor/)

  [ElGamal guide](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/elgamal/)

## Sealed-bid auction

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/sealed-bid-auction/

> Bids stay hidden from other bidders and the public, every bid is readable by the auctioneer from the moment it's placed, and a zero-knowledge proof makes the auctioneer pick the right winner.

In an open auction, every bid is visible, so late bidders can shade their bid against the others,
and on a public ledger the same thing happens automatically: anyone can read every bid in the
mempool and on-chain. A **sealed-bid** auction fixes that. Each bidder submits one hidden bid, and
the highest wins.

The usual way to seal a bid on a blockchain is **commit and reveal**: publish a hash of your bid,
then reveal the bid after the deadline. That has a weak spot. A bidder who sees they're losing, or
who wants to disrupt the auction, can simply **not reveal**. Forfeiting a deposit is the most you
can do about it, and the auction then ends with a wrong price.

This design closes that gap. Each bid is **encrypted so that only the auctioneer's key opens it**,
and a zero-knowledge proof shows the hidden bid is valid. The auctioneer can read every bid from the
moment it's placed, so there's nothing left to reveal and no way to back out. A second proof then
forces the auctioneer to settle honestly: it reads the bids but can't change who wins.

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### The zero-knowledge idea

**A bidder proves "this ciphertext, which only the auctioneer can decrypt, holds a bid between the
reserve and my deposit". The auctioneer later proves "decrypting every bid in the lot, the earliest
highest bid is bid number `w`, at price `p`".**

Two building blocks make this work:

- **ElGamal encryption on the Jubjub curve.** A bid `b` becomes a ciphertext `(A, B)` under the
  auctioneer's public key. Anyone can encrypt; only the auctioneer's secret key decrypts. ZeroJ's
  `ZkElGamal.encrypt` lets a circuit prove what a ciphertext contains without opening it. See
  [Commitments & encryption](https://zeroj.dev/learn/commitments-and-encryption/).
- **Groth16 proofs.** One per bid (`BidProof`), and one for settlement (`SettleProof`), each checked
  by the auction's validator on Cardano.

Bidders lock the **same deposit**, so the ADA moving on-chain doesn't leak the bid. The deposit is
also the upper limit: a bid can never exceed what the bidder has locked.

### What stays private, what's public

| Value | Bidder | Auctioneer | Seller | Public |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Its own bid | Knows it | Decrypts it | — | Hidden |
| Other bidders' bids | Hidden | Decrypts them | Hidden | Hidden |
| Auctioneer's secret key | — | Holds it | — | Hidden |
| Who bid, and how many bids | Public | Public | Public | Public |
| Deposit, reserve, deadlines, item | Public | Public | Public | Public |
| Bid ciphertexts and bid proofs | Public | Public | Public | Public |
| Winner and winning price | Public after settlement | Proves them | Public after settlement | Public after settlement |
| Losing bid amounts | Only its own | Decrypts them | Bounded, never published | Bounded, never published |

The winning price is public by design: the seller is paid in ADA, so the amount shows up in the
settlement transaction anyway.

Losing bids never appear on-chain in the clear, but they aren't fully hidden either. Every bid is
proved to lie between the reserve and the deposit, and settlement proves the winner is the earliest
highest bid. So once the price is public, everyone knows each losing bid lies in `[reserve, price]`,
and a losing bid placed before the winner's lies strictly below the price.

### How it works

1. **Register the auctioneer's key.** The auctioneer publishes its ElGamal public key in an on-chain
   key registry, with proofs that it knows the matching secret key.
2. **Open a lot.** The seller locks the item in a lot UTxO and sets the deposit, the reserve, the
   bidding deadline and the settlement deadline. The lot names the auctioneer's key from the
   registry.
3. **Bid.** Each bidder encrypts its bid to the lot's key, proves `reserve ≤ bid ≤ deposit` in
   zero knowledge, signs, and adds exactly the deposit to the lot. The validator appends the bid to
   the lot's datum. The proof is bound to the bidder's key hash, so a copied ciphertext and proof
   fail for anyone else.
4. **Close.** After the bidding deadline the validator accepts no more bids.
5. **Settle.** The auctioneer decrypts every bid privately, finds the earliest highest bid and
   proves it. The validator checks the proof against **every** bid in the datum, then checks the
   payouts: the seller gets the price, the winner gets the item plus the rest of its deposit, and
   every other bidder gets its deposit back.
6. **Refund.** If nobody settles before the settlement deadline, anyone can return every deposit
   and give the item back to the seller. A lot with no bids goes back to the seller.

### The circuit

Both circuits are from the demo's `auction/circuit` package. This is the bid proof, as in the demo
apart from the Javadoc:

```java title="BidProof.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.*;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkElGamal;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkElGamalPublicKey;

@ZKCircuit(name = "sealed-bid", version = 1)
public class BidProof {

    @Prove
    void prove(ZkContext zk,
               @Public ZkField bidderInt,                      // the bidder's key hash, as a number
               @Public @UInt(bits = 32) ZkUInt deposit,
               @Public @UInt(bits = 32) ZkUInt reserve,
               @Public ZkField pkU, @Public ZkField pkV,       // the auctioneer's public key
               @Public ZkField aU, @Public ZkField aV,         // the ciphertext (A, B)
               @Public ZkField bU, @Public ZkField bV,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 32) ZkUInt bid,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) ZkUInt k,             // encryption randomness
               @Secret ZkField bidderSquared) {
        // A public input that no constraint uses doesn't affect Groth16 verification, so the
        // bidder is bound with a trivial constraint. Without it, a proof could be copied.
        bidderInt.mul(bidderInt).assertEqual(bidderSquared);
        var key = ZkElGamalPublicKey.fromVerifierFixedPublic(zk, pkU, pkV);
        ZkElGamal.encrypt(zk, bid, k, key).assertAffineEquals(zk, aU, aV, bU, bV);
        bid.lte(deposit).assertTrue();
        bid.gte(reserve).assertTrue();
    }
}
```

The settlement proof is the interesting part. The auctioneer's secret key `sk` and the decrypted
bids `m_i` are private inputs. For each bid it reuses the encryption gadget **backwards**: encrypting
`m_i` with randomness `sk` under the "key" `A_i` must give `(PK, B_i)`. That says `[sk]·G = PK` and
`[m_i]·G + [sk]·A_i = B_i`, which is exactly "`m_i` is the decryption of bid `i`". Then it picks the
winner and checks the price. This is the core of the demo's `SettleProof`:

```java title="SettleProof.java (core)"
for (int i = 0; i < bids; i++) {
    // m_i is the decryption of bid i under the auctioneer's key
    var handle = ZkElGamalPublicKey.fromVerifierFixedPublic(zk, cts.get(4 * i), cts.get(4 * i + 1));
    ZkElGamal.encrypt(zk, m.get(i), sk, handle)
            .assertAffineEquals(zk, pkU, pkV, cts.get(4 * i + 2), cts.get(4 * i + 3));
    isWinner[i] = w.isEqual(zk.constant(i + 1));
    selected = selected.add(isWinner[i].asField());
    price = price.add(isWinner[i].asField().mul(m.get(i).asField()));
}
selected.assertEqual(one);                // exactly one winner
price.assertEqual(p.asField());           // the published price is the winner's bid
for (int i = 0; i < bids; i++) {
    m.get(i).lte(p).assertTrue();         // nobody bid more
    // a bid before the winner must be strictly lower, so the earliest highest bid wins ties
    ZkField beforeWinner = zero;
    for (int j = i + 1; j < bids; j++) beforeWinner = beforeWinner.add(isWinner[j].asField());
    beforeWinner.mul(one.sub(m.get(i).lt(p).asField())).assertEqual(zero);
}
```

| Circuit | Constraints | Public inputs |
|---|---|---|
| `sealed-bid` | 7,011 | 9 |
| `sealed-bid-settle`, 1 bid | 6,950 | 8 |
| `sealed-bid-settle`, 2 bids | 13,330 | 12 |
| `sealed-bid-settle`, 3 bids | 19,710 | 16 |

There's one settlement circuit per bid count, so the demo caps a lot at three bids.

### On Cardano

The demo's `SealedBidAuction` is one JuLC multi-validator: a minting policy for the one-shot lot
token and a spending validator for the lot. Its actions are:

| Action | What the validator checks |
|---|---|
| **Open** (mint) | The seller signs; exactly one lot with the item and no bids; the key matches the auctioneer's current registry entry |
| **Bid** (spend) | Before the bidding deadline; a new bidder signs; exactly the deposit is added; the datum is the old one plus exactly this bid; `BidProof` verifies |
| **Settle** (spend + burn) | Between the two deadlines; `SettleProof` verifies over every bid in the datum; the seller, the winner and every loser are paid |
| **NoBids** (spend + burn) | After bidding, with no bids, signed by the seller: the item goes back |
| **Refund** (spend + burn) | After the settlement deadline, submitted by anyone: every deposit and the item go back |

Every payout goes to the recipient's exact address and carries a datum naming the lot token, so one
output can't count as a payout for two lots at once.

Measured on Yaci DevKit with mainnet protocol parameters (ADR-0008 r4 in the demo repository, at
commit `814b2f0`):

| Transaction | CPU steps (share of the per-transaction limit) | Fee |
|---|---|---|
| Open | 3.3% | about 0.51 ADA |
| Bid | about 46% | about 0.90 ADA |
| Settle, 3 bids | 60.7% | about 1.03 ADA |
| Refund | 4.1% | about 0.53 ADA |

These were measured before ZeroJ PRs #85 and #86 cut the cost of the on-chain Groth16 verifier, so
bids and settlements cost less on ZeroJ 0.1.0-pre13 and later.

### Security considerations

- **The auctioneer sees every bid.** It's trusted for confidentiality, not for the outcome. It could
  leak bids to a favoured bidder while bidding is open, and nothing here prevents that. Removing
  that trust needs a different design, such as a key split among several trustees.
- **Demo custody.** The demo server holds the auctioneer's decryption key, and `GET /api/auction`
  returns the auctioneer's view (`auctioneerView`, every decrypted bid) to anyone who calls it.
  That is the demo operator's view. Privacy here holds against chain and mempool observers, not
  against the demo server.
- **No forward secrecy.** The ciphertexts stay on-chain. Whoever holds the auctioneer's secret key,
  now or in the future, can read every bid ever placed in its lots.
- **The auctioneer can refuse to settle.** Bidders then wait until the settlement deadline and
  refund. They lose time, not funds.
- **No Sybil protection.** The first three distinct keys fill a lot, so one party with three keys can
  shut others out. A real auction needs more bid slots or bidder admission.
- **The settlement argument needs review.** Reusing the encryption gadget as a decryption check is
  the demo's own argument. Its design reviewers checked it, but it hasn't been externally reviewed.
- **Development setup.** The demo's circuits use a single-party development setup, so whoever ran it
  could forge proofs. Real keys come from a multi-party ceremony
  ([Trusted setup, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/trusted-setup/)).
- **Not audited.** ZeroJ's ElGamal profile is experimental and not externally audited. Treat the demo
  as a blueprint, not a production auction.

### Try it

The demo is the **Sealed-bid auction** tab of the [`pedersen-commitments`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/pedersen-commitments) app in zeroj-usecases. With Yaci DevKit
running (see [Run the demos](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/overview/#run-the-demos)):

```bash
./demo.sh pedersen
# opens http://localhost:8093; pick the "Sealed-bid auction" tab
```

To run it without Docker, use Java 25 and `./gradlew -p pedersen-commitments bootRun -PwithFrontend`
from the repository root.

The first start runs development setups for every circuit, which takes several minutes; later
starts reuse the cached keys. In the tab you can open a lot (default: "Painting", 100 ADA deposit,
10 ADA reserve), place bids from Alice, Bob and Carol, watch the auctioneer's private panel, settle,
and try the cheats:

- a bid above the deposit or below the reserve: no bid proof exists, so the app refuses it;
- the auctioneer naming the wrong winner: no settlement proof exists;
- copying another bidder's ciphertext and proof: the validator rejects it, because the proof is bound
  to the original bidder.

The DevKit end-to-end test also submits a late bid, which the validator rejects.

### Related

- [Commitments & encryption](https://zeroj.dev/learn/commitments-and-encryption/): what ElGamal encryption is and why
  it adds up
- [Selective disclosure](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/): choosing between revealing, proving and encrypting
- [Encrypt for an auditor](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/encrypt-for-an-auditor/): the pattern behind sealed
  bids
- [ElGamal encryption guide](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/elgamal/)
- [Confidential payroll](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-payroll/): the same "readable by one authority"
  idea for salaries

## Confidential loyalty points

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-points/

> Customers hold and move loyalty points with hidden amounts on Cardano, wallets recover their balances from chain data, and an auditor can still read every amount.

Put a loyalty programme on a public chain and every customer's balance, every gift to a friend and
every purchase becomes public. Anyone can see that Alice holds 1,000 points, sent 700 to Bob and
that Bob spent 120 at the shop. Hiding the amounts fixes that, but it creates a new problem. The
retailer still has to account for the points it owes, and a regulator or auditor may need to see
every amount. Nobody should have to trust a database that the retailer runs.

This page follows a demo in which amounts are hidden from the public. Holders recover their own
balances from the chain, and a designated auditor reads every amount. For notes created by a
transfer or a redemption, a proof guarantees that what the auditor reads is the real amount.

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### The zero-knowledge idea

**Each holding is a _note_ on-chain: a sealed amount that the owner and the auditor can open, and
that a proof keeps honest when it moves.**

A note has three parts:

- **A Pedersen commitment** `C = v·G + r·H` to the amount `v` with a random blinding `r`. It hides
  the amount, and the owner can't later claim a different one. Commitments add up, so a proof can
  show that a spent note equals the notes it creates. See
  [Commitments & encryption](https://zeroj.dev/learn/commitments-and-encryption/).
- **Sealed openings.** The opening `(v, r)` is encrypted on-chain twice: once to the owner's
  viewing key and once to the auditor's. Each sealed copy is an 89-byte *delivery*. A reader accepts
  an opening only if it recomputes the commitment.
- **Audit limbs.** The amount is also split into two 32-bit halves, and each half is encrypted to the
  auditor's ElGamal key. The transfer proof shows that these limbs encrypt exactly the committed
  amount, so the auditor's view is enforced, not just delivered.

Moving points is a proof: "the note I spend holds exactly as much as the two notes I create, and
each new note's limbs encrypt its amount". The verifier sees only commitments and ciphertexts.

### What stays private, what's public

| Value | Who can see it | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Amount of each note | Owner and auditor | Hidden from the public by the commitment, until it's redeemed (see below) |
| Blinding `r` | Owner and auditor | Part of the opening; inside the deliveries |
| Viewing keys and spending keys | Their holder only | Open deliveries; sign spends |
| Auditor's ElGamal secret key | Auditor only | Decrypts the limbs |
| Commitment `(u, v)` | Public | Stored in the note datum |
| Owner (key hash) | Public | The ledger checks the owner's signature on a spend |
| Deliveries and audit limbs | Public, but unreadable without a key | Stored in the note datum |
| Redemption price | Public | The shop is paid a visible amount |
| Auditor's public keys and generation | Public | Published in the registry |

Amounts are hidden; the transfer graph is not. Anyone can see that Alice's note was spent in the
same transaction that created a note owned by Bob.

Redeeming tells observers something about the note it spends, because the price is public.
Redeeming a whole note (price equal to its amount, no change) publishes the note's amount. A partial
redemption shows that the note held at least the price.

### How it works

1. **Register the auditor.** The auditor publishes an ElGamal public key and a viewing key in a
   registry UTxO that holds a one-of-a-kind token. The registry validator verifies a proof that the
   auditor holds each secret key. Rotating the keys bumps a generation number.
2. **Issue.** The retailer creates a note for Alice: a commitment to 1,000, deliveries for Alice
   and the auditor, and the auditor limbs. For points, issuance is *trusted*: nothing proves that
   the limbs match the commitment.
3. **Transfer.** Alice sends Bob 700. Her wallet spends her note and creates a 700 note for Bob and
   a 300 note for herself, with a proof that `1,000 = 700 + 300` and that each new note's limbs
   encrypt its amount under the current auditor key.
4. **Redeem.** Bob spends 120 at the shop. The price is public; a proof shows his note covers it
   and returns 580 as a new hidden note.
5. **Recover.** Each wallet scans the ledger's UTxOs and opens the deliveries meant for it. No
   server keeps balances.
6. **Audit.** The auditor decrypts every note's limbs, cross-checks its own delivery, and labels
   each note *proof-enforced* (created by a transfer or redemption) or *issuer-claimed* (issued).

### The circuit

This is the core of the demo's `NoteTransferProof` (one note in, two out), with the audit-limb
helper inlined for the first output. Amounts are 64-bit, blindings and ElGamal randomness are
252-bit, and limbs are 32-bit.

```java title="NoteTransferProof.java (core)"
// Each note's opening must produce its public commitment (u, v).
var in   = ZkPedersenCommitment.commit(zk, inAmount, inBlinding);
var out1 = ZkPedersenCommitment.commit(zk, o1Amount, o1Blinding);
var out2 = ZkPedersenCommitment.commit(zk, o2Amount, o2Blinding);
in.assertAffineEquals(zk, inU, inV);
out1.assertAffineEquals(zk, o1U, o1V);
out2.assertAffineEquals(zk, o2U, o2V);

// in = out1 + out2 as whole numbers (the gadget refuses layouts that could wrap around).
ZkPedersen.assertBalanced(zk,
        List.of(ZkPedersen.Term.of(in)),
        List.of(ZkPedersen.Term.of(out1), ZkPedersen.Term.of(out2)));

// The auditor's key is a public input that the validator takes from the registry.
var key = ZkElGamalPublicKey.fromVerifierFixedPublic(zk, pkU, pkV);

// amount = L0 + 2^32·L1, and each limb is encrypted to the auditor's key (repeated for out2).
o1L0.asField().add(o1L1.asField().mul(zk.constant(TWO_32))).assertEqual(o1Amount.asField());
ZkElGamal.encrypt(zk, o1L0, o1K0, key).assertAffineEquals(zk, o1a0u, o1a0v, o1b0u, o1b0v);
ZkElGamal.encrypt(zk, o1L1, o1K1, key).assertAffineEquals(zk, o1a1u, o1a1v, o1b1u, o1b1v);
```

The full circuit has 24 public inputs: the three commitments, the auditor's key and the 16
coordinates of the four limb ciphertexts. It compiles to 34,184 constraints. The redeem circuit,
with a public price, has 18,366.

Why two 32-bit limbs instead of one 64-bit ciphertext? Decrypting exponential ElGamal ends in a
search for a small number. The auditor can search 2³² values quickly with a lookup table; 2⁶⁴ is out
of reach.

### Recovering notes from the chain

A wallet doesn't need a server to know its balance. It reads the note UTxOs at the ledger address
and hands the owner deliveries to ZeroJ's `NoteScanner` with its viewing key:

```java title="Wallet scan"
List<NoteScanner.Candidate> candidates = new ArrayList<>();
for (var note : ledgerNotes) {            // read from the chain: datum fields of each note UTxO
    boolean mine = Arrays.equals(note.owner(), myKeyHash);
    candidates.add(NoteScanner.Candidate.of(note.ownerDelivery(), note.u(), note.v(), mine));
}
NoteScanner.Scan scan = NoteScanner.of(myViewingKey).scan(candidates);

scan.opened();           // openings that recompute their commitment: spendable if the note names you
scan.unopenableOwned();  // notes that name you as owner but don't open: report these
```

A note counts as yours only if it names your key hash as owner **and** its delivery opens to its
commitment. A note you own but can't open is reported rather than skipped. On-chain the ledger can
only check a delivery's length, so a sender could put random bytes there; the unopenable note is
your evidence.

The auditor works from the same chain data. It decrypts the two limbs of each note with its
ElGamal key and opens its own delivery with its viewing key, then compares the two. For a
proof-enforced note the limbs are guaranteed. For an issued note they are only the issuer's claim,
and a disagreement with the delivery is flagged.

Scanning decrypts data that anyone can put on-chain. Run it in the user's own wallet process, not on
a shared server. The demo's server scans on its wallets' behalf for convenience.

### On Cardano

- **`NoteLedger`** is one JuLC multi-validator: it mints the note tokens (issue, split, receipt) and
  guards the note UTxOs (transfer, redeem). It verifies the Groth16 proofs and requires the owner's
  signature on a spend. It also reads the auditor key from exactly one registry reference input and
  rejects limbs encrypted to a retired key.
- **Exact-address policy.** Every output under the ledger's payment credential must sit at the
  ledger's exact enterprise address and hold only ADA and one note token. A note sent to a variant of
  the address with a stake credential is rejected.
- **`AuditorRegistry`** holds the auditor's keys under a one-shot token, so there is only ever one
  current entry. Registration and rotation verify two key-possession proofs on-chain.
- **Datum size.** A note's datum is about 0.6 KB (commitment, generation, eight limb coordinates and
  two 89-byte deliveries), so each note UTxO holds about 3.5 ADA.

Measured on Yaci DevKit for the complete transaction (zeroj-usecases ADR-0007 r3, fee figures with
mainnet protocol parameters after commit `814b2f0`):

| Transaction | CPU steps (of per-tx limit) | Memory | Fee |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transfer (one note in, two out) | 75.8% | 13.8% | about 1.16 ADA |
| Redeem | 57.8% | 11.5% | about 0.98 ADA |
| Trusted issue (one note) | 2.1% | 4.3% | about 0.47 ADA |
| Registry init / rotate | 76.8% / 77.2% | 6.2% / 6.9% | about 1.22 / 1.23 ADA |

These figures were measured before ZeroJ PRs #85 and #86 reduced the on-chain Groth16 verifier's
decompression cost, and haven't been re-measured since, so 0.1.0-pre13 and later should come in
somewhat lower.

### Security considerations

- **Points issuance is trusted.** The retailer chooses what to encrypt for the auditor when it
  issues, and the ledger can't check it. The auditor labels such notes *issuer-claimed*. The
  [confidential payroll](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/confidential-payroll/) demo uses proved issuance instead, so an
  employer can't under-report a salary.
- **Deliveries are only length-checked on-chain.** A sender can give the recipient a delivery that
  doesn't open. The recipient's wallet reports the note as unopenable, but the points are stuck.
  The auditor's limbs are the part a proof enforces.
- **Redemptions reveal amounts.** The price is public, so redeeming a whole note publishes its
  amount, and a partial redemption shows the note held at least the price.
- **The transfer graph is public.** Owners are key hashes in the datum, so who paid whom is visible
  even though the amounts aren't.
- **Key custody in the demo.** The demo server holds every wallet's keys and the auditor's keys,
  and scans on their behalf. Its API is the operator's view, so the privacy described here holds
  against chain and mempool observers, not against the demo server. A real deployment keeps viewing
  keys and scanning in each user's wallet, and the auditor's keys with the auditor.
- **Development trusted setup.** The demo's Groth16 keys come from a single-party setup. Whoever
  ran it could forge proofs. See [Trusted setup, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/trusted-setup/).
- **Unreviewed assumptions.** ZeroJ's confidential-note profile rests on assumptions (A1–A3 in
  ADR-0055) about delivering the same opening to several readers, which still await external
  review. Nothing here is audited.

### Try it

The demo is the **A. Confidential points** tab of the [`pedersen-commitments`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/pedersen-commitments) app in zeroj-usecases. With Yaci DevKit
running (see [Run the demos](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/overview/#run-the-demos)):

```bash
./demo.sh pedersen --run
# opens http://localhost:8093; --run plays a happy path in every tab, starting with points:
# 1,000 issued to Alice, 700 moved to Bob, and a redemption by Bob
```

To run it without Docker, use Java 25 and `./gradlew -p pedersen-commitments bootRun -PwithFrontend`
from the repository root.

The first start compiles the circuits and runs development setups, which takes a few minutes;
later starts reuse the cached keys. In the tab, issue points to Alice, transfer to Bob and redeem.
Then try the cheats: transfer more than a note holds (no proof exists), send a garbage delivery,
under-report an issuance, encrypt limbs to a retired auditor key, or send a note to a stake-variant
address. The ledger evaluates rejected transactions locally and doesn't submit them.

- [Choose how to disclose](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/)
- [Share with chosen readers](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/share-with-chosen-readers/) and
  [Hide a number](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/hide-a-number/)

## Proof of solvency with hidden balances

Source: https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/private-solvency/

> An exchange proves its locked reserves cover every customer balance while hiding each balance and even the total. Customers and an auditor check their part from on-chain data.

The [proof of reserves](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/proof-of-reserves/) page hides every customer balance but
publishes the total liabilities. Sometimes the total is sensitive too: it tells competitors how big
the exchange is and how fast it's growing. And a Merkle inclusion path shows a customer hashes of
their neighbours' leaves.

This variant hides the total as well. Each customer balance becomes a **Pedersen commitment**, a
sealed number that can still be added up. The exchange proves the hidden balances fit under a
reserve it locks on-chain. Each customer opens their own entry from the chain, and an auditor opens
only the total. It follows the Provisions approach (Dagher et al., CCS 2015).

_The web version of this page has an interactive illustration here._

### The zero-knowledge idea

**The exchange proves "these committed balances are each between 0 and 2⁶⁴, and together they add
up to at most the reserve locked in this vault", without revealing any balance or the total.**

Two properties of Pedersen commitments make this work. (See
[Commitments & encryption](https://zeroj.dev/learn/commitments-and-encryption/) for an interactive introduction.)

- **Hiding and binding.** A commitment `C = v·G + r·H` with a random 252-bit blinding `r` reveals
  nothing about the balance `v`, and the exchange can't later claim it holds a different number.
  The proof opens every commitment inside the circuit, so it sums exactly the published balances.
- **Adding up.** Commitments add: `C₁ + C₂ + C₃ + C₄` is the commitment to the total, with the sum
  of the blindings. Anyone can compute that point from the chain. Only someone given its opening
  can read the total, and the exchange gives that opening to one auditor.

Each customer gets their own opening the same way, as a small encrypted **delivery** next to their
entry in the datum. They read it with their viewing key, so what they check comes from the chain,
not from the exchange's say-so. See
[Share a value with chosen readers](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/share-with-chosen-readers/).

### What stays private, what's public

| Value | Exchange | Customer | Auditor | Public |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Each balance `v_i` | Knows | Only their own, from their delivery | No | No |
| Total liabilities `L` | Knows | No | Opens it from its delivery | No |
| Blindings `r_i` | Knows | Their own | Only the sum | No |
| Customer identity | Knows | Their own salted `idHash` | No | Only salted hashes |
| Commitments `C_i`, reserve `R`, customer count `N` | Public | Public | Public | Public |

### How it works

1. **The book.** At the start of a period the exchange has its customer balances. In the demo,
   Alice 500, Bob 1,200, Carol 300 and Dave 0 ADA. Each customer receives a fresh 32-byte salt for
   the period with their account statement.
2. **Commit and deliver.** For each customer the exchange builds an entry: a salted id hash
   `blake2b_256(I2OSP2(len(id)) ‖ id ‖ salt)` (the length as two big-endian bytes), the commitment `C_i` to the balance, and the opening
   `(v_i, r_i)` encrypted to the customer's viewing key (89 bytes). It also encrypts the opening of
   the sum, `(L, Σr_i mod l)`, to the auditor's registered viewing key. Every attestation draws a
   new salt and a new blinding for every customer and shuffles the entries into a fresh random
   order, which the proof and the deliveries follow too.
3. **Prove and lock.** The exchange proves `Σ v_i ≤ R` with Groth16. It then locks `R` lovelace in
   the period's vault with the entries as the inline datum, **before the period starts**. The vault
   verifies the proof against the datum's commitments and the locked amount.
4. **Customers check.** During the period, each customer derives the period's vault script
   themselves, reads every live attestation, and looks for their `idHash`. Then they open their
   delivery with their own key and compare the result with their statement.
5. **The auditor opens the total.** The auditor adds the on-chain commitments and opens the sum
   with its own delivery. It learns `L` and checks it against `R`, without learning any single
   balance.
6. **Release.** Once the period is over, the exchange spends the vault and burns the attestation
   token. Nothing can be added or released while the period runs, so every attestation in the
   period is locked at the same time and the same reserve can't back two of them in turn.

### The circuit

This is the demo's `HiddenLiabilitySolvencyProof`, with the constructor check trimmed. It opens
each commitment in the circuit and sums the hidden balances. The public inputs are
`[R, u₁…u_N, v₁…v_N]`: the reserve and the coordinates of each commitment, read from the datum.

```java title="HiddenLiabilitySolvencyProof.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.annotation.*;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.zk.ZkPedersenCommitment;

@ZKCircuit(name = "hidden-liability-solvency",
           nameTemplate = "hidden-liability-solvency-n{customers}", version = 1)
public class HiddenLiabilitySolvencyProof {
    private final int customers;

    public HiddenLiabilitySolvencyProof(@CircuitParam("customers") int customers) {
        this.customers = customers;   // the demo allows 1 to 16
    }

    @Prove
    void prove(ZkContext zk,
               @Public @UInt(bits = 64) ZkUInt reserves,
               @Public @FixedSize(param = "customers") ZkArray<ZkField> liabilityU,
               @Public @FixedSize(param = "customers") ZkArray<ZkField> liabilityV,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 64) @FixedSize(param = "customers") ZkArray<ZkUInt> balances,
               @Secret @UInt(bits = 252) @FixedSize(param = "customers") ZkArray<ZkUInt> blindings) {
        ZkUInt total = null;
        for (int i = 0; i < customers; i++) {
            // C_i opens to (balance_i, blinding_i)
            ZkPedersenCommitment.commit(zk, balances.get(i), blindings.get(i))
                    .assertAffineEquals(zk, liabilityU.get(i), liabilityV.get(i));
            total = total == null ? balances.get(i) : total.add(balances.get(i));
        }
        total.lte(reserves).assertTrue();   // Σ balances ≤ R
    }
}
```

- `@UInt(bits = 64)` on the balances rules out a negative "balance" that would quietly shrink the
  total. With at most 16 balances below 2⁶⁴, the sum can't wrap around the field.
- The blinding is a 252-bit secret, as ZeroJ requires for a hiding commitment. See the
  [Pedersen guide](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/pedersen/).
- With four customers the circuit has 10,042 constraints.

### Customers and the auditor check

Both checks use only chain data and the reader's own viewing key. They run with ZeroJ's
confidential-note API, `NoteScanner`. The result of a customer's check is one of five outcomes:

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `LISTED_ONCE_CORRECT` | Their `idHash` appears exactly once, and the delivery opens to their balance |
| `MISSING` | No entry with their `idHash`: they were left out |
| `LISTED_TWICE` | Their `idHash` appears more than once in the period |
| `UNOPENABLE` | The entry is there, but its delivery doesn't open with their key |
| `WRONG_BALANCE` | The delivery opens, but to a different balance |

Anything other than `LISTED_ONCE_CORRECT` is evidence against the exchange. In particular the vault
can only check that a delivery is 89 bytes long, not that it decrypts. An exchange can attest with a
garbage delivery, but the customer it targets finds out.

These snippets are simplified from the demo's `SolvencyAttestation`. The commitments and deliveries
come from the attestation datum.

```java title="SolvencyChecks.java"
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.JubjubPoint;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.NoteOpening;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.NoteScanner;
import org.zeroj.circuit.lib.jubjub.NoteViewingKey;

import java.math.BigInteger;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

public final class SolvencyChecks {

    // Customer: open my own entry's delivery against its commitment.
    static Optional<BigInteger> myBalance(JubjubPoint commitment, byte[] delivery, NoteViewingKey me) {
        JubjubPoint c = commitment.normalized();
        return NoteScanner.of(me).open(delivery, c.affineU(), c.affineV()).map(NoteOpening::value);
    }

    // Auditor: add up every commitment, then open the sum with the auditor's delivery.
    static Optional<BigInteger> totalLiabilities(List<JubjubPoint> commitments, byte[] auditorDelivery,
                                                 NoteViewingKey auditor) {
        JubjubPoint sum = JubjubPoint.IDENTITY;
        for (JubjubPoint c : commitments) sum = sum.add(c);
        JubjubPoint s = sum.normalized();
        return NoteScanner.of(auditor).open(auditorDelivery, s.affineU(), s.affineV()).map(NoteOpening::value);
    }
}
```

`open` returns empty when the delivery doesn't open, or when the decrypted opening doesn't
recompute the commitment. The exchange side builds each delivery with `ConfidentialNotes.seal`.
See the [confidential notes guide](https://zeroj.dev/guides/confidential/confidential-notes/).

### On Cardano

The demo's `SolvencyVault` is a JuLC multi-validator. One script is both the attestation minting
policy and the vault address. Its parameters fix the exchange's key hash, the number of entries,
the period `[periodStart, periodEnd]` and the verification key, so each period has its own vault
script.

- **Attest (mint).** The validity range must end at or before `periodStart`, and the exchange must
  sign. Exactly one attestation token goes to one output at the vault's exact address, holding
  only lovelace plus the token. The vault checks the datum
  `Attestation([Entry(idHash, u, v, delivery)] × N, auditorDelivery)`: 32-byte id hashes, canonical
  coordinates and 89-byte deliveries. It then builds the public inputs from the locked lovelace and
  the datum's coordinates and runs `Groth16BLS12381Lib.verify`.
- **Release (spend and burn).** The validity range must start at or after `periodEnd`, the exchange
  signs, and the attestation token is burned.

The demo measured the attest transaction with four customers at about 4.41 billion CPU steps and
1.25 million memory units in the JuLC VM. That was before two later cost reductions: the demo's
datum-access optimization (zeroj-usecases commit `814b2f0`) and ZeroJ's cheaper on-chain Groth16
verifier (ZeroJ PRs #85 and #86). Each extra customer adds two public inputs, and the demo's own
estimate puts the per-transaction limit at about 19 customers per attestation. A larger book needs
batching.

Like every validator, this one checks a proof against the data it can see. It doesn't know where
the reserves came from or that every customer was included. Those gaps are listed below. See
[Application security](https://zeroj.dev/guides/verifying/application-security/).

### Security considerations

- **Borrowed reserves.** The vault proves the funds are locked for the period, not that the
  exchange owns them. It could borrow them for exactly that window.
- **Who ran the setup matters.** If the exchange ran the Groth16 setup itself, it could forge a
  proof. The verification key must come from a ceremony the exchange can't subvert. The demo uses
  a single-party development setup ([Trusted setup, explained](https://zeroj.dev/learn/trusted-setup/)).
- **Omissions are caught only by customers who check.** Leaving someone out, or understating them,
  is detected only if that customer runs their check. Make the check easy and automatic in the
  wallet.
- **The customer count is public.** Pad with commitments to 0, which look like any other
  commitment, to hide the real `N`.
- **The auditor learns one subtotal per attestation.** If a period were split into several
  attestations, the auditor would learn each one's total, and an attestation holding one real
  customer plus zero-padding would reveal that customer's balance. The demo makes exactly one
  attestation per period.
- **Fresh per attestation.** Reusing a salt, a blinding or an entry's position would link a
  customer's entries across periods. An earlier version of the demo reused every salt and blinding
  when it re-attested, and kept entries in book order. Now each attestation draws fresh salts and
  blindings and shuffles the entries with `SecureRandom`, so two attestations of the same book
  share no id hash, no commitment and no position. A customer finds their entry by this period's
  salted id hash, never by position.
- **Outside the period the attestation proves nothing.** It covers `[periodStart, periodEnd]`
  only.
- **The exchange's key.** The exchange's signature makes an attestation the exchange's, so the
  demo generates its wallet key randomly and keeps it, owner-only, in the data directory next to its
  deployment state. If that state exists but the key is missing or doesn't match, the demo stops
  instead of creating a new key.
- **Demo custody and operator view.** The demo server holds every wallet's keys and scans the chain
  on everyone's behalf, and its API is unauthenticated. `GET /api/solvency` is the public view (the
  period, the vault and its on-chain entries, with no customer ids or balances). `GET
  /api/solvency/operator` is the exchange's private book, shown in the UI's "Private" panel. That
  is the demo operator's view: privacy here holds against chain and mempool observers, not against
  the demo server. Real customers scan in their own wallet. The off-circuit
  commitment and sealing code is for offline, isolated use; see the guides for the exact rules.
- **Maturity.** ZeroJ's Pedersen and confidential-note APIs are experimental and haven't been
  externally audited. Treat this as a blueprint, not a production system.

### Try it

The demo is tab "C. Hidden-liability solvency" in the [`pedersen-commitments`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/pedersen-commitments) app in zeroj-usecases. With Yaci
DevKit running (see [Run the demos](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/overview/#run-the-demos)):

```bash
./demo.sh pedersen
# opens http://localhost:8093; pick the solvency tab
```

To run it without Docker, use Java 25 and `./gradlew -p pedersen-commitments bootRun -PwithFrontend`
from the repository root.

The first start compiles the circuits and runs development setups, which takes a few minutes. In the
tab you can edit the book, attest with locked reserves for a period that starts about 45 seconds
later and lasts 180 seconds, run each customer's check, and let the auditor open the total. Try to
cheat: lock less than the book (no proof exists), give one customer a garbage delivery (their check
reports `UNOPENABLE`), or attest again or release inside the period (the vault rejects it).

Design notes: ADR-0006 (demo C) and ADR-0007 (on-chain deliveries) in the zeroj-usecases
[`docs/adr`](https://github.com/bloxbean/zeroj-usecases/tree/main/docs/adr) directory.

### Related

- [Proof of reserves](https://zeroj.dev/use-cases/proof-of-reserves/): the Merkle-tree version, with a public total
- [Commitments & encryption](https://zeroj.dev/learn/commitments-and-encryption/): Pedersen commitments, explained
- [Hide a number, prove facts about it](https://zeroj.dev/selective-disclosure/hide-a-number/)
